en: The Sūtra-based Exposition.
// Anuvyākhyāna //

I bow down to Nārāyaṇa, whose singular body consists of all perfect qualities, who is free from defects, who is the most supreme object to be attained by all through excellent words, who is worthy of worship in every respect because he is the source of this universe, and who is eternally my dearest beloved. (Manusmṛti 1.1)

Having bowed down with immediate ease to that very source of the treatise, the teacher of the teachers of the world, I myself shall now provide an explanation of my supreme knowledge, specifically for you. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.2)
Having appeared as Vyāsa Hari, requested by Viriñca, Bhava,
and others, he composed this unsurpassed treatise known as the Higher Knowledge (paravidyā).
Bādarāyaṇa is the teacher of teachers and the source of the scriptures;
for that which was uttered by him is authoritative, as it pertains to the meaning of the [Vedas] beginning with the Unborn (Aja).
When there is the attainment of harmony among the speaker, the listener,
and the subject matter, it is so by virtue of being the word of a trustworthy person (āptavākya) and likewise by virtue of being rooted in the Śruti.
And because it is rooted in reasoning, the great threefold authority of the Brahma-sūtras is seen everywhere in one way and not otherwise.
Therefore, nothing else is considered a more authoritative means of knowledge than this;
even though it has been composed by myself, its commentary is being provided for the sake of clarity. (Manu Smṛti 1.7)
In this regard, it is held that Tārā is the root of all weapons;
because she is present everywhere, she is separately honored by everyone.
For the syllable *oṃ* denotes that which is pervaded; it expresses the state of being pervaded by those [qualities].
That very thing is the meaning of the word *brahman*, as expressed by the term *nārāyaṇa*.

That very meaning of the word *bhargas* is also [the meaning] of the *vyāhṛtis* by virtue of their abundance (*bhūmatas*), and because of their manifestation (*bhāvanāt*) and their being well-born (*sutvāt*); thus he is also called "this Person" (*puruṣa*).
That very meaning of all the Vedas is here enjoined as the object of inquiry;
therefore, the man of knowledge is dearest to Me, and it is only the knower who becomes immortal.
For, by the force of such statements as "He whom [the Lord] chooses,
by him He is attainable," one is liberated through His grace alone from the knowledge born of the desire to know (jijñāsā).
Substance, action, time, inherent nature,
and the living soul exist through its favor and do not exist through its neglect.
"Nothing whatsoever is done without you," and so forth;
for otherwise, even by virtue of the nature of knowledge alone, liberation might occur for someone somewhere without Hari. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 1.1.14)
Viṣṇu is the giver of knowledge to the ignorant, and he is the giver of liberation to the wise;
Janārdana alone is the giver of bliss to those who are liberated.
From this statement, it follows that the falsity of bondage does not depend at all upon liberation;
nor indeed can the falsity of bondage be established, because it contradicts direct perception.
If falsity regarding suffering and so forth were established prior to those statements,
then the capacity of that which is false to prove [its object] would not be established for the opponent.
And that [duality] is established by you either through a false means of knowledge or through one that is real.
If it were established by a real one, then duality would be proven; yet a real means of proof for something else has not been established.
Therefore, by one who desires the establishment of an existent thing through that witness, the capacity to prove is indeed accepted;
yet, conversely, the incapacity to prove is established for that which lacks distinction.
And since that [validity] must be established by means of another cognition that is itself without distinction [from the first], there would be an infinite regress;
therefore, for those who do not accept the reality of the entire universe, that [status of being a speaker] cannot be maintained.
Therefore, all worldly transaction is established as being "true";
it is from this that the term "conventional truth" (vyāvahārika-satya) has come to be.

Furthermore, its status as a means of proof from the perspective of conventional reality is as previously stated. It is now asked: by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is this threefold nature of existence established? 1.22.
For that [non-existence] as well, there is no proof whatsoever in the manner already described;
by this, the distinction between existence and non-existence is also refuted.
Furthermore, for one who asserts that the existent is itself differentiated, how could there not be a differentiation of the non-existent universe by that same [existent]? (1.24)
If it is argued that "it arises from everything," then the established distinction of existing things would remain;
consequently, even Brahman’s nature as pure existence (sanmātratva) would not be possible.
Furthermore, even the fact that [the world] is sublated by knowledge is not established for the opponent;
for it is held that the correct cognition of something already cognized is precisely what constitutes its being otherwise.
In order to distinguish it from the non-existent, that which is to be known must indeed be understood as non-existent;
therefore, how can the cognition of the non-existent be prevented by that [definition]? 1.27.
Therefore, alteration is non-existent; it is perceived only in error.
Thus, the very perception of existence must be accepted as belonging to that which is non-existent.
If that [ignorance] were itself indeterminable, there would indeed be an infinite regress;
for how could anything be veiled by ignorance when the Self, devoid of distinctions, shines forth by its own nature?
Even the distinction of falsity depends precisely upon the establishment of ignorance;
and since ignorance is not a non-existent obscuration, it is not accepted as such by that [falsity].
Since an insentient object is by nature non-luminous, ignorance is not attributed to it;
and due to the absence of ignorance, the entire scripture would become useless.
And if one conceives that the falsity of ignorance [is known] through ignorance itself, there would either be an infinite regress or else a mutual dependence. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.32)

If it is argued that the doctrine of ignorance regarding intrinsic nature is faultless and therefore not [inherently] impossible, then the self (ātman) would likewise be such [an impossible entity]. // MAnu 1.1.33 //
Therefore, those who are virtuous should reject the doctrine of Māyā, which is devoid of [proper] qualification, subject matter, fruit, and connection, and is corrupted by endless defects.
Because it is true, and because it contradicts the direct perception of suffering and so forth,
the Veda cannot in any way declare that the individual soul possesses the nature of Brahman.
Just as the status of being the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) does not belong to the sacrificer according to the Vedic scripture,
so too the status of the Brahman-priest does not belong to the individual soul (jīva), since there is no distinction [between them] from the perspective of direct perception.

The Śruti proclaims that the Lord, who possesses qualities such as omniscience, is distinct from the individual soul; indeed, it is only by depending upon that very [distinction] that the scripture which teaches non-duality functions.
Due to its contradiction with that which is to be relied upon, this [Smṛti] cannot possess authority;
for even in the case of the status of being independent and distinguished, as well as the oneness of the self and the immortal, [it would be contradicted].

Since the statement of identity regarding similarity is rightly held to have scope as you desire, how can the scriptural mention of difference—which lacks such scope—not be very powerful? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.39)
Since ignorance itself is impossible, false duality is thereby refuted;
consequently, for one bound to reality, there can be no liberation without the grace of Viṣṇu.
For it is because [the truth] has not been ascertained that the desire to know it is enjoined here;
just as a king, being pleased by a true vision, releases one from bondage. (Manu 1.41)
Thus perceived, that Blessed One would effect the dissolution of bondage;
yet there would be no "task to be accomplished" (kāryatā) without [the cognition of] it being a means to achieve a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā).
For an effect is not pervaded by an action, since that which is prohibited is equal [to what is enjoined];
nor will the Lord create an effect that has not yet come into being through an action—so it is said.
An action must indeed be performed; it is not intended that an action which cannot be performed be considered a duty.
Likewise, that which is prohibited is accepted as a means [to the goal] precisely because of its similarity [to what is enjoined].
The Blessed One is the means for accomplishing what is desired; he is the chosen deity.
Or rather, according to the Vedic revelation, he is the most beloved object of the mind.
Since vital breath, intellect, mind, ether, self, body, offspring, wealth, and so forth,
became dear through contact with Him, what else indeed could be dearer than He?

"Since expectancy, proximity, and compatibility [are established] by such statements as these, it is intended that the linguistic competency (vyutpatti) regarding the entirety [of the Veda] be sought in this very [text]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.47)

"Your brother has *attyapūpān* (eaten cakes)," and so forth—due to insertion (*āvāpa*), as well as due to deletion (*udvāpa*), due to the state of being present, and also due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.48)
A child does not acquire proficiency from such sentences as "Bring the cow," since proficiency is possible through the very perception of the object being brought. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.49)
Why indeed would this person wait for something yet to come in order to bring it? However, when the word for action refers to the present tense, it will apply to the future as well.
Furthermore, through perception alone, one will subsequently acquire proficiency in hearing words,
in the sequence of the present, the past, and the future.

Since the derivation of an injunction is necessarily accompanied by expectancy and the like, how could there be expectancy for a word on the part of one who has already cognized the meaning of that word through perception? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.52)
Therefore, the first [cognition] is etymological derivation;
once that has passed into the present tense, everyone desires what is intended and does not depend upon actual activity.
Whether direct or indirect, knowledge is the means for attaining what is desired;
for desire may exist somewhere for that purpose, just as eating is for the sake of experiencing flavor.

While the mere knowledge of the meaning of a sentence might sometimes be desired, there can be no intentionality (tātparya) of the Veda regarding such things as the sacrificial ladle, the dipping-spoon, or the fire.
Whatever else one might perform would otherwise merely be a sacrifice;
therefore, for the sake of spiritual cultivation, one should possess an intent directed toward the true goal.
Thus, when the word "iti" is employed, the inference "in the fire" arises and memory is produced;
for there are indeed many utterances that exist entirely devoid of the word "iti. (Manu 1.57)
The passages beginning with "the self alone," etc., apply equally to Yoga and to the sacrificial fire;
for they constitute a single coherent statement throughout the entirety of the Veda.
"A split in the sentence would not be appropriate, and there should be a connection with the great fruit"—this is what one should say;
thus spoke the word that had gone into the fire standing nearby. *Manu Smṛti* 1.1.59.
If there were to be a complexity of conceptualization when a separate intended meaning is possible, then indeed,
due to that very complexity of conceptualization, the word-meanings would not exist at all.
If it is argued that the intention [of the Veda] consists in being understood through valid means of knowledge, then it is exactly so;
therefore, the intention applies both to the meaning of the individual words and to the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
And the status of being a distinct sentence arises from a distinct syntactical connection;
since these are intermediate sentences, a division of sentences is not a defect.
Furthermore, because they have accepted that each individual word-meaning is connected with the verb separately, there is the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). 1.1.63.
Therefore, since a figurative meaning is possible when there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge,
one should not assume that the primary sense of a word is not intended even when there is no such contradiction.
Therefore, actions have knowledge as their fruit; for knowledge alone is the primary bestower of grace from Viṣṇu, and that [knowledge] arises from the desire to know (jijñāsā).
Therefore, an inquiry [into dharma] must be undertaken on the basis of the authority of the Vedas;
for the authority of the scripture is indeed intrinsic, just like that of perception.
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress, and thus invalidity would arise from another source;
therefore, whatever contradicts the Veda results in false cognition, deception, and the like.
Indeed, even the eternity of the Vedas is not to be accepted;
for the establishment of dharma and other matters would never be possible without an eternal word.

Non-deceptiveness, the knowledge of that [truth], and its being produced by that [knowledge] must also be postulated; because of the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava), human speech is not a means of valid cognition.
When it is argued that "the Dharma is perceptible to someone because it is a real entity," the inference strikes back: "The Buddha could not be a seer of the Dharma because he is male."
For the speech of those who speak unrighteousness is indeed devoid of purpose;
therefore, even the absence of dharma would not be perceived by us through direct perception.
Therefore, when doubt has arisen, a sentence is a means of valid cognition just like perception;
and the capacity of words to denote their own meanings as connected [with others] is experienced.
Therefore, the theory that words denote meanings as already connected (anvitābhidhāna) is simpler; otherwise, there would be the assumption of a greater complexity.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the denotation of the impossible occurs, nor is activity possible in either of the other two ways.
All of this has been explained at length in the treatises on logic and indeed in the Brahmatarka; however, because each science is distinct, it is indicated here only in brief.
The proper study of the means of valid cognition and logic is carried out through the science of reasoning (tarka-śāstra);
however, the purification of the objects of knowledge is achieved through Mīmāṃsā by means of those established proofs and principles.
And that same Lord, the Sovereign, composed the Brahmatarka,
extracted from the Nārāyaṇa-tantra which extends to fifty crores [of verses].
Having extracted five thousand [verses], Bādarāyaṇa composed this work;
therefore, he indicated its purpose by saying "ataḥ" (hence) as a summary.
Since all this is established through direct experience, and for this reason as well,
it has not been made overly extensive, even though it is occupied with matters difficult for the gods to comprehend.
For these arguments directed against [the doctrine] are indeed contemptible;
for one who is capable of perceiving through direct perception, what position could he possibly regard here?
Therefore, because he is not on our side, Viṣṇu has been disregarded in this treatise on liberation by the Blessed One himself; it was stated previously that [he is] Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said: "For by him the divine scripture has been eclipsed;
the beginning and the end of the divine scripture were indeed composed by the Blessed One himself."
By his command, Paila and Śeṣa quickly composed the middle [portion].
Therefore, because the state of being Viṣṇu is established therein, he indicated it as "Brahman. (Manu 1.82)
Since the words *doṣa*, *ara*, and *chidra* are synonyms, it should be understood that the *guṇas* are called *nārās*; he who possesses them is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
For this word "Brahman" also denotes the fullness of qualities;
therefore, it is the inquiry into Nārāyaṇa alone that is enjoined here.
Since the word "Brahman" is established as referring clearly to Viṣṇu in the Śruti,
he who was spoken of in the verse "In the boundless waters" is designated by the term Nārāyaṇa.
For he himself is proclaimed as being within the waters;
he who, by his own will, bestows the status of Brahmā, Rudra, and the other gods, accompanied by Śrī herself.
And [he spoke] of Viṣṇu as the source from whom they stand,
and of that which was declared as "in whom the gods abide," and of the ocean as the very place of origin.
That which is called "name" is indeed the syllable *oṃ*, which is declared to be the *ṛc*;
and that from which [all things] were produced, he called that very thing Brahman.

That which resides within the ocean and is the cause of the production of the universe is characterized by the definition "from whom the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]," as stated in the well-spoken Upaniṣads and other texts.

For in these sacred scriptures, the creation, maintenance, and destruction [of the world], as well as destiny, knowledge, concealment, and even bondage and liberation, are always said to belong to Hari.
Since all names truly enter into Him— according to the Vedic revelation that "He who [is the goal] of the gods"—
therefore all names belong to Viṣṇu alone.
Therefore, the name does not primarily belong to anyone else;
for since the qualities have been heard [in this way], there would be no fault regarding the meaning of the Veda.
Because of their delight and because they are intent upon liberation, there is no intention whatsoever in them toward finding fault;
for indeed, the great purport of all these statements lies herein.
In case of conflict with that [Veda], there is no authority; for liberation is the fruit [indicated] by the Vedic statement.
There can be no authority for the Purāṇas and so forth regarding a matter contradicted by the Śruti.

Because they are rooted in other philosophical systems and for the purpose of deluding [the ignorant], these others do not possess the status of "all" (sarva) according to Hari’s command; indeed, it is nowhere stated in the Śruti that they do so.
Furthermore, because there is no statement of fault regarding Hari in the Veda,
ignorance, dependence, and even non-existence at the time of dissolution are necessarily [denied] of Him.
And the incapacity of all others has been declared in the Śruti;
therefore, by the words "from whom the birth, etc., of this [world arise]," this is the specific defining characteristic of Viṣṇu alone.

In the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, he himself declared that his own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the state of being the cause of the origin and so forth of this [universe], under the guise of the chariot drawn by black horses.
Therefore, that Teacher of the World also rejected the identity of the individual soul [with Brahman];
for the individual soul could not be the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.99)
Furthermore, the Lord himself will indeed speak of the fault of performing what is harmful and so forth;
and by that very Lord himself, the charge of being devoid of qualities has been refuted.
But when the primary meaning is possible through differentiation alone, why resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)?
How could there be oneness for this eternally distinct quality by means of abandoning its qualities?
If this [world] were always possessed of qualities, then that which is devoid of qualities would always be distinct from it;
nor could there be the state of having false qualities, because that which is inexpressible (anirvācya) has been refuted.
In that case, there would be a state devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), and otherwise, there would be a demonic state;
whether there is a distinction between the characterized and the characteristic, or non-distinction, or both.
When this is asked, there is no way at all to establish their identity;
for since identity is non-difference, that [reality] cannot be known through scripture, but is known through its own self-luminosity.
If difference were false, then the reality of difference would necessarily follow by force;
and if both difference and non-difference were to exist, there would indeed be an infinite regress.
If it were self-sustaining, then even the external [object] would be its sustainer;
there would either be a distinction between synonyms or an infinite regress in both cases.
Even in the case of [the Brahman defined as] "truth, knowledge," and so forth, there is no purpose served by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
If that which is excluded were indistinguishable [from what remains], then that [Brahman] would be partless, and thus [the claim of its being] "partless" would be refuted.
By this, [the doctrine of] featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) would become like saying, "I am mute. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.107)
For this distinction necessarily follows even when there is no difference;
thus, the possessor of the distinction and the distinction itself must be self-establishing.
But in that which is devoid of difference, there exists that which is called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), which is the regulator of other synonymous terms; it exists in all things whatsoever.
These particulars are also infinite and mutually distinctive;
they exist in all things without exception, being capable of establishing themselves by their own nature.
Therefore, Brahman is said to possess infinite qualities even though it is without differentiation;
likewise, the Śruti declares its non-difference from all phenomena by saying, "Thus [are] the dharmas."
But by means of the visible fruit obtained from the Śaiva and other Āgamas,
and by analogy with their words, other [scriptures] are inferred to possess the status of valid authority.

If it is argued that [the Veda] is authoritative because it is the word of Īśvara, then there would be an inference of its lack of authority based on the fact that he is fallible; furthermore, Īśvara himself would not be something to be inferred separately.
By the very power of the cause that constitutes its masculinity, and by the path already described,
the status of the scripture as the source [of Dharma] arises through the force of this cause.
From such statements as "The truth is not reached by one who lacks the Veda, nor by mere reasoning," it follows that reasoning can in no way lead to the knowledge of the Lord.

For it is indeed easy to establish that the Lord, who is the subject under discussion by virtue of His being the creator of the forest and so forth, possesses some degree of knowledge simply by His being a person. (Manu 1.116)
"Because of his masculinity, he knows every tree, just like Caitra"—
an inference such as this, which vies with [the authority of] the Supreme Lord,
is not capable of making Him known; moreover, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if one were to infer in such a manner.
Because it is a real entity, a horse has horns; the sky is like a flower; and [the earth] is joined with sons.
Citriṇī is the sixth taste because it is a taste; therefore, it would be superior.
From the signs such as the commencement [of the treatise], there is no other inference than this.
When these [meanings] are correctly investigated by those who follow the lineage of tradition,
the primary meaning of all scripture is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, and none other.
Because He is that which is to be beheld, Viṣṇu can only be denoted [by words] and not otherwise;
for if He were ever seen as something to be indicated (lakṣya), the question "What is that? would lead to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, specific qualities such as sweetness and so forth are always expressed by their respective words;
for even the meaning of a sentence must be expressed by the very word "meaning of a sentence."

How could a wise man, by saying "there is nothing that cannot be said because of such [reasons]," assert that something is inexpressible? It would be like a mute person saying, "I am mute. (Manu Smṛti 1.1.122)
He replied with the word "lakṣya" (the object to be defined) regarding that which was called "lakṣya":
"For when even a single word is accepted in its secondary sense by the wise," (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.123).

Great shame arises wherever all sounds are said to have non-primary meanings; how then can shame not arise for one who follows that path to claim for himself the status of being a true scholar of the scriptures? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.124)

When words such as "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman" directly denote the Full [Reality], and Brahman is defined as the cause of birth and so forth, then [the identity of the two is established]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.125)

Having conceptualized the object of reference as being like the son of a barren woman, variegated by illusion, and even as something expressible, one speaks of the pure reality through words without any means of valid cognition.
Knowledge of that very thing denoted by the word "Self" is not a means to liberation;
for this would involve the abandonment of what is heard in scripture and the fabrication of what is not heard.

And it may be that in every case where even one person in the world feels disgust, both [the act and its result] will certainly belong to him who holds both views—his own and that of others. (Manu Smṛti 1.128)
This man is always adorned with ornaments that are truly difficult to acquire;
his two garments shall be perpetual darkness and constant suffering.
"Blissless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those who lack knowledge, not the wise. (Manu Smṛti 1.130)
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of their own selves."

Scriptural passages such as these are the authority here by the hundreds on all sides; and because there is no statement of its being something to be discarded, the Self heard in the Śruti is not secondary. 1.1.132.

"Know that alone as one; abandon all other speech"—thus has the Self been described. How could it be secondary (gauṇa), for it is heard in scripture as belonging to the category of what is to be abandoned?
Even those things which are to be accepted as attendants must be abandoned from the perspective of the primary essence;
having taken the fullness of the Full, only the Full remains.
Thus, the dissolution of the full [Self] into the Full has been illustrated;
how could that which is delimited by *māyā* be the primary Full? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.135)

And how could he say that the "state" (pada) is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) in a figurative sense? If that state is characterized by the absence of qualities, even then it is denotative [of its own nature].
Therefore, how could this doctrine— which is the great abode of all faults through its door of infinite regress—
be respected by wise and discerning people?
Nor did the Blessed One compose these sūtras for the purpose of refuting the Sāṅkhya;
for he does not accept that the Pradhāna is "not based on scripture" (aśabda).
When concomitance (anvaya) is asserted, the very fact that it is within the scope of verbal expression must first be established; for in the absence of that, how could there be concomitance?
And how could one who maintains the theory of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) speak of the concordance with Brahman?
That concordance would apply only to that which is the primary meaning of the word. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.140)
The Lord has directly declared that the cause of birth and so forth is the one with whom [the scriptures] are in harmony;
that alone is what must be investigated. What room is there here for anything devoid of qualities?
And how can there be the impossibility of that primary meaning being set aside?
By what means of knowledge (pramāṇa) could that which is inexpressible, unknowable, and devoid of qualities be known?
If it were immeasurable, the scripture could not in any way function with respect to it;
therefore, that ocean of virtues belonging to us is what is to be investigated by means of the scripture.

The supreme Brahman, known as Vāsudeva, who is without a second and is the highest of all, is to be understood as being free from all distinctions such as being that which is to be known, that which is denoted by words, or that which is indicated by them.
If that [Brahman] were something outside the range of mind and speech, let it be so;
let the disputant not speak of it, for it is certainly not contained within our scriptures.
Having stated that the unspeakable is speakable, why does he, like a madman, falsely strive to plunder our scripture while simultaneously subverting his own words? (Manu 1.146)
That which is the cause of birth and so forth, which is directly named Nārāyaṇa—that is Brahman; let the Vedas declare it, and this scripture [the Mahābhārata] does so for that same purpose.
Furthermore, for those who deny that cognition is self-luminous,
how can there be omniscience without the apprehension of one's own cognition?
Let it be that what has proceeded is inexpressible by you; do not speak of it in any way whatsoever.
For that which is inexpressible by all words, once spoken, again becomes the object of those very words.
Having bound you with scripture and reasoning, we shall properly investigate our own treatise with respect, by means of both scriptures and reasonings.

"Because it is marvelous, it is inexpressible; and because it is inconceivable and unknowable, and because it is filled with infinite qualities—thus says the Śruti of the Paiṅgins. Even in the world, that which is most wonderful on earth is called 'inexpressible'. (Manu Smṛti 1.1.151)
Thus, the Unborn One declares, in the chapter beginning with "consisting of bliss," the systematic unity [of the Vedas] through their distinct divisions as understood from the scriptures.

In the first quarter [of this chapter], there is the reconciliation in Viṣṇu alone of those words well-known elsewhere that denote the general category of the possessor of qualities (guṇin). *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā*, 1.1.153.
And first, the Lord declared the concordance of those words expressing qualities;
the Śruti [describes Him] as reclining upon the ocean and as the source of all sources.
"That alone is the supreme Brahman"—thus he declared with certainty;
therefore, because the word "Brahman" is restricted to that very thing, [it refers to that]. (Manu 1.155)
This [meditation] occurs through the practice of such forms as "Food is Brahman" in the Taittirīyaka,
and likewise in thousands of other instances across various Vedic branches (śākhās) that possess this same form.
Hari himself is denoted by such words as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and others;
words beginning with "consisting of bliss" serve merely as indicators.
Because this Sūtra consists of few syllables, it serves to determine the meaning of all branches [of the Veda];
furthermore, because it provides the means of attainment, there is another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning it.
For the Śruti declares: "All the Vedas proclaim that state";
yet, because of the statement regarding the "tail" of Brahman, it refers to Brahman in its form as consisting of bliss.
For the name "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is indeed due to the attainment of the state of Brahman in its entirety;

knowledge has been declared by means of the mind and is also expressed through higher realization (*vijñāna*). (Manu 1.188)

the root "man" is proclaimed to have the meaning of "breathing" and "understanding."
By the very statement that "there is no happiness in the small," its nature as consisting of bliss is declared;
thus its infinity is well-established, for perfect bliss does not reside in what is limited.
For this reason, the expansion mentioned in the words of the Mantras is performed here in its entirety by means of the supreme [Veda], since no other [source] is mentioned in this context.
"He who knows the Puruṣa shall be liberated; indeed, no other path exists"—according to this Vedic revelation, how can one who knows anything else attain liberation?
The Supreme Person, the Self-born, Brahman, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great Bliss, Viṣṇu, Bharga—He is proclaimed as "Om. (Manu Smṛti 1.197)

thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti, for by no other knowledge is one liberated.

and Hari, who is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa), is primarily Hari himself.
That which shines everywhere as space is primarily Hari;
because his nature consists of strength and knowledge, he is Vāyu, Agni, and the one who leads the immobile.
He is called *āpaḥ* (water) because he protects (*ā-pālanāt*), and he is known as *pṛthivī* (earth) because he extends (*prathitaḥ*).
Since he serves as the refuge for plants (*uṣadhīnām*), he is likewise named *oṣadhi*.
Viṣṇu resides within herbs; he may be resorted to by those who are hungry.
Because he lies within the city (puri), he is therefore celebrated as Puruṣa.
The manifestation of Hari as the initiator of activity is his birth;
for there is no other [birth] in the elements such as space, since the presiding deities possess self-conceit (abhimāna).
The manifestation of the body of the conceited one occurs directly from the primary elements;
thus, everything down to the body and so forth is indeed Hari himself.
He reflects upon that very [Self] in order to know its fivefold nature;
having abandoned everything beginning with the elements, the Śruti says, "That indeed is this. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.207)
He who is designated by the word "self" (ātman) and resides within the body of the living being—
this Lord consists of the essence of food alone, not of the food of the world.
Thus he distinguishes that [Self] residing in the body by the word "rasa" (essence);
it is designated as "this," like the all-pervading Lord when He is covered by a garment.
The individual soul (jīva) arises from the head and so forth, because it is established in the head and so forth;
by knowing that, one attains liberation for this [soul], but never through the knowledge of anything else.
Because of the teaching of distinction—“This [Self] is in the sun and in the person”—there is no non-difference between Him and the individual soul; nor is inference a matter of arbitrary choice.
Since bodies are considered diverse as the abodes for my enjoyment,
the notion that "these are bodies" and so forth is indeed required for the knowledge of reality.

Since it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, and is devoid of both direct observation and authoritative scripture, where would an inference driven by mere whim not find no place? (1.1.213)

Therefore, the divine Nārāyaṇa is primarily designated by words that express all qualities without exception,

By the aphorism "janmādy asya," the definition of Brahman was proclaimed for the sake of establishing its entire range of attributes, since that [definition] is rooted in the sacred scriptures.
The lineage of all words is that which makes known the entire essence of qualities,
because the primary application of the causes for the occurrence of words resides within it.

The denotative power of words with respect to other meanings arises from their being used frequently in those senses, due to the scarcity of usage for the primary meaning and because they serve as its cause.

The Vedic conventional meaning of a word must be derived from its etymological derivation;
therefore, keeping in mind that Viṣṇu is the primary referent, the Lord [Manu] says: [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.237].

furthermore, it must refer to Hari because of the subsequent mark of being "greater than the great" (parato 'pi varīyastva).
To dispel such doubt, the name "Ākāśa" is given;
furthermore, based on the preceding indicative mark, the state of being even more excellent than the former belongs to Hari.

Whether verse by verse, word by word, or even syllable by syllable,
according to their respective fitness through various specific methods of reasoning, scripture, and logic.

for since actions are impermanent, how indeed could they constitute its essential nature?

for it is the absence of that [non-existence] which contradicts its presence, and nothing other than that.

Likewise, the state of being approached by the liberated, superiority over all things including the vital breaths, the distinctness of one's own nature, and action preceded by discernment; Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.3.11.

The state of being nameless and formless, the status of being the foundational authority for all distinctions,

The perfect knowledge of Viṣṇu is eternal, free from increase or decrease,

But such qualities as these are employed even when all [other factors] are present;

Therefore, because of the extreme remoteness of defects and because even doubt is impossible—

Intending to express the sense of absolute sovereignty, even words denoting defects are applied to Viṣṇu;
and the Vedic scripture concerning Vāsudeva declares that there is indeed no inauspiciousness in Viṣṇu.

Faults do not at all produce harm in Hari when they are spoken of with the understanding that He is their locus;
therefore, those very words denoting faults signify virtues in His case.

Even if this is accepted, there is no fault in the consistency of the statement;
for ritual action and the like are possible as being for that purpose, [the teaching] being intended for those of limited intellect.

"Who knows the application of the Vedic meters?"—from this Vedic revelation, he who knows the true meaning of yoga understands that Brahman alone exists and there is no other; for the word "who" (ka) has a dual significance here. (Manu 1.4.19)
Since it is certain that even for that eternally established [relation], the cognition [of the relation] is itself [eternal],
the eternal connection of words with their meanings is not at all negated;
and all words denoting women, as well as those denoting negation, are expressive of Brahman.
These various stations serve, in every respect, as distinct points of convergence for those who prohibit women, being the causes for the abundance of all opposing views.

Contradiction with all [authoritative] measures, the impossibility of [proper] linguistic derivation, mutual contradiction, contradiction between the action and its possessor, the feminine gender, and negation— these are the reasons against the prima facie arguments. (Manu 1.4.22)
The restriction that faults do not touch [the Veda], the multiplicity of word-meanings, as well as the multiformity of the Lord characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation. 1.4.23.
The production [of the world] from one's own body, as well as the non-manifestation of the wicked—
these and other such arguments establish the final doctrine directly here.
"The etymological derivation of all words cannot be easily known"—
by stating this, he expresses the view of Jaimini and others that leads to aversion toward the world.
The Lord, the Master of Knowledge, the Sovereign himself, set forth his own doctrine in part for the sake of the renown of his disciples. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.26)
Having understood this, he spoke here concerning the relative gradation of men, since their proficiency in various subjects has been acknowledged.
Because there are many purposes and because each of those is non-contradictory,
and by virtue of the power of the instructions and so forth, his capacity is understood to reside in Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, when there is a contradiction, its status as a direct denotation is set aside;
but when there is no contradiction, these [words] are considered to have multiple meanings because they are rooted in this [Veda].

For here [in this work] others have attained their established status; for here [in this work] they are the basis upon which this depends. Its establishment relies on them, and that dependence occurs by the will of Hari.
Therefore, there are three modes of operation for a word: supreme primacy in Viṣṇu, primacy elsewhere, and the secondary mode which is indicative. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.31)
The abundance of causes for engagement should be understood as the state of being supremely primary;
therein, if there is an abundance of practice, what need is there to mention devotion? (Manu 1.4.32)
Both are observed in the case of Viṣṇu with respect to all words:
there is the mere abundance of usage, which is called "conventional meaning" (rūḍhi). Mānava 1.4.33.

It should be understood that the cause of figurative usage (vṛtti) is either similarity associated with application or a relationship in a secondary sense; when the primary sense is impossible, there is recourse to the latter. *Manusmṛti* 1.4.34.
For it is said here that they call him by names such as "Śatarcī" and others precisely because he exists in this very way; thus, the word "santam" (existing) serves as a restrictive emphasis.

He clearly demonstrates, through the very intent of the text and with etymological explanations, the predominance of usage based on yoga (etymology) and the usage among the learned that pertains thereto, many times over.
The syllable *a* is declared to be Brahman; by its explanation, one is likewise considered to have fulfilled the purpose regarding all words as well as names. (Manu 1.4.37)

Then, speaking of the letter *ṇa* and the letter *ṣa* as consisting of strength and activity, he declared that the name Viṣṇu possesses the nature of both meaning and form, beginning with the *saṃhitā*.
Likewise, the study of the *saṃhitā* is preceded by that knowledge;
and let there be the prefix *vi-* because it denotes a state of being, while *un-* likewise has the sense of habituality.
The letter *ṇa* and the letter *ṣa* are considered to be name and form;
therefore, there is a complete correspondence in Viṣṇu of the nature of vowels, consonants, and words.
How much less could there be a connection for the Veda as a collection of sentences?
For all sounds are the Vedas, and all the Vedas are that single Word.
"The first creator, the bestower of names upon all the gods, is Indra, Mitra, and likewise Indra"—such is the Vedic revelation (śruti). 1.42.

"Regarding the subject matter not already mentioned by the means of valid knowledge, that very [matter] has been stated from the beginning"—thus did the Blessed One himself declare the entire sequence. (Manu 1.4.43)
It is not merely the denotability by words that is denied here of the Pradhāna,
because it is included within all the Vedas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of Prakṛti bind the imperishable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.45)

Where the meaning is intended to be nothing other than that expressed by such statements as these, or if even the primordial material cause consisting of fire, water, and earth is intended; (Manu 1.4.46)

When it is asked, "What is the primary cause of this beginningless offense?", the Śruti declares, "The one unborn [Prakṛti]. At that time, what fault could there be if [the cause] were entirely insentient and subject to transformation? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.4.47)
For us, however, the Blessed One alone is the supreme primary object;
everything else is accepted as being established merely by way of being secondary.
Since the secondary (gauṇī) and other [figurative] functions of all words are impossible [in that context],
Hari spoke with the intention of referring to two meanings.
They know that the cause of all effects is the first, the highest object of speech is the word, the supreme perfection of yogas is the ultimate goal, and that is your station.
Thus, because both [words] are established through etymology and conventional usage,
and because there is no reason to abandon either when they are brought together in the intellect, it is accepted that they possess both meanings.

In the absence of a contrary means of valid cognition, the prior ascent [of a word's meaning] is the cause; where that [prior ascent] would be rendered futile because it is an error, as in the case of a delusion, that scripture declares *pradhāna* to be the material cause of the world. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.52)
That which consists of the three qualities, unmanifest, eternal, and composed of both being and non-being—
what they call Pradhāna and Prakṛti, undifferentiated yet possessing differentiation.
Five, five, four, and likewise ten—
those who know the primary principles recognize this group of twenty-four as the Pradhāna.
Thus spoke the Lord himself, the sovereign of knowledge, in the Bhāgavata:
"And by the word *prakṛti*, Brahman is not called the material cause."
The Self is forever changeless, eternally pure, and eternal; Hari is always possessed of uniform consciousness and power, and has bliss as his very nature.
Changeless, imperishable, pure, free from affliction, undecaying, and immortal;
non-universal yet the creator of the universe, unborn—he who is thus described is called the Supreme.
That which is changeless, incomparable, eternally of one taste, and imperishable—
what the people learned in the Vedas know as Brahman and the Supreme Self.
Thus, according to what is stated in the Śruti and Purāṇas, Janārdana is not subject to modification;
for him there is no acquisition of qualities dependent on another, nor any irreversible change of state.

If it were intended that Hari’s very nature as the material cause (apādānatva) constitutes his being the source of transformation, then there could never be any modification of him, such as milk and the like.
That was accepted by Bhava as if he were a father; however, there is no transformation in the Universal Soul, nor is there any such change in the spider, its progenitor, or its mother.
Because it possesses consciousness, that food indeed exists in the form of an effect;
through its status as the material cause, the agency of the Creator over the universe is preceded by intelligence.
It has been stated with reverence in the Bhāllavi-Śākhā and in the Brahmatarka that the creation of the immutable Lord occurs at all times by his mere will.
This is the inherent nature of the Infinite One by which the world came into being through passion; Janārdana formerly consumed the universe at his own will, beginning with his own body.
The Lord, himself eternally changeless, transforms primordial matter (pradhāna) like a mother and father, or like a spider, [bringing forth the world].
For wherever there is an insentient thing, it could never be a transformation of consciousness;
nor could a conscious being ever be a transformation of the insentient. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.66)
Nor is the nature of one thing ever seen to be the nature of another, even when it has undergone transformation;
for nowhere is the curd ever seen by anyone to be anything other than the milk.
For the world is indeed experienced as being other than the omniscient Brahman;
yet if non-difference were based merely on existence, it would follow that even a donkey and gold are identical.
If transformation occurs through a portion, then there must indeed be a distinction between the portions;
that portion which would not undergo modification is, for us, the Lord himself.
If it be argued that the name "Brahman" refers to the collection of differentiated things,
then Brahman could never be the material cause of the universe at any time.
From a horn comes an arrow, from sheep's wool dūrvā grass, and likewise from cow dung a scorpion; in such cases as these, the status of the ablative (apādāna) is accepted.
Even though here the state of being a portion of the material cause is observed,
the very state of being the source [of creation] should serve as the illustrative example for Brahman.
For here, it is not merely the material cause [that matters], because of the weight of the external parts;
nor does consciousness arise there from that which is unconscious.
It is not by way of being a material cause; rather, for this conscious principle residing in the body as its effect, it is observed to be merely the instrument (upādāna).
"Truth became that which is true"— by this statement, its being the universe is not asserted,
because the universe was already established prior to that through the very act of its creation.
Because it exists, because it is understood, because it is Vedic, because it cannot be correctly described,
because it is the substratum, because it is its own substratum, because it is knowledge, and because it is difficult to know.
Because it possesses the seventy forms of conduct, because it is unattainable by the wicked,
and because it is eternally characterized by the pervasive qualities of the virtuous and is the form of the Controller,
Brahman alone is indeed described as such through its form pervading the world.
For the manifestation of the aforementioned qualities among men occurs in relation to the Supreme Person (puruṣa); thus, the expression "it was" and so forth is appropriate here. (Manu 1.4.78)
Therefore, the Lord of Ramā— who is the sole creator of all without exception and is devoid of transformation—
is designated by words such as "prakṛti" and others that possess feminine grammatical gender.
"May I become many"— it is for this very purpose that the world was created by Him through the aforementioned method, assuming various forms in accordance with that intent.
And that which is this very Brahman, unmodified, yet falsely perceived as the universal self by those of dull vision—that is called "creation. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.81)
Was that limited vision of his directed toward that very Brahman, or toward something other than him?
If it was directed toward Brahman, how can he be omniscient; if it was directed elsewhere, then his difference from [Brahman] is inherent.
The vision of one who is not joined with a body does not exist by itself; if embodied beings were not possessed of causes, their bodies would not exist, except through delusion.
If even the distinction therein is produced by delusion,
then since delusion is rooted in ignorance, it depends upon that very distinction.

Nothing can be considered a product of ignorance, since that would involve mutual dependence; nor does this statement apply to the state of error, for error is included within that [category of ignorance].
For its status as conventional reality depends indeed upon its being non-sublated;
that which is sublatable cannot perform a causal function, yet even a dream is not entirely false.
Since that [dream] is also admitted to be produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
and because of the scriptural statement "for he is the agent," the notion that it is waking is indeed an error.
For even in cases such as the delusion of a snake, there certainly exists a cognition of that very kind;
it is precisely that [cognition] which performs the purposeful action, and it is that alone which is the real producer of the effect.
The Veda, however, is effective in purposeful action, whether through extrinsic means or by itself;
for it has been accepted as such by that very [Veda] itself, yet its validity is not extrinsic. (1.4.89)

Since we two always agree that the non-primary truth-cognition is a means of valid knowledge, let that [primary] cognition remain as a means of valid knowledge; for there can be no disagreement between us on this point. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.90)
For one who is perverted in his understanding cannot establish anything anywhere; rather,
the probative power of truth belongs to the witness, for that which is correctly agreed upon by both of us should not become a matter of dispute.
If nothing whatsoever has been accepted, then even the state of non-acceptance is not itself accepted;
thus one would be mute, and so there is no disagreement with us.
"All that he has perceived is true," "He knows the essence of this according to its true nature"—all such scriptural passages declare the reality of the universe. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.93)
The reality of the sky and so forth is established by the perception of the witness;
that which is established by the witness can never be sublated, because of its faultlessness.
The fact that [the self] is not sublated at any time is perceived by the witness-consciousness itself;
for time is directly perceived by the witness, as is evident from the experience during deep sleep.
The past and future times as well are not within the range of direct perception;
since it is impossible to take them as the subject of inference, inference does not apply there.
All this— whether it be the entire field of perception or the range of memory—
indeed exists as inlaid with time, which is established by the Witness.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever can be remembered or seen without that [Self];
for since it is eternally established, there would be no occasion for inference.
Therefore, the truth of that which is perceived as faultless is held by the witness;
for by that very [witness], the truth of the investigation and so forth must also be held.
Otherwise, why is it not suspected that the entire universe might suddenly cease to exist, despite the existence of means of valid cognition such as scripture and reasoning?

If there were no course for transmigratory existence because it did not exist prior to this [creation], then [the world] would arise from speech and inference; and the authority of those two would depend upon a witness. (Manu 1.4.101)
The validity of that [scripture] is established exactly as a witness establishes it:
by remaining steadfast at all times and by excluding any deviation. (Manu 1.102)
Why, then, would he not establish the reality of the universe—which is proven by its being perceived through the senses—on the basis of his own faultless power of knowledge? (Manu 1.4.103)
If it is asserted that the universe was created by a single knower, then the rebuttal to that would be that the universe was created by many knowers. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.104)
Even while knowing the reality of another, why would one who is a thief of his own self say "another does not exist," speaking like a madman? (Manu Smṛti 4.105)
For speech is useless in the absence of an opponent; if he does not speak at all, then one should answer that thief with a whip, a goad, or the like.
If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease;
this duality is merely illusion (*māyāmātra*), for in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is non-duality (*advaita*).

If conceptual construction were to cease because it had been imagined by someone, then this teaching would be for that purpose; for duality does not exist in one who knows [the truth]. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 1.4.108)

In this context, the two words "if" (*yadi*) and "would cease" (*nivarteta*), as well as the two [concepts] that they declare the reality of the universe and the very origin of knowledge—[these are the points to be understood]. (Manu 1.4.109)
For from this root *vid*, in the sense of "origination," it is indeed origination itself;
for the fivefold diversity of phenomenal expansion is generally characterized by cessation and pervasion. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.110)

The distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, likewise the distinction between the insentient and the Lord, the mutual distinction between individual souls, the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul,
and the mutual distinction between insentient things— this is the fivefold phenomenal world of distinctions.
This reality is indeed beginningless; for if it had a beginning, it would be subject to destruction.
Therefore, the view that duality does not exist belongs to the ignorant.
Thus, according to the Śruti, that which is measured and protected by the knowledge of Hari known as Māyā is the supreme reality;
Hari alone is the highest object, while everything else is middling or inferior.

That which is initiated by speech and based on convention is called a derivative name, and it is manifold; whereas that which is eternal is the Vedic designation, such as "mṛttikā" (clay) and so forth.
Because of its preeminence, by knowing it, even an ordinary ignorant man is called "learned" by the virtuous; thus is one who knows the eternal Self.
The wise declare that "the eternal truth" (satyātana) refers precisely to the permanent; furthermore, there is an application of this term later on: "if old age were to overtake it."
This body perishes; what remains of it thereafter?
It is not slain by murder, nor does it decay through old age.
"This is the true City of Brahman" is stated precisely because of its eternity;
for when it is said that "all is a mere modification of speech," to claim it is false would be an unwarranted assumption not supported by scripture.
Furthermore, it would follow that the name [of the Veda] is a mere tautology, rendering it purposeless; and the terms "a single lump" and "a gem" would likewise be redundant. (Manu 1.4.119)

If one intended to express that they are mere modifications [of the original], then there would be no cutting with a single nail, nor would everything be made of black iron; therefore, it is precisely because of their similarity [that the term is applied].
But here, by the path already described, the intention is toward eternity and preeminence;
and the detailed account of creation and so forth is for the purpose of establishing that preeminence.
Therefore, by no means whatsoever should there be an adherence to the doctrine of non-return;
since it is fraught with innumerable faults, those who seek what is auspicious must certainly abandon it.

Because the faults [of the world] are innumerable and for fear of excessive prolixity, [the discussion] is here concluded. Therefore, Viṣṇu, who is free from exertion and whose nature consists of perfect remaining qualities, creates the universe like a father according to his will.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

The systematic concordance has been stated; here, the absence of contradiction is directly established. First, that of the fourfold [means of knowledge] is treated, and therein also the contradiction with Smṛti is addressed.

Since that [Speech] possesses four forms, all her feet are each fourfold in nature; and the portions of those feet, as well as the forms [of the gods], are derived from the [Vedic] syllables according to tradition.
Trustworthiness arises from the power of equanimity, impartial vision, and equal learning;
it consists of following all [traditions], lightness [of conduct], and the absence of fruit due to not perceiving distinctions.

The fulfillment of desired results and the logical arguments found in the prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣa) serve as the constraints; these very factors, when possessed of great strength, are the determinants of the final conclusion (siddhānta).
How could the Śruti— resembling the script of ants— ever contradict a matter declared by authoritative persons after perceiving it directly, for those [authorities] are all-pervading?
If it is argued that Rudra and the others, headed by Hari, are all-knowing, why are they not considered omniscient? For the same authority would apply to both cases.
And certainty regarding attainment cannot be established there because of the possibility of deviation;
nor, even if there is such deviation, is its status as a means of valid cognition ever lost.
Since the qualification prescribed in the Vedas is always difficult to determine,
it is indeed impossible to know whether there is strict adherence or deviation from it.
For it is said that eligibility is easily obtained in other scriptures;
however, the eligibility declared in the Veda is difficult for all human beings to attain.
Even for those born as Caṇḍālas, the status of a Brahmin is gradually established through entry into the circle [of initiates] in other traditions.

Having declared that the qualification [for dharma] is difficult to attain, he has now stated it to be very easy; having declared the means of accomplishment to be impossible, he has stated them to be easily performed for the sake of attaining that fruit.
Therefore, what was said is indeed subject to deviation even with respect to the result.

How could it attain the status of a valid means of knowledge because of its eternity, and how could it not become authoritative when it has been cast aside by those originating from human beings who are free from all defects?
"By means of eternal speech, O Virūpa, [the Veda is eternal]—both eternally and non-eternally," and so forth;
by such scriptural passages, the Veda is understood to be eternal. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.13)
The script of the ants is also authoritative because it is not contradictory,
just as that which was composed by Ulūka for the son of Droṇa served as a means of awakening.

That which is not contradicted is valid, whereas that which is contradicted is sublated precisely because of the contradiction; since no contradiction is perceived, the authority of the Veda is therefore accepted.
Since the Smṛtis have their root in that [the Veda], there is no contradiction anywhere;
yet it is precisely where there is a contradiction with either direct perception or scripture that a conflict is said to exist.
When there is a contradiction between two scriptural authorities, reasoning is required;
however, when there is a contradiction with the Veda, which is the source upon which all others depend, one must interpret the other text in a different sense.
Perception should generally be relied upon, and reason as well in some cases;
for among those who hold scripture alone as the authority, that [scripture] itself is what must be relied upon.
If the meaning of a scripture is understood as being both reasonable and unreasonable, then only the reasonable meaning should be accepted; and that reason is considered to be threefold.
Pervasion is that which is established through perception, as well as through reasoning and scripture;
however, in such cases, reasoning rooted in perception and scripture is the most authoritative.

Validity consists precisely in accordance with reality; that is the primary sense of both "knowledge" and "word. Being an object means being an objective thing; it is not considered to apply to actions.
The status of being an object of knowledge is primary in relation to the object of cognition, while it follows immediately thereafter in relation to the word-meaning;
those logical arguments which produce knowledge of an object as it truly is are considered to be valid.
For these words of the Akṣapāda and the Logicians are indeed secondary means of knowledge;
therefore, the authority of a restatement is not lost, nor even that of a traditional Smṛti.

If it is accepted that the very meaning of the word "validity" (prāmāṇya) intended here is simply "conformity with reality," then what contradiction could there be in the validity of memory and other such cognitions?
Nor should fruitlessness be asserted for all Smṛtis and restatements;
nor do we intend to claim that their authority consists in possessing a fruit. (Manu 2.1.25)
Furthermore, what fruitfulness is said to exist in the perception of grass and such?
For even in memory, some degree of pleasure, pain, and so forth is observed.
Furthermore, valid cognition (*pramā*) is not merely that which performs the function of delimitation;
for in this context, it is declared that perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises from faultless sense organs. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.27)
Prakṛti and pure consciousness are considered to be the two-fold sense-faculties;
the pure ones reside in the Lord, Śiva, and liberated souls, while elsewhere they are joined with the products of Prakṛti.

Consciousness alone is indeed without fault; elsewhere, both are held to exist—pure consciousness, even among those in the cycle of transmigration, remains untainted despite its objects such as pleasure and pain.
Because it is faultless and possesses absolute certainty, that [knowledge] is considered the most powerful.
Due to the distinction between the five senses and the mind, ordinary perception is traditionally held to be sixfold.
Inference is said to be nothing other than reasoning, and it is traditionally held to be nothing other than pervasion (vyāpti).
For when pervasion alone is stated for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā), that is inference. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.31)
What remains here for one who understands that mark?
If the mark were unestablished, how could it possess the status of a means of valid cognition? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.32)
If it were merely a means of recollection, there would be no purpose for the rememberer here;
nor would the dispute reach its conclusion upon the statement of the five-membered syllogism.
In the case of examples and so forth, the means of proof would likewise be required;
and even when the logical mark (liṅga) is stated, the conclusion of inference would certainly be established in this same manner.
Contradiction and lack of connection are direct refutations of the reasoning;
indeed, "lack of connection" is said to be the absence of a relationship between the reason and the proposition. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.35)

Contradiction also occurs in only three ways: contradiction with the meaning of the proposition, lack of a logical mark, and non-pervasion; whereas deficiency and excess pertain to the verbal expression.
The non-pervasion of the probans consists in its absence where the pervader of the probandum is absent;
even when there is a contradiction with a weak [opposing] means of knowledge, it does not render the [valid] means of knowledge ineffective.
Even if there is a contradiction with one's own statement, [the argument] will not attain the status of a proof;
moreover, these very points, when accompanied by a failure to state a corroborative instance, constitute grounds for defeat (nigraha).
For those who understand, there are three types of discourse: debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*);
these serve to establish the ascertainment of truth, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
But mere talk, debate, and chatter depend upon matters such as wealth and the like;
it should be known that only the discourse of the virtuous is true *kathā*, whereas *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) belongs to the wicked or to those who appear virtuous but are not.
Without disclosing one's own established doctrine, one should first state the refutation of the opponent's position;
once they have stated their proof, its refutation must then be articulated.
Vitaṇḍā (cavil) and jalpa (disputatious debate) must be preceded by an examination of knowledge,
since victory and defeat depend upon the determination of superiority and inferiority.
For without a definitive determination of the truth, there can never be a discernment of superiority or inferiority through mere disputation and the like; such is the examination of knowledge.
Through debate, the distinction between superior and inferior status becomes clearly known;
thus, debate comes first, for the other two [means] would be useless if that [distinction] were not established. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.44)
But once proficiency in many sciences has been established, even debate— preceded by the assembly, the speaker, and the judges— is not at all the cause [of success], even for rivals.
Only debate (vāda) serves both purposes, bringing about both determination and victory;
whereas the sole fruit of cavil (vitaṇḍā) and wrangling (jalpa) is the mere failure to reveal the truth.
If it were possible to examine knowledge without debate, then even wrangling (jalpa) and the like might sometimes be considered true debate; otherwise, they would not be.
Indeed, even such a debate might be called mere "chatter," and its conclusion might be established by a mere assertion, as was the case with Yājñavalkya.
The assembly, the president of the assembly, and the assessors should be devotees of Viṣṇu;
the members of the court should be free from passion and hatred and well-versed in all the Vedas.
And those who are ignorant of this, as well as the members of the assembly who stand at a distance from them,
shall serve as authorities for a decision, provided they are free from partiality.

In both debate and disputation, the means of proof and refutation should be established by both parties; however, the virtuous should employ only the traditional scripture (*āgama*), which is effective for proving one's intended position.
For, according to their own tenets, [the opponents] infer what is non-existent;
yet, by resorting to contradictions with perception and scripture, they merely establish something else entirely.
In this context, the fault to be observed in scripture is the contradiction of the gender;

whereas conformity with the gender and the favoring of the primary meaning [of the word] constitute the subordination of the direct statement (*śruti*) and the other criteria. *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 2.1.53.

If one were to claim that inference must necessarily consist of either three or five members, or even two members, one should ask him: if such [a minimal form] is not inference, then by what means could the members of the probandum be conceived?
When the specific members [of the syllogism] are not established, the proof is by means of pervasion alone.
Therefore, that alone must be performed by him; for that reason, it is considered to be inference (anumā).
If direct experience is the means of valid knowledge, by what is memory sublated?
When it is asked, "What is the proof for that which was previously experienced?", what could be the answer?
For that mental cognition is indeed a means of knowledge through direct perception;
just as the past and the future are directly perceived by yogis,
so too is that which was previously experienced understood by the mind alone.
"Even that which was previously known by the mind as 'this was done by me' is established through direct experience; how indeed can it be set aside? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.60)
Thus, regarding these three means of knowledge characterized in this way, the Veda alone is the authority for entities such as Brahman and the rest; and its authority has been established.

Nevertheless, how could words such as "clay" or "water," which denote [substances] like intellect (*buddhi*) or speech (*vāk*), serve as a means of valid cognition (*māna*) in that regard, since they would contradict observed pervasion (*vyāpti*)? 2.1.62.
Therefore, it is stated here that another person may exist who bears that same name,
provided this is established without contradicting reason and scripture.
Even without relying on the conventional usage of children, by resorting to the conventional usage of the learned,
these [beings] are indeed designated by their respective names as they identify with their respective objects.
Their power is said to be especially superior to that of others, and their pervasiveness is declared according to the tradition; they are perceived by those who possess the requisite qualifications.
Furthermore, proficiency in the subject matter taught in the scriptures arises from the indications found within those scriptures;
such proficiency is indeed superior to that which comes from mere book-learning, for the latter is the proficiency of a fool.
But when there is a contradiction with a firm argument, this principle applies everywhere:
an argument joined with even a few words may be more numerous and thus more powerful than one that contradicts it.
When it is asked, "How can there be a determination of the truth in various such cases?
the established principle is that it is due to the abundance of contradictory arguments. (Manu 2.1.68)

Since there is an abundance of reasoning for what is logical and of scriptural authority for what is based on tradition, how could one not reach a definitive conclusion? For it is not the case that there is no valid reason [to do so].
In some instances, the meaning of the Veda is established through the Vedic texts themselves and through logical reasoning;
however, in the fourth chapter, the absence of contradiction is thoroughly demonstrated.
If it is argued that "just as a non-existent effect is seen [to arise], so too is the cause," we say no; for that which is of the sole nature of negation possesses no agency.
For here, agency is determined to be activity preceded by intelligence;
however, the negative nature of an entity arises from its character as a non-existence,
and due to the identity of the property and the possessor of the property, it does not consist of that [non-existence] alone.
Moreover, the existence of non-existence is both a property (*dharma*) and a substratum (*dharmin*);
yet here, such reality is said to consist merely in the absence of cognition. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.73)
In the initial cognitions, the state of being a subject consists precisely in being qualified;
for here, the nature of existence and non-existence is defined by the forms of affirmation and negation.
Since a person remains virtuous even amidst total ruin,
this destruction— even if it is considered contested— must possess a surviving agent, because it is a form of destruction.
Furthermore, the destruction of all men has never been seen, nor is it observed anywhere;
even though man must be accepted as the substratum of merit and demerit during the dissolution.
How could there ever be a cause that is beginningless if it has never been observed?
If what is seen later arises from what was not seen before, then how can there be no subsequent [effect]?
If the unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) were not the cause, what would be the basis for dissolution?
For nowhere is an intelligent being ever seen to be the agent of creation and destruction.
Why is a creator not inferred everywhere by means of that same analogy? However, this inference is to be established as a valid means of knowledge when supported by scripture.

In the absence of the support of scripture, reasoning would not be established; however, for that which is rooted in perception and scripture, its establishment is indeed possible. Otherwise, its lack of foundation would be contradicted by one's own words.
Nor is it the case that the doctrine of a Lord (Īśavāda) is not accepted by disciples;
therefore, what is here prohibited is the agency of the remaining [entities], such as the individual soul (jīva).

The birth of the mind from non-existence, as expressed in the passage beginning "He made that mind," is refuted by the preceding statement, for [the mind] could not have arisen suddenly without a cause.
The procreation of offspring from one who is not [legally] fit is prohibited here out of concern for it;
however, the specific remedy is specified as merely the statement of the authoritative injunction.
Having observed in some cases that a form is produced by a living being, and in others that it is produced from a conscious agent,
one infers in other instances likewise, because of its substantiality, on the basis of the Vedic revelation.
Nowhere has anything ever been seen to have attained a state of difference from itself;
therefore, the individual soul can never become Brahman.
How could that which was seen in some places as distinct be seen as non-distinct?
For such a thing has never been seen before, nor is it seen now.

As for the view that [the world] becomes the enjoyer, from what source did Hari state "because of the attainment of the status of an enjoyer" (Bhoktrāpatti)? And how is there non-difference between them? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.1.87)
When the immutability of the world has been established by the aforementioned reasoning,
it is therefore the status of being an independent cause that is here negated.

"Substance, action, time, inherent nature, consciousness, and fortitude—these exist through his grace and do not exist through his neglect. Since this is heard [in scripture], the state of being under his control is not due to anything else. Thus, [it is established that] he alone is the cause. (Manu Smṛti 2.1.89)
For although Hari is capable of acting otherwise,
he always creates this world by means of fixed causes alone, according to the restriction of his own will.
For there is indeed a constant distinction by way of the efficient cause (*nimitta*), while by way of the material cause (*upādāna*) there are two;
that which is non-existent in the form of the effect exists, however, as the nature of the cause.
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress regarding the origin and destruction of everything;
for even the Lord Viṣṇu, though capable, could not act otherwise than he does.
"The Unborn One creates the universe, which is non-different from Himself yet different from His causes"—
thus, according to this scripture, the stated meaning has been concluded in its entirety.
Salutations to that Self-existent One who truly bestows upon the soul— even though it possesses no inherent parts— some measure of capacity for its various duties.

If Hari were not to employ the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti) through its portions in all activities, then he would either have to exert his entire effort everywhere himself, or else he would be merely a part. (Manu 1.95)
For those things such as cloth which are wholes are called "wholes" because they possess parts that are indeed distinct from one another; but sentient beings are not like this at all.
Therefore, the Vedic revelation applies the term "partless" to these very things,
even though they possess multiple natures, solely on account of their specific [essential] nature.
Indeed, the state of having many forms exists among them precisely because they possess parts;
since multiplicity is invariably concomitant with it, distinctness necessarily follows.
If the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, were not the establisher of such a rule,
then because of his possession of infinite power, it would be appropriate for him to have been born even with armor.

In the second chapter, the contradiction regarding the preeminence of all [deities] is refuted; however, in this chapter on Nārāyaṇa, other such contradictions occurring here and there are likewise addressed.
The mutual non-contradiction of the statements concerning creation and dissolution, as well as those denoting the nature of the individual soul (jīva), is the subject matter of the second chapter.
Because of the distinction between the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, there is no tautology;
the Lord's constant activity arises solely from His own nature.
"Just as certain gestures of a man may be devoid of any specific intention, so too does the Śruti directly declare: 'This is the very nature of the Divine.'"
"Having made play the motive, creation is not in contradiction with the Veda"—
thus has the Lord himself determined that it is indeed mere sport (*līlā*).
