The Śruti prohibits desire for the sake of one's own personal interest; it does not do so because of the fact that such interests possess utility. Therefore, the Teacher of the World says: [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.1.105]
Those who are certain regarding creation hold that "the creation of the Lord is merely His will";
this is established through praise, from the Vedic texts concerning desire, through reasoning, and by virtue of the primary purport [of scripture]. Thus, mere will is not denied.

Since the Vedas have liberation as their purpose, and since He, out of His grace, desires to lead [the soul] upward— as indicated by scriptural statements and in accordance with worldly observation— [He is the Supreme Lord].
Since [the Veda] has desire as its motive, in the absence of that [desire], how could it—devoid of great purpose—attain the status of a valid means of knowledge? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.1.108)
Even in the case of a statement, it is its very accordance with reality that constitutes its authority; yet even such a statement attains authority only when it possesses a complete purpose.
Partiality and cruelty are indeed the grounds for the invalidity of the Vedas;
therefore, nothing other than these, such as that which is called partiality and so forth, should be accepted.
Since both virtues and faults depend entirely upon him,
how could he not possess virtues, and how could he not likewise possess faults?
For by such words as well, which establish all dharmas,
the Blessed Lord Hari is determined to be free from all defects and endowed with every excellence.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Śrībrahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

Memory, reasoning, sacred revelation, and the qualities of virtue—these four kinds of arguments, being manifold in their application, are by no means contradictory when directed toward the same conclusion. (Manu 2.2.1)
Although it has been determined by the first quarter-verse,
the dull-witted person again entertains a doubt because various philosophical systems continue to be active due to persistent inquiry.
For conventions have existed from beginningless time by way of a continuous flow;
since there is no destruction of any convention whatsoever, it is therefore all-pervading.
He clearly demonstrates that these [views] are rooted in error,
by means of most firm arguments as well as through the words of those who propound traditional scripture.
Because those of pure intellect are rare, because those of little knowledge are numerous,
because the world is characterized by darkness and prone to false cognition,
and because there is constant hostility toward the supreme reality and those who know that reality. (Manu 2.5)

Due to the connection with beginningless latent impressions, because of the great number of asuras, and because they are seized by stubborn dogmatism, these systems always prevail. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.6)
Nevertheless, for those of pure intellect who are joined with the grace of the Lord,
reasonings consistent with the scriptures shall always destroy darkness.
Thus Vidyāpati has thoroughly refuted the objections to the observances for the sake of sharpening the intellect of his own devotees. (Mānavadharmaśāstra 2.2.8)
Those who deny the existence of a Lord (nirīśvara) assert that reality consists of only two principles: the sentient and the insentient.
Among these, the insentient is divided into five groups of five;
the sentient is innumerable and distinct from it, and into this latter [the former] dissolves.
The agency of that which is insentient is proclaimed as being independent; furthermore, the mutual distinction among effects would have its locus [in such an agent]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.10)
Some say that for the enjoyers there is consciousness, while others say even that does not exist;
[they maintain] that the state of being an enjoyer arises from the power of the consciousness inherent in one's own nature and from self-luminosity.

Those who maintain that there is no experience [of pleasure and pain] say that it is precisely the failure to grasp the distinction between the nature of Prakṛti and the Self that constitutes experience; they hold this because of their perception of a difference between the two.
Liberation is taught for those who possess enjoyments; that same liberation is also taught for those who maintain the doctrine of non-enjoyment.
However, because the Lord is free from attachment, neither of those two [doctrines] is tenable in His case.
When the production of a cloth is seen to follow from volition and desire, who can prevent another thing from having such a nature, given that it is a real entity? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.14)
Nor is there any Vedic revelation that serves as a means of valid cognition regarding the goal to be attained;
for, according to the path already explained, the status of the speaker as a reliable authority is simply not possible.
Even by accepting the intrinsic invalidity [of all cognition], like a magician, one would negate everything one has said oneself; and nothing at all would be established.

"This [world] is not under the control of the insentient, because it is a real entity, like a perceived object"—since this [position] has been thus refuted, what could serve as the basis for an inference? (MAnu 2.17)
And how could such an independent composition exist in that which is insentient?
To claim that insentience is independence is contradicted by the very nature of the Self.
For the wise know that sovereignty is indeed the state of acting according to one's own will;
how could there be will for one who is unconscious? And if it is conscious, how could it be insentient? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.19)
For it is by virtue of one's own experience that one says, "I desire";
thus, when the desire for insentient things has ceased, there is no apprehension of difference here.
How could that [self] not belong to the jar? Because of the distinction "my mind," and because the mind is also grasped, it follows that [the self] possesses the nature of both.

But for desire, the mind is the object of desire; it is seen to have a twofold nature through the distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant. Therefore, how can there be a failure to perceive this distinction?
Because the formation [of the world] is impossible, that [world] does not follow from the inference of an omniscient being;
the world is insentient, and milk, water, and so forth are not [valid] analogies for its creator.
Even though there is this twofold division of the conscious and the unconscious according to the words of the Praśāstṛ, how can the self possess ownership over desire and the rest? 2.24.
That which has ascended to the level of direct experience can never be sublated;
ownership by will alone is what is meant, and nothing other than the possession of that will.

Even when one has come under the sway of something else, ownership remains as it does in the world; how much more so, then, for the Supreme Lord, who possesses all things as His own self and is independent of desire?
Nor is even the Vedic word capable of negating the fact that the mastery over desires is based on experience; therefore, that [Vedic statement] refers to something other than that.
If there were someone else who, being already liberated, would desire liberation for another, what use would that be for one desiring liberation? And who would strive for their own destruction?
The state of being an enjoyer is perceived only for that which possesses the state of being an agent;
and there would be no evidence whatsoever anywhere for a separation between these two.
Initiated into the singular, perverse initiation that opposes all of Manu,
this man may be compared to a proponent of illusion (māyāvādin), yet he is refuted by the word "that" (tat).

But the Sāṅkhya who maintains the existence of a Lord (Seśvara) says: "There exists a self-existent Lord, possessed of the power to favor the field (kṣetra), who is free from afflictions, karma, and the like. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 2.2.31)

That very [Prakṛti] possessing the power of the field is Nature; the individual soul possessing the power of the seed is the living being; and the Lord possessing the power of fate is known as being like the rain-cloud.
"The Pradhāna is like the earth, and the individual soul (jīva) is like the sower of seeds by virtue of its mere proximity; thus the Lord himself has declared here. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 12.33)
Elsewhere there is no power whatsoever that acts independently; for the Lord alone impels those powers directly, and they are always dependent upon Him.
For all cognitions and activities regarding existence, primordial matter, the individual soul, and the powers proceed eternally from that which is eternal by its very nature.

Just as the eternal Lord, by virtue of his eternity and eternal power, constantly governs all things, so too does he do so through you, according to the Vedic revelation: "There is nothing other than you."
Intrinsic nature, the living soul, karma, substance, time, the Vedas, and ritual actions—
by whose grace these exist, and by whose disregard they do not exist.
Thus, according to scripture, even existence and the like do not exist apart from Nārāyaṇa;
therefore, the systems of Patañjali, Vindhya, and others do not grant the supreme goal of human life.
The Cārvākas say that the only means of valid cognition is that which is born of the senses; there is no other anywhere.
The body is the self, and the human goal consists of nothing other than sensual pleasure and wealth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.39)
What purpose, then, is served by such a view regarding the scope of direct perception?
For men have already obtained that very [truth] from the scriptures; what else is there, apart from delusion?
Since it is devoid of benefit for oneself or others, why does this treatise, according to its own view, fruitlessly prattle on in vain like a madman? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.41)

To embodied beings, the self appears through experience as distinct from the body, just as it is always clearly evident that "this is my body" in the same way one says "this is my wealth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.42)
By what means is it determined that perception alone possesses authority?
If it is the means of establishing that [authority], why would it not also apply to the authority of the Veda? (Manu 2.43)
Furthermore, no other form of validity is ever established by any means of valid cognition;
such a position, being devoid of meaning according to its own tenets, should be disregarded. (MAnu 2.2.44)
Even if the insentient proceeds because of the proximity of the sentient,
nevertheless, since it would lack prior intelligence, the aforementioned fault would remain the same.
The fact that the Puruṣa alone is the principal (aṅgin) is experienced by everyone;
moreover, by asserting that everything else is merely his subordinate (aṅga), one would be a denier of all things.
How much more so for this Lord of All, from whom everything indeed proceeds? (Manusmṛti 1.2.46)
If he alone possesses the status of being the principal agent, then he does not have complete independence;
for since he is incapable of impelling [others], another independent being must be required.
Nor can he possess independence, because that would contradict perception and other means of knowledge;
furthermore, it would entail defects such as performing what is unbeneficial. Therefore, may you be well; the doctrine of a non-god (anīśvara) is not accepted.

Those who do not accept that there exists another, distinct from transmigrating beings, who is the Lord of all, omnipotent, incomparable, and upon whom this world of sentient and insentient entities— beginning with the living beings— depends, are all equal to these [who deny the Veda]. (Manu 2.49)
Therefore, by means of the authority of the Vedas and through logical reasoning, it is firmly established that Hari is the Supreme, eternal, and must be accepted as such by everyone.

Others say that Īśvara is endowed with eternal knowledge, effort, and desire, as well as the five qualities beginning with number; impelled by His will and *adṛṣṭa*, all atoms, which consist of the four categories, join together in pairs.
From two atoms alone, that which is called a dyad (dvayaṇuka) is produced;
from three dyads, a triad (tryaṇuka); and from four of those, [a tetrad] consisting of them is formed.
Therefore, the existence of parts and wholes occurs without any fixed rule;
and consequently, the production of all wholes likewise occurs without any fixed rule.
In that regard, the inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa) is said to be the atoms and so forth;
however, the Lord’s will, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and time are considered the instrumental causes (nimitta-kāraṇa).
Generality, ultimate particularity, and inherence—these three are eternal;
action is non-eternal; and quality and substance possess both forms [eternal and non-eternal].
In the case of an effect, the inherent cause consists of the qualities and actions;
however, the qualities and so forth residing in the cause, as well as conjunction, are the causes of substances.
Even though this is the established doctrine, a distinction is postulated therein:
namely, that the binary compound and the atom possess respectively shortness and sphericality.
"The cause does not possess the qualities of its effect; rather, dissimilarity is the cause in that regard"—so they say.
To them, the Lord himself, the Master of Knowledge, then spoke:
Furthermore, largeness and length are attributed to triads and other such [composite bodies];
from that, a similar effect is produced in their subsequent effects.
Just so, indeed, from minuteness and also from spherical dimension,
a similar effect would arise in the product, because of their equality.
If it were not so, then [the effect] would not arise from that which is large or even from that which is long;
for there can be no connection whatsoever between a cause and an effect that are dissimilar.
If it is argued that [the atom] would thus be imperceptible because of its atomicity in its effects,
we say no; for since magnitude exists even in the minute atom,
how can it be said that atomicity does not exist in the triads and those prior to them?
Perceptibility and its opposite depend upon the person;
however, minuteness and magnitude depend upon the object itself. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.63)
Since all things indeed exist in a state of gradation,
just as there is a limit to greatness, so too is a limit to minuteness accepted.
If it is argued that [the atom] is not so because it possesses magnitude, then even magnitude would have no ultimate limit;
for "infinite" is what is perceived, and thus infinity exists even in the atom.
The Lord is not limited by the quality of the principle of Mahat as being "only this much," nor is He ever delimited by the minuteness of an atom.
If it is understood that some infinite part remains at rest,
it simply cannot be determined because of the contradiction itself.
By the mere act of witnessing, neither time nor space has an end; the witness perceives the infinitesimal atom as having no limit in both respects.
If that greatness is not accessible through direct perception, by what means is it apprehended?
For its degree of repose is indeed observed through inference.
If that greatness is understood from scripture to be infinite,
why is its minuteness not likewise determined to be infinite?
No ultimate limit for either greatness or minuteness is ever found;
for infinity is indeed something distinct from both greatness and minuteness, yet equal to them both.
Just as in arithmetic one perceives both multiplicity and scarcity,
so too the infinity of the single parts is indeed counted as their very measure.
The Blessed One, as proclaimed in the Āgamas, is both the subtlest and the greatest;
the word expressing infinity maintains its status as a valid means of knowledge even with respect to the two kinds of infinity.
The smallness of qualities does not diminish, nor does the smallness of time depend on status;
for that which exists at all times may remain present even during a short period.
If it is argued that even a small quality may belong to one who possesses great qualities, you yourself would not exist [as such]; nor is this our view regarding even a single region.
For one who knows the Veda has declared that even the vastness [of Brahman] is as small as a minute space;
if it were not situated in a minute location, it would not exist anywhere at all.
For one who remains within limited spaces, omnipresence would indeed be impossible;
how much less can there be residence in all things for one who does not abide even in a single place? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.77)
That which has no stability even in a single location must be nothing but emptiness;
therefore, there is no resting place for either atomicity or magnitude anywhere.
Therefore, if that which is endowed with both kinds of infinity were to be the primary "Great" (mahat),
it would be the supreme Brahman itself, directly possessed of all infinities at all times.

If the witness were self-evident, by what means would he be known? Furthermore, the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge would either be established [by themselves] or there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, all objects always possess parts;
yet, because they are connected in all directions, their indivisibility constitutes the state of being an atom.
If the birth of things were to occur from an indefinite conjunction of those two, by what means could it be determined that there is a conjunction of only two? Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.82.
Therefore, the qualities of the cause would also exist in the effect; for all things, whether large or minute, exist according to their respective degrees of intensity.
Moreover, mere imagination cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge regarding the creation proclaimed by Him;
for how could it ever refute that which has been directly perceived by the Witness?
If this [matter] is not established by direct perception, nor does inference apply there,
since it is impossible to make it the subject of an argument (pakṣa), how indeed could there be any inference?
Who could reach that realm where there is no setting down of a footstep?
Terms such as "another country" and so forth are like terms such as "the horn of a hare."
Indeed, what similar instance of the same class exists for our position,
by which— through that very same manner— in which something unestablished is inferred, the existence of things such as a rabbit's horn could likewise be postulated?

Only that [correlation] for which there exists either perception or scripture as a restrictive authority constitutes valid pervasion (*vyāpti*); no other [pervasion] is so, because its basis is doubtful. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.88)

Inference based on mere observation does not establish pervasion; for pervasion is established only when there is either sense-perception or scripture that excludes [the probans] from the absence [of the probandum], or when it is determined through reasoning. That alone is [pervasion]; it is certainly not anything else.
Otherwise, even the existence of a seventh taste would follow by inference; for inference, acting according to its own whims, leads to all manner of undesirable conclusions.
Furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect, as well as that of the fivefold group beginning with the qualities (guṇas),
is held to be inherence (samavāya), which is distinct from [the other categories].
Because it shares the quality of being distinct [from them], its connection with those two would certainly be established;
if it were self-sustaining, why should it not likewise be a substance? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.92)
If a distinction such as being located therein and so forth is perceived in what is non-different,
for what reason could there be a negation of the forms of qualities, actions, and the like?

Therefore, substance itself, by virtue of its nature as having infinite particularities, is always the cause of manifold worldly transactions; its infinity consists precisely in these particularities.
Furthermore, that which is the qualified and that which is the qualifier exist by means of their own nature, like inherence;
for, due to the fault of conceptual complexity, they do not constitute separate categories of existence.
Having merely conceptualized the six categories along with their non-existences,
if that distinction resides in the One alone, why was it forgotten before?

By that which is established through direct perception, all worldly transaction occurs through the distinction between existence and non-existence; without it, such transaction is not possible in any way whatsoever.
And the cognition of non-difference regarding this category of entities— which begins with cause and effect and ends with non-existence— is determined as being accompanied by specific qualities.
How can all properties such as residing in that [substratum] be excluded by disputants from categories like universals, even though the underlying reality is one? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.99)

How could there be no distinction between the fact that an effect resides in its respective cause and the qualities (guṇas) and so forth being all-pervasive? If you say that this [distinction] is merely another property (dharma), [we reply: it is not so. MĀnu 2.2.100.
For even if there were no fixed number of categories, there would be a surplus beyond the six categories;
moreover, because a property arises from the continuum of properties, it would lead to an infinite regress.
For this reason, the universal of a universal and the quality of a quality have not been accepted;
if they were, there would be an infinite regress somewhere.
In our view, qualities and the like are indeed possessed by their substrates;
because they are non-different [from them], there is no infinite regress, and likewise, there would be no distinction at the time of destruction.
Since a specific rule is indeed more powerful when it relies upon another specific rule,
and since both are authoritative as direct perceptions, how can there be a contradiction between two scriptural injunctions?
Since both contradiction and non-contradiction reside within the scope of perception,
how can wise men attribute contradiction to that which is actually perceived?
The Blessed One is non-different from his own nature, yet he possesses differentiation through that which is other than it;
however, all his attributes are eternal and are therefore not distinct from him.
In other cases, phenomena that involve total annihilation possess both natures;
for if those very things were to exist, they would be annihilated, and all others would likewise be so.
Since there is no difference between the part and the whole, the conjunction of the parts is indeed the conjunction of the whole;
thus, even if there is no finality regarding the parts, there is no infinite regress.

If another conjunction were to arise only when one [conjunction] has already arisen, then there would be an infinite regress; but if the conjunctions were identical, where would that regress occur? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.109)
And since conjunction is observed to occur in parts, what is this infinite regress?
If conjunction does not reside in the parts, how could there be magnitude in composite effects?
"It is a marvelous statement that there is no largeness in an atom or a minute particle;
yet, even in a triad [of atoms], that largeness exists without depending on the largeness of the atoms.
How can this statement—that there is largeness in an atom—be possible? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.111)
This non-difference of the whole from its parts, while there is indeed difference from each individual part, is an object of all direct perception; how then can it be set aside?
Conjunction, disjunction, and indeed distinction are each perceived separately in both cases through their mutual opposition.

The term "divided" (*bhinnāḥ*) refers to what is observed as a collection of divisions; likewise, the expression "the difference between these two things" is used in the same manner. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.114)
A distinction characterized by two properties is observed here from that, and there from this;
in that regard, the singular number is used, as for example in "the feeding of the Brahmins. (Manu 2.115)
In this same way, even such states as "humanity" and so forth are understood through their respective attributes;
there is no single entity that possesses all attributes, for a collection consists of distinct elements.
And such similarity among objects exists individually;
for even when one [object] has perished, it is seen in another.
How can one who has attained the state of ashes be expected to attain humanity again?
There is no proof for their identity, and even the Śruti declares so with reverence.
All things, though distinct and possessing distinct properties, are nevertheless non-distinct from their own respective properties and from their own essential natures in every respect.
But phenomena whose destruction has not ceased possess both forms;
therefore, the Blessed One is not non-different from his own qualities.
For even this etymological derivation is understood through similarity alone;
the word "all" (sarva) applies simultaneously to all things that are similar.
Nevertheless, because of the attainment [of the result], because of the singular number,
and especially because the capacity for understanding resides in similarity, there would indeed be comprehension of the intended meaning.
And this word "that" clearly indicates that it is of such a nature;
if [it is argued] it is by way of genus (*jāti*), how could it apply to those [individuals]? If [it is argued] it applies to them, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).
In the same way, the cognition of an individual is vitiated by the absence of individuality;
if that [individuality] exists, there would likewise be an infinite regress regarding its specific qualities.
If it is asked how even the nature of the universal (svarūpatva) is known as something recurring, [we reply:

if it were to extend to the limit of a single conceptual derivation, it would be vitiated by faults such as infinite regress; therefore, because of the excessive complexity of such a hypothesis (kalpanāgaurava), the postulation of a recurring entity is not tenable.
Is that same entity then something else when qualified by adventitious attributes?
If it is the very same thing, then what is said regarding its "fire-possessing" nature?
If it were merely contact with fire, that would be proving what is already established;
for if there is contact with fire in a mountain, what else could the genitive case signify? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.2.127)
If it is the inherence [of the universal], then because that is one, you are merely proving what is already established.
If its distinction is due to limiting conditions (upādhi), how can its oneness be maintained? || 2.2.128 ||

For it is not held that the two [states] are indescribable; otherwise, since they would be real by virtue of being adventitious, what distinction would there be? How else could one be a proponent of Māyā? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.129)
If that [universal] were produced by adjuncts (upādhi) and cognized through them, it would be adventitious (aupādhika).
In both cases, there would be infinite inherent relations (samavāya) here and there;
since distinctness exists in all of them, what distinction is there for that which is apprehended by adjuncts?
Since another [entity], namely inherence (*samavāya*), is not actually present,
let there not be an inference that makes it known by means of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
In the same way, the production of a non-existent thing through the inherence of existence is considered [impossible];
for even in that case, there is no remedy whatsoever for the faults already mentioned.
In our view, since a particularity (viśeṣa) is admitted everywhere, there is no fault; for in some cases it is indeed existence, and in others it is non-existence.

The properties of non-existence would be existences, and all those [properties] belong to them; since all this is established by the means of perception, it is not possible to refute it. Therefore, at all times, all things—both existences and non-existences—are real entities. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.134)
Nevertheless, that which is first the object of a cognition of negation is non-existence;
but that which is first the object of a positive cognition is the other [existence].
Therefore, that which has its distinctions and so forth destroyed is understood simply as "existent":
there exists non-existence, there exists destruction, and the non-existence of the body is the state of ashes.
All this is consistent with direct perception and other means of valid cognition;
likewise, mutual non-existence, difference, and distinctness are each established individually.
Whatever they conceptualize, that too has vanished due to the weight of conceptualization;
for all those words are indeed known as synonyms.
But as for those who claim that difference is the very nature of things and thus assert emptiness,
they are truly marvelous, since it is accepted that one thing must serve as the counter-correlative of another.
For this distinction belongs to the counter-correlate and not to itself in any way;
through such division there would be merely a reduction in size, so how could there be emptiness?
For the existence of a real entity is not admitted to arise from the conjunction of empty things;
moreover, the verbal root *dhā* signifies the sense of splitting and denotes the quality of division.
For even though his mouth was not split apart, his lips were split;
therefore, because it is the speech of a madman, the doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda) is to be disregarded.
Nor is the Lord— whose ocean of infinite qualities flows with an unceasing stream of constant bliss—
to be measured by means of the eightfold attributes, because He is beyond being so measured.
In me, who am infinite, possessing infinite qualities and infinite forms by virtue of those qualities,
there exists a great ocean of knowledge, power, and majesty consisting of infinite attributes.
"Nārāyaṇa is supreme; he is the highest state beyond all sentient beings"—thus is it determined by such Vedic passages and countless other statements.
How indeed can the infinite quality of Viṣṇu be denied,
if even his infinite specific attributes, such as his knowledge and so forth, are excluded?
How can that specific objectivity be enjoined for the sake of omniscience?
For a distinction based on limiting conditions (upādhi) has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, for those who deny that cognition is self-luminous,
how can there be omniscience without the apprehension of one's own cognition?
"One knowledge is that which transcends the universe, while the other is the supreme object of that knowledge;
by means of these two knowledges alone, the Supreme Lord is omniscient. (Manu Smṛti 2.2.149)
If it is argued that this very object is determined by that cognition, then self-luminosity alone would be the case; for cognition is indeed the qualifier here.
If it were known by another cognition, there would indeed be an infinite regress;
therefore, its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) would unavoidably follow as a consequence.
Otherwise, the pervasion that one must be either possessed of happiness or possessed of suffering would not hold;
for the state of being free from suffering and possessing great bliss is declared of the Lord by the Śruti itself.

And that [knowledge] is expressed in such passages as: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, as well as sorrow and the rest, knowing the bliss of Brahman, is free from evil," and so forth. (Manu 2.2.153)

If it is argued that God’s will is such [that He causes suffering] because of the limiting condition (upādhi) of being a sufferer, what answer could one who is intent on disregarding the Vedas possibly give? (Manu 2.154)
Nor could there be a desire for one's own suffering; therefore, this [desire] is prohibited.
Merely by seeing [this], one becomes a denier of the Vedas.

For how could one not infer that even sacrifices and the like are causes of sin because they are joined with violence, if the only limiting condition (*upādhi*) [for their being sinful] were their prohibited nature? (Manu 2.156)
And how would the fact that [others] are not suffering not constitute a qualifying condition for their non-mention?
Everything else is free from suffering, but living beings alone are subject to suffering;
it is for the sake of removing their suffering that this Vedic revelation proceeds. (Manu 2.157)
If the supreme Veda, the very word of the Veda, is the authority, then what need is there for inference—which is like a nipple on the neck—to establish the effect? (Manu 2.158)
If an object perceived through revelation were set aside by inference in the manner previously described, then neither God nor Dharma would exist,
nor their fruit; therefore, in this matter, revelation alone must be the authority.
Since the existence of the Lord is established through inference, the Veda must be a means of valid cognition regarding its nature;
for by that [Veda], the Lord is declared to be complete with all auspicious qualities.
Inference of his lack of bliss would not be a valid means of knowledge, because it contradicts the cognition that apprehends the subject; therefore, mere inference is of no use here.
Because the Supreme Lord possesses eternal desire, because atoms exist eternally,
and because the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and time also exist, the effect would necessarily be produced at all times.
For in their view there is no distinction of time, whereas in our view,
Hari’s desire for this creation and so forth exists at a specific time and is eternal.
Furthermore, all specific divisions of time are always subject to the will of Hari;
for the Śruti itself declares with reverence that "all [time] consists of moments. (Manu 2.2.164)
Even his speech utters the power known as Time;
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in Time being subject to Time.
Because desire is characterized by an inexhaustible variety,
the Lord, as well as place and time, are always inherent within it at all times.

"Those two (the individual soul and the material world) are eternally dependent on the Lord, supported by Him, and subject to Him"—thus the Śruti also declares, specifically regarding Time as designated by itself. (Manu Smṛti 2.2.167)
Therefore, the Lord always desires only that which is created at that specific time;
for that time exists only then, since time is inherent within itself.
For this desire of the Lord arises from his very nature, according to the Vedic revelation;
yet it has been stated previously that even his nature is subject to the will of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, scripture states that they are both eternal and non-eternal, being dependent upon that [Primal Nature].
Due to their form, touch, and other qualities, the atom is non-eternal.
And because the Vedic texts are contradictory, that doctrine is not to be accepted as inferable;
therefore, this consistent synthesis is free from contradiction.
The Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas [hold that] the world is momentary by its own nature, and that it is a collection of atoms produced by time, karma, and causes.
At the time of their origin, those who are joined [to existence] perceive themselves as momentary,
yet they also perceive a constant continuity of these [moments] existing in the form of the five aggregates.
The persistence of formative predispositions, form, consciousness, and perception as suffering in essence is [the nature of existence];
they call the absence of suffering, as well as the continuity of formless cognition, "happiness."
For that liberation arises from a combination [of causes] and not from either one alone; nor does it result from both [acting] independently, since it depends upon their combination.
Therefore, because they would be mutually dependent, a collective entity is not tenable;
for it is through mutual dependence that a person is perceived as a collective.

If it is argued that even though that [proximity] is constant, it is caused by nearness—and thus the cause is merely that which is occupied with the production of the effect—then [we reply]: MAnu 2.177.
But a cause cannot be engaged in specific effects;

therefore, because the self lacks the nature of being a conjoined entity— which is the nature of the cause consisting in the contact between the object and the sense organ— it does not possess even the status of that cognition.
If a cause is held to produce effects characterized by specific differences,
how can there be uniformity among the effects in every respect?
Therefore, since anything whatsoever could be the cause of anything else due to the lack of fixed necessity,
how could that [cause] bring about a specific distinction even for that which is unseen?
Whatever distinction one might establish for anyone at all—
be it the effect or the cause, whatever it may be for whomever it concerns.
Since there is no restrictive factor [to determine this], by what means of knowledge can it be understood that "this alone is the cause" for eternal destruction? (Manu 2.182)
In the case of the statement "this is not produced from that," there too no cause exists;
for destructions and productions are never seen to be eternal.
Stability is perceived through recognition in all things;
it is especially inferred everywhere by means of fruits and the like.
If momentariness were established by existence alone, then it would apply to space as well, since there is no distinction between them.
Since everything exists [in some form], why is it not inferred that there is no distinction?

If space were not existent, how could it ever be understood as having the status of a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) to entities such as humans? Thus, the existence of space is established through its relationship with existing subjects.
For indeed, non-existence is never observed anywhere without those two;
thus, the state of being a counter-correlative to a non-subject is understood in the case of space.
Through the acceptance [of the former] and the rejection [of the latter] regarding all things— both those unseen and those seen—
he who is not insane applies himself even more intensely to virtues.
Since a preceding entity perishes merely through the arising of its successor, it is not logical for anything anywhere to impart a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.189)

Therefore, since [the notion] "this is known by me" and so forth is not to be known, how can there be inference? Having abandoned the oneness residing in experience, one is free from pride; for how could there be any distinction regarding the self and other such things, since experience is like that of a child? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.190)
And how could the subsequent [moment] necessarily possess the preceding latent impression without the cause and the effect being simultaneous? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.191)
Only that which is connected transmits its entire impression (*saṃskāra*) elsewhere; how could something previously unconnected be the cause of an impression in what follows? (2.192)

Without a conjunction [of causes] occurring at the same time, how could the persistence of all things for even a single moment be admitted on the basis of their own latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*)? (2.193)
A moment (kṣaṇa) is held to be devoid of prior, middle, and subsequent parts. Does the effect arise from the existence of that [moment], or from its destruction? (2.194)

If destruction were simultaneous with production, then all things to be produced would arise at once; if it occurs later, then that [destruction] would not be the effect, and what proof is there for the arising of an effect?
In the case of the body, a lamp, a fruit, and so forth, the perception of their specific differences is logical for us, based on our direct experience, despite their lack of essential difference.
If the perception of a specific quality were the means of valid cognition, how could there be a perception of stability?
Furthermore, by the example of space regarding the pleasure of direction, if existence were real, it would have to exist somewhere.
He who, having abandoned the universe as perceived by direct observation, would speak of it as being merely inferred,
should be shunned like a proponent of illusion (māyāvādin) by one who desires prosperity.
How can that which is always established by all means of valid cognition as distinct from the intellect be the intellect itself? And what else could the entire universe possibly be measured against?
Since the entire world is constantly afraid of this direct experience,
why would one who denies it— not being a proponent of a position devoid of valid means of knowledge— not be feared?
Thus, these very experiences— such as "I am happy," "the sky always exists," and "the directions exist"—
are always directed toward the antidotes for that [false view].
Therefore, who indeed—save for a host of demons—would ever embrace such a wicked doctrine, which is devoid of pride and serves as an antidote to all means of valid cognition? (Manu 2.202)
Another [teacher] says that everything is empty, beyond the reach of mind and speech,
devoid of distinctions, self-luminous, untainted, and free from old age and death.
"Free from all defects, infinite in space and time,
and in its true essence— that [Self] am I. By making this constant meditation directly manifest, one leads the yogi to that state which is free from defects such as passion and the like.
Through that very beginningless conventional reality, the world, consisting of various diverse forms, appears as if real; its reality is held to be merely conventional.
But ultimate existence belongs nowhere to anything other than emptiness;
all worldly discourse occurs solely by means of conventional truth.

"From the void, through the application of conventional reality, this entire universe proceeds; then, at the time of creation and again at the end, it becomes still and returns to the void. Addressing him, the Teacher of the Worlds said: MAnu 2.207: "The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) spoke thus regarding that [void]: 'In the beginning, this world was indeed non-existent; from that, the Existent was produced. It was enveloped by the void; therefore, people say, "In the beginning, this world was non-existent. Then, having seen it, he strove for its production; from that, the Great Principle (Mahat) arose, and from the Great Principle, the Ego-sense (Ahaṃkāra). MAnu 2.208: "From the Ego-sense, the five great elements were produced in succession. Because they are composed of those [elements], these bodies are called *tanmātra* (composed of the subtle elements). MAnu 2.209: "The earth, water, fire, air, and space—these are the five great elements. From these alone, the worlds arise, and into these, they dissolve again. MAnu 2.210: "The earth, water, fire, air, and space—among these, each subsequent element acquires the quality of the preceding one. MAnu 2.211: "Thus, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these are known as the five qualities of the elements, each following in order after the preceding one. MAnu 2.212: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these five qualities belong to the elements; they are perceived by the five senses in their respective order. MAnu 2.213: "The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose—these are the five sense organs, which perceive sound and the other objects in their respective order. MAnu 2.214: "Speech, hands, feet, the organs of excretion and generation—these five are the organs of action, which perform various functions. MAnu 2.215: "Mind, intellect, ego-sense, and the heart—these four are the internal faculties, which perceive the objects of the senses. MAnu 2.216: "The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose—these five are the organs of perception; they are called *buddhīndriya* (organs of cognition) because they are instruments of cognition. There is no coming into being of a non-existent world, for the birth of the non-existent has never been observed;
as for the existent, there is no means of knowledge [for its production], and direct perception alone is superior to everything else.
If this were so, then from the seventh taste, sweetness,
there would arise corpulence for people, just as a cat's claw is fatal to a cow.

One who seeks an effect would never, under any circumstances, take up a real cause; nor would one engage in activity for the sake of what is desired, because that which is desired cannot arise from what is empty.
The restriction of place, time, and so forth would arise here from that which is empty;
for if anything were produced in accordance with human desire, [such restrictions would not exist].

Why is it not inferred that everything likewise arises from the Puruṣa because of its being a real entity? Furthermore, there is no non-existence [of anything], for the entire universe is understood to be existent.
Since perception is obstructed, from where could there be any speech for the proponent?
This [world] is perceived merely through conventional reality, just like a dream or an illusion.
If, because of existence, no delusion whatsoever were to cease here; or if the cessation of this beginningless universe is desired,
then that cessation itself would have to cease, since it is possible for it to be a delusion.
If that which is seen were an illusion, how could there be no delusion regarding that which is unseen?
For the horns of a hare do not become horned simply because cows possess horns.
But for us, everything is consistent by virtue of the means of valid cognition, the grace of the Lord, and the authority of the scriptures as expressed through the stated method of interpretation.

If it is argued that this [world] is false because it is perceptible, like a dream, then if it were false, the probandum would not be established; yet if it were not false, there would be no deviation [in the reason]. MĀnuv 2.217.

The probandum is the capacity to prove that which is unreal, because there is disagreement on this point; and if that [capacity] were also to require proof, there would be an infinite regress. Furthermore, its existence is established through direct experience.
If falsity were established by contradiction with experience, let there be no [such contradiction];
for even the past and future times are within the range of our witness-consciousness,
and the existence of the perceived object as related to those times is likewise known through the witness.
That which is seen with firm conviction is [true] perception; anything other than that is a semblance of perception.

This distinction between error and conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) is characterized by non-deviation, and it has been correctly accepted even by him; for us, that indeed constitutes truth. (Manu 2.220)
If one were to say that this [cognition] might sometimes deviate from consciousness, then that would not be valid knowledge;
nor can it be valid knowledge, because it would contradict itself. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.2.221)

If it is argued that difference depends upon the perception of the qualified object, its attributes, and so forth, then because of the resulting circularity, it would be difficult to grasp; yet this is not the case.
The nature of a thing is its difference; for as long as that [nature] is not apprehended, there is no apprehension of it.
Otherwise, it would not be appropriate to say, "This is different from that."
When difference is not apprehended, then there would be the apprehension [of the object] as being "from itself";
however, this is contradicted by experience, for no one would speak in such a manner.

If the state of being the subject (dharmitva), the state of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitva), and their mutual difference were apprehended simultaneously, then the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation would likewise be grasped at once.
What contradiction is there? For it is precisely difference that, having been apprehended in its own nature, is then apprehended specifically as "this is distinct from that."
Furthermore, as for the one who asks how difference can be apprehended,
he has stated a circular argument, because the apprehension of difference depends upon the apprehension of the substratum and so forth.
If difference is not apprehended, how can there be mutual dependence?
If difference were already established, how could there be mutual dependence? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.228)
Both the Māyī and the Mādhyamika are speakers of such things and are mines of fallacious rejoinders; therefore, they should be avoided by those who desire their own welfare.
That which is the Void for the proponents of emptiness is precisely Brahman for the proponents of Māyā;
for there is no difference in their defining characteristics, because both are devoid of distinctions.
The characteristic of both [truth and untruth] is their opposition to falsehood and so forth;
since the opponent has no need for his own statement, there is no requirement for him to provide a corroborating statement.

"In that position," [the Creator] refuted [the theory] through dissimilarity (vaidharmya), stating "not like dreams and so forth," and by saying "unborn" and "without effort," he indicated its contradiction with perception and its lack of valid proof (*apramāṇatva*). (Manu 2.232)
Cognition alone shines forth as the single form of all objects of knowledge;
therein, the distinctions of continuity, its own internal differences,
and the distinctions [between objects] appear as conceptual constructs upon the various planes of conventional reality.
This too is not tenable for us; for the world does not appear as consciousness, because that would contradict experience itself and is therefore untenable.

Because cognition is momentary while the object of knowledge is of a stable nature according to the aforementioned method, and because these positions contradict all the scriptures as well as direct experience, they are inauspicious.
The Kṣapaṇaka said: "The universe is both existent and non-existent, dual and non-dual;
all this is both dual and non-dual, eternally characterized by the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī)."
This is not tenable for a single entity, because it contradicts perception;
for by what rule can it be prevented that the very form in which the universe is cognized as both being and non-being is indeed its true nature?
If one whose vision is wavering becomes tainted by all those very faults for which he has adopted various [observances] as his own essence, then [those observances are futile]. (Manu 2.238)
Having disregarded the rule established by authoritative means regarding existence and non-existence—
[a rule that is] entirely consistent and always free from pride— it is rendered utterly contradictory.
For one who speaks in every possible way, there indeed arise all such faults as the abandonment of what has been seen, the failure to grasp [the truth], and self-contradiction. (Manu 2.240)
He speaks of himself as his own radiance, yet even that [self] which is measured by the body is subject to corruption,
because it enters into various bodies and undergoes transformation.
It is an established principle that whatever entity undergoes change is impermanent;
according to that view, the impermanence of the person (pudgala) is unavoidable.

In our view, however, impermanence does not apply to consciousness and other such defining attributes; for if those defining characteristics were to cease, that [impermanence] would never exist in the conscious principle.
However, impermanence would occur only upon the cessation of such characteristics as being composed of warp and woof in a cloth, or the arrangement of limbs in the body. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.244)
In our view, it is only material form and the like that are pervaded by destruction;
for that which undergoes transformation is not what we describe as impermanent.
Likewise, for one who possesses form and so forth, in order to establish that the world is subject to destruction,
the self would be impermanent because of its transformation, due to that pervasion.
Even this liberation, which is described as an eternal upward movement,
how could it not be a transformation for one who has reached the non-worldly space (alokākāśa)?
And what kind of alteration is intended as the cause of destruction?
If it is the departure of the [original] configuration, that is certainly not the case in the instance of the earth, the ocean, and so forth.

If any kind of transformation were liberation, and if that were the case, then there would be a modification of the body itself; thus, those who maintain the permanence [of the self] are not truly understanding the non-self.
He said: "Indeed, there may be a change of state even in bodies such as those of elephants;
for what specific quality does the soul possess, which undergoes transformation upon becoming an elephant so as to pervade that body, yet lacks it in the body of an immobile being? (Manu 2.250)

"From its song comes the acquisition of flowers and fruit; from touch, emaciation; from its sap, stability—even in the case of a tree these are observed. Thus, there would be a plurality of selves; and for this very reason, the knower of the Veda has declared that the self is not all-pervading. (Manu Smṛti 2.251)
[Sadāśiva] is endowed with all qualities such as omniscience and the like;
he is the creator of the manifold arrangement of the universe and is free from all defects.
The Pāśupatas say that this [practice] is also not to be accepted because it contradicts the many Śrutis; for this is the doctrine of this god who dwells in a pit—praise him! (Manu 2.253)
He crushed his head; I praise the Lord of Beings, the Foot, so that Rudra, drawn by me, may strike down him who seeks to harm Viṣṇu’s supreme [abode].
"Whomever I desire with my bow, O fierce ones, let him not [escape], O you whose deity is the phallus!
Having slain those whose deity is the phallus, he alone remained—that supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, Rudra and Samprasāda both performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
by means of the sacrifice, they sacrificed the sacrifice, binding Puruṣa as the victim.
"Rudra, the lord of beings, the bull who moves within the threads"—
by the power of such scriptural passages as these, [it is established that] birth and death involve dependence on another.
Dependence on others, attainment of what belongs to another, ignorance, and non-existence at the time of dissolution—these are perceived as defects; therefore, Paśupati is not the Lord (Īśa).
Since he is bodiless, no connection with the world can ever be established for him through agency; this is because [agency] is seen to belong only to one who possesses a body and knowledge.
Nor can the universe belong to him in the same way as his body and so forth, because enjoyment is impossible [in that case].
An agent is perceived as performing an action while remaining situated within a substratum;
however, at the time of the dissolution of the elements, he has no connection with such a substratum.
If he were bodiless, he would be eternally non-omniscient, like stone or wood;
if he were embodied, he would necessarily be subject to an end, as illustrated by the example of Yajñadatta.
And all this does not apply to Viṣṇu, due to the weight of the authority of the Śruti;
for we perceive that Viṣṇu alone is he who is characterized by mind and intellect.
That very body is consciousness, sovereignty, and exalted power;
O Viṣṇu, that body of yours, O Viṣṇu, did not appear before you as Vāsudeva.
In the beginning, there was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara.
Beyond him, another [principle] was placed within the navel of the Unborn by means of a measure.
He whose body is truth, whose fragrance is happiness, whose light is knowledge, and whose prowess is real;
he who is the knowledge of knowledge and the bliss of bliss—he is Viṣṇu, the supreme imperishable.
In the beginning, O Ānanda, there was only the one Lord Nārāyaṇa;
Priya was the head of that Hari, and Modas and Pramoda were his two arms.
Ānanda was from the middle; Brahmā was the tail, and nothing else existed anywhere.
From his mind Brahmā arose, and from his forehead Śaṅkara.
On his two wings were Garuḍa and Śeṣa; from his mouth issued Sarasvatī;
he was the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
On the strength of such collections of scriptural passages, it is understood that the entire universe manifested from the body of Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of eternal qualities.
What contradiction can possibly be found anywhere for that which possesses authority?
For both non-contradiction and contradiction are indeed understood through authoritative means alone.
Therefore it has been said: "Everything pertaining to Vāsudeva is appropriate;
and the Vedic texts associated with names such as Śiva and others are expressive of Viṣṇu. (Manusmṛti 12.271)
He who alone bears all names as the bearer of the names of the gods—he is Hari himself; Viṣṇu is the one who possesses all names, and no other.

"The names of Nārāyaṇa do not apply to others besides Hari"—such scriptural passages are the authority in this matter, and thus the systematic reconciliation (samanvaya) has been stated. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.273)
The Purāṇas are not authoritative because they contradict the Purāṇas and other [scriptures];
nor are they a means of knowledge regarding things that contradict them, due to internal inconsistencies between earlier and later parts.
Furthermore, because of the contradiction with the equality of Brahman, due to the restrictive rule regarding the Vaiṣṇavas as well,
and because of the statement intended to delude [the ignorant], Viṣṇu alone is the ocean of qualities.
The doctrines of Skanda, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and others have been refuted in their entirety by means of logic,
without exception, in accordance with our established tenets.
When the specific [manifestation] is set aside, the Great Goddess—who possesses power, who is distinct, who utters the syllable *hrīṃ*, and who is the cause of all—is refuted;
she is designated by such names as Tripurā, Bhairavī, and so forth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.277)
That from which Sadāśiva and others, as well as gods and humans, are born— that this [universe] consisting of the elements and their derivatives should also arise from that— is not tenable.
Procreation is always observed from men, or especially from both women and men;
it is certainly not from women alone, because birth from them [without a male] is impossible.
The Mahāvāma doctrine is not to be honored; something else is proclaimed by the Vāmas.
Śakti, with Śiva as her subordinate, created this universe on all sides.
Thus, that [objection] is not valid because Śiva is not an agent;
for others might say that the Lord is omniscient precisely because he is bodiless.

It is not proper for the two [the Veda and the Smṛti] to be mutually contradictory, because they both enter into the doctrine of the Lord (Īśa) as being endowed with qualities such as omniscience through the conception of the Guru.
For it is not logical that there should be only one Lord as the sole motivator;
since the faults already mentioned apply to that position, it is not further refuted here.
Because it contradicts the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas in their entirety, and because it is loathed by the virtuous, that doctrine must certainly not be accepted.
If they cite these [Vedic texts] for the purpose of prohibiting the Pañcarātra, that is highly contradictory, since he (Manu) has stated in the Mahābhārata: [2.285]
Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra;
O Indra among kings, this [system] is superior to all these other systems of knowledge.
But those who know the Pañcarātra, O King, who are devoted to its sequential practice and have attained single-minded devotion, they enter into Vāsudeva.
Thus the Gītā is declared to be a summary of that scripture;
for it has been said that [the goal is attained] through the Veda, the Pañcarātra, devotion, and indeed sacrifice.
"I am visible, not otherwise visible even in hundreds of millions of years"—
this is the statement of Varāha, and the words "iti ślokāḥ" (thus the verses) are heard in the scripture.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme object of meditation according to both the Vedas and the Pañcarātras;
the Pañcarātra and the Vedas are indeed one single knowledge, though they are designated as two.
By such Vedic statements as these, the Pañcarātra is set aside;
for how could there be any fault here, and what is its origin? Thus it is said. (Manu 2.2.291)
What has been stated here is not said again there; rather, it is taught that the individual soul (jīva), bound by beginningless karma, wanders within the circle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
For his statement that [the soul] wanders eternally by the will of Vāsudeva is indeed [untenable];
for nowhere in the Pañcarātra is it taught that the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) has a beginning.
The birth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the presiding deity of the individual soul (jīva), is said to be from Vāsudeva;
and likewise, the birth of Pradyumna is said to be from him.

For one who takes pride in the mind, how can the manifestation (vyūha) of Hari himself— which occurs in some instances under names such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others, and which possesses eternal, inconceivable, and vast power— be declared wicked by first describing it otherwise? Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.2.295.
Just as one might say, "If he should know the four Vedas," there is a completion of the Vedic requirement;
why then is there such hatred toward the *Pañcarātra* in the conduct of Śāṇḍilya?
Therefore, the refutation of the Pañcarātra raised by the Asuras out of hatred for the Supreme Teacher is not even worthy of consideration.
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa— the sustainer of the entire world without exception, a faultless ocean of vast virtues—
is determined through the intended meaning of the collection of Vedas.
"Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance; into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, they enter who do not merely despise it. (Manu Smṛti 2.2.299)
Then, he who understands both knowledge and ignorance together,
having transcended these through the knowledge of their defects, attains immortality by means of knowledge.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

Then the Lord, intending to dispel all contradictions with the entirety of the sacred tradition (samāmnāya) regarding the divine, the elemental, the individual soul, and the supreme Self, [proceeded].
With this chapter, the one of immeasurable luster demonstrates the absence of contradiction among the various statements for the purpose of determining their true nature.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with experience, reason, and many scriptural statements;
moreover, all this would result in the equality of the existent and the uselessness of the means [to liberation]. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.3)
It follows established views and reasoning, does not contradict other meanings, accepts well-known names, and conforms to many scriptural statements. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.4)
Conformity with worldly views, equality with living beings, beginninglessness,
thorough knowledge of each respective stage, and likewise the scriptural teachings on the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas).

The state of having an origin, the non-experience of one's own qualities, the assumption of a limited [intellect], the existence of various Vedic texts, and diversity— these are the arguments belonging to the prima facie position.
The impossibility of a fixed rule, independence, conformity, primacy, possession of power, diversity, and universal inclusion [are the characteristics of the Veda]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.7)

The movement [of the soul], the power of the Lord, the non-contradiction with all means of valid cognition, the clear establishment of the fulfillment of desires, the reversal of what is established by scripture,
and the specific cause— these are the proofs for the very tenet [of the Self].

"Primordial Matter (prakṛti), the Person (puruṣa), Time (kāla), the gods who preside over them, and [the principles] beginning with the Great One (mahat) are born, characterized by dependence on another. He creates all this"—thus is the state of being subject to birth declared here. (Manu 1.3.9)"
Space is merely the absence of obstruction; otherwise, how could it arise?
If there were no space previously, what was this world made of—was it a dense mass of material form?
Furthermore, if there were no space, there would be a state of total material density;
for corporeal substances indeed always abide within space.
Therefore, the deity of that [element], Vināyaka, who is denoted by the word "space," is declared by the Śruti to have been born together with the birth of the body.
Even though it is real, that which is unseen is indeed within the range of divine vision;
for the unmanifest space arises as an object of perception for the witness.
It should be understood as a "region," for that [space] is eternal and does not arise.

Nevertheless, that which is endowed with specific qualities dependent upon prior relations is what the Vedic term "originating" intends to express, even though it is [in its ultimate nature] merely space.
Primordial matter, the person, and time—
all these together are proclaimed to be produced through their specific dependence upon the Lord.
Time alone is the one eternal reality, and it possesses no specific distinctions;
it is the single *rāmā* (delight) that presides over the Puruṣa, the Unmanifest, and Time itself.
Having attained that specific state of desiring to create through the direct will of the Blessed Lord,
it is called "creation" even though it is the primary matter (pradhāna) which is itself subject to transformation.
"Men are said to be subject to creation because of their connection with the body; likewise, even at the time of dissolution, he whose higher and lower nature is manifest remains so."

The primary vital air (mukhyaprāṇa) is eternally uniform because it is the cause of the body's production; it is designated as "born" only by virtue of its particular states dependent on other factors.

Nothing whatsoever exists that is not born from that Supreme, except for the state of being devoid of birth; for if birth were dependent on something else, there would be the consequence of grossness.
If the word "birth" (janman) is used while omitting the preceding word [“of”], then for Lakṣmī there is no birth at all, nor indeed for pure consciousness alone. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.3.21)
And for the primary Veda, as well as for each individual Veda, there exists a specific manifestation by the will of the Lord; therefore, it is indeed dependent upon that [will].
In this context, the arising [of the universe] is described because the Supreme Self is independent;
there is no arising whatsoever for that which is other than Him, for it is not independent.
Having divided even the indivisible soul in many ways and granted it various enjoyments, Hari causes it to attain unity once again.
Therefore, when Keśava brings the entire world— both sentient and insentient— which is under his control, from a state of non-distinction into distinction,
what indeed is impossible for the Supreme Lord? Thus it is said.
Even though this is so, some maintain that the individual soul is one with the Supreme Self,
on the basis of such Vedic texts as "He who is I am He," and by the strength of inference.
That is not correct, because Viṣṇu is indeed declared to be distinct;
for in the state of liberation, difference is declared in such passages as "He whose eye is wisdom, he who is light," "This bliss," and "The supreme equality. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.27)
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained a state of similarity with me;
they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution.
Having attained that light, he reaches its true nature;
there he moves about, laughing and playing, ever happy.
"Tell me that liberation which the wise proclaim,"—
when thus addressed, the Goddess of Speech spoke to Prajāpati concerning the supreme liberation.
The great rivers flow around, branching out from branch to branch;
they carry parched grain and cakes, are filled with meat, and are always muddy with milk-rice.
That imperishable syllable which the gods, headed by Agni, together with Indra and the hosts of Maruts, worshipped with the most excellent sacrifices— they worship that.
Having been liberated, those who enjoy worldly pleasures enter the Supreme God and remain right there; yet, impelled by the Supreme Lord Himself, they emerge again at their will.
Due to the perception of duality and the conceit of agency— even through action performed without attachment— one regards Brahman as possessing qualities, as a person, and as the Bull among Men.
Having united again in due time with the form of the Lord,
when the intermixture of the qualities has ceased, he is born once more just as before.
One sits nourishing the Ṛg-verses, always impelled by the Supreme;
whatever he desires, that he creates truly, and he creates that even by his own self.
Having transcended those qualities, he enjoys his desires together with Brahman;
having abandoned suffering and the like, he is exempt from the activities of the world.
"He enjoys exalted pleasures together [with them]," according to such scriptural authority;
for since the liberated one is understood to possess distinction, how indeed can there be non-difference? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.38)
Nor can inference establish the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord.
If it is argued: "The difference under dispute is false, because it is a difference, like the difference in the appearance of the moon," [we reply:
this property to be proven (the predicate) must be either existent, non-existent, both, or neither. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.39)

If it is argued that what is existent is an "unestablished conclusion" (apasiddhānta), while that which is non-existent is precisely that [same thing], and if neither is the case, then it is not established; this is the refutation of the means of valid cognition (māna).
And this cannot be established anywhere by another means of knowledge;
if it were by inference, then indeed that same infinite regress would occur.
There is no scriptural authority for that meaning, nor would [the scripture] say "it was non-existent";
therefore, by process of elimination, if it were to be established, the Supreme Self must be inexpressible.
For in that case, only inexpressibility remains as the residue;
there is no other means of knowledge for that which is the counter-correlate of both existence and non-existence.

There is no direct perception [of such a thing], nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) accepted [as proof], because it is impossible for that which exists to be sublated; indeed, it is precisely because there is no sublation [that it is established].
How can an object be sublated? For it is that which exists which is sublated;
indeed, the son of a barren woman cannot be killed—it is Yajñadatta who is killed.
Where is this pervasion—that "what exists is subject to sublation"—observed? And what is this "sublation" that has been designated; for there can be no destruction of what is non-existent.
Furthermore, how could the cessation of that which has never come into being be possible?
If the knowability [of an object] consists in the cognition that "it did not exist, it exists,
and it will exist," then its non-existence is once again admitted by that very same [cognition], should there be a sublation.
By saying that there is no cognition of what is non-existent, he does not deny that [cognition];
for the negation of something uncognized is in no way possible.
Nor can there be a comparison here, for its existence is established by direct perception;
moreover, the distinction of one's own self from the Supreme Lord, who is accessible through scripture, is clearly perceived.
How can oneness be asserted in contradiction to experience? For it is experienced by everyone that [the self] is both an agent of some action and a sufferer. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.50)
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is heard of as omniscient and omnipotent;
for this scripture speaks of Him as distinct from what has been experienced.

But how could the Śruti declare identity, which contradicts what it itself provides as a basis for livelihood, when the authority of that which expresses difference will have been established? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.3.52)

If that very [cognition] is the apprehender of the substratum (dharmin), how could there be no distinction from it? Why should that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the essential nature [of the substratum] not also be so for its property (*dharma*)?
Through the cognition and representation of a single [object], both would become non-measures;
if that one were not a measure, then neither of those two would exist here.
Therefore, the contradiction with the cognition that apprehends the substratum is a defect of that means of knowledge;
for here, non-difference is not to be accepted as something to be relied upon, since in some cases difference is established by the force of scriptural revelation.
And Brahman is never an object to be attained by another means of knowledge;
for whatever means of knowledge it were attainable by, difference would be understood through that very means.
If the Lord is somehow to be accepted as consisting of all-knowledge,
then His distinction [from others] is understood precisely through that quality of omniscience.
Nowhere does the experience of suffering ever become a false experience;
for indeed, no sublation of the experience of suffering and so forth is ever observed.
If it is determined that the experience of suffering is an illusion,
then by what means is it not understood that the scriptural teaching on the absence of suffering is likewise an illusion?
The nature of the Veda and its meaning are determined by means of valid cognition alone;
if that means of cognition has been grasped by you, why this delusion regarding the experience of suffering?
And there is no specific criterion for sublation such that only that which remains unsublated is [valid];
for if sublation occurs regarding an experienced object, how can a definitive conclusion be reached?
For no matter can be determined by one who speaks out of delusion;
since both delusion and non-delusion are established through experience, if one person is mistaken therein, how can the other be free from error? (Manu Smṛti 2.3.62)
For all that is to be known—whether it be error or non-error—is indeed witnessed by the Witness (Sākṣin).
If that Witness were to be subject to defect anywhere, how could a definitive conclusion be reached? (MDh 8.63)
All these specific details fall within the scope of the evidence of witnesses;
and having accepted all of them, legal procedure proceeds. Legal procedure is defined as that which is determined by witnesses.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing all well-known worldly transactions,
we must always accept one witness who is indeed free from defects.
When the pure witness is established, how can suffering be prevented? For that very means of valid cognition upon which one depends is precisely what apprehends difference.
Therefore, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is firmly established by the power of the Śruti.
Nevertheless, qualities such as consciousness and bliss, which are similar to that [Brahman],
remain as its essential nature even in liberation.
Therefore, these scriptural texts indeed proclaim [the identity] as if there were no difference;
and the Puranic statements do so by resorting to non-difference through similarity.

They say that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with the Lord (īśa) is due to similarity, preeminence, and independence; never, however, do they speak of an identity of essential nature (svarūpa).
For one who is liberated, there is identity of place and unity of mind, which is indeed superior;

however, for insentient things, there is only similarity and specifically the two [identity of place and unity of mind]. With the Supreme Self, there is only the third, which is a very slight similarity.
Likewise, for the forms, actions, and qualities of the Lord,
as well as for his limbs, identity with his essential nature is primary in every respect.
"Just as water rained upon a mountain precipice flows away in different directions,
so too one who perceives phenomena as distinct runs after those very things.
According to this scriptural teaching, neither of the two— namely, difference nor non-difference— is accepted.
One alone is without a second; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death.
"Thus, from the phrase 'as if heard,' there is the rejection of both difference and non-difference;
and in the determination of the word *iva*, it is taught that both [words] signify similarity. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.74)
The refutation of that position follows from the statement regarding liberation as a state of distinction;
for if non-difference is intended to mean a similarity in qualities such as consciousness, we have already accepted that, but never the identity of essential nature. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.75)

There is no non-difference with anything whatsoever, nor is there difference-and-non-difference anywhere, except for Viṣṇu’s aggregate [of attributes], or even apart from his own qualities and so forth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.3.76)
Thus, according to scripture, there is no distinction or non-distinction of it by anyone;
for the scriptural statements regarding non-distinction are due to its being a part, and its similarity is indeed its state of being a part.
A portion (aṃśa) should be known to be of two kinds: that which is identical in nature (svarūpāṃśa) and that which is distinct (anya).
A distinct portion would possess limited power and be endowed with only a slight degree of similarity.
One [of these] is the sun, possessing the conceit of being its own light;
then there is Sūrya, and the lord of the waters of the outer ocean beyond the seven seas.
By virtue of its solidity, even Mount Meru and the earth itself have the goddess Dharā as their deity;
in this very same way, the one imperishable Lord Viṣṇu,
possessed of perfect qualities, eternally exists in various forms of incarnation.

Just as those who are conceited about their excrement, urine, eyes, and so forth are fallen deities distinct from the sun and other celestial bodies, even so is this transmigrating being distinct from the Supreme Self.
Because they are corrupted by bodily defects, these deities— known as *apabhraṣṭa* (corrupted)—
are distinct from the gods such as the Sun and are always to be favored by them.
In this very way, individual transmigrating beings are considered distinct from Viṣṇu;
