they are to be favored by Him alone, and through His grace, they become liberated.
But it is not intended that forms such as fish and so forth are objects of grace;
for, because he is complete with all qualities, there is no difference between him and the others in their primary sense.
And all these are merely partial appearances of the Supreme; they are not His parts in the primary sense.
Just as this shadow exists in a man, so is that [universe] spread out within Him.
"But these individual souls are not like the feet of a person;
rather, they are the full qualities of that Supreme Self existing in the form of manifestations.
Thus spoke the supreme Śruti to Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord Viṣṇu is inexhaustible, the abode of Lakṣmī, and established in dissolution;
he is eternally meditated upon by the liberated ones, beginning with Brahmā, who exist within the gradations of being.

Nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), time (kāla), and the Vedas—this fourfold set is eternal by its very nature; yet, because it merely attains specific manifestations from Viṣṇu, it is said to have an origin. Lakṣmī is the one who presides over that [nature]. (Manu 1.89)
Then, from this [Prakṛti], the male named Brahmā was born from Vāsudeva;
he is the Sūtrātman and is also called Prāṇa, while the two goddesses are those who assume the form of Prakṛti.
From that [Brahmā] was born Rūpa, the great ego (ahaṅkṛti) of Brahmā, who is Śiva;
from Brahmā, named Buddhi, was born Nāma; from him was born Indra, called Manas; and from him Skanda and all the other gods were born.
Among them, each preceding one is superior in all qualities taken together;
and Lord Viṣṇu is superior even to them, for they are always dependent upon him.
Birth, maintenance, dissolution, ignorance, destiny, knowledge, worldly existence, and liberation—all these remain entirely dependent upon Him; their subordination to Him is never lost.

"Even in liberation, He alone is independent and possessed of perfect, auspicious qualities"—this has been declared by the Lord in this chapter through both scripture and reasoning. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.3.94)
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Where the meaning of a Vedic text appears to be contradicted by either the Veda itself or by reason, the Lord settles that matter through highly distinguished arguments; in such a case,
the Vedic text is considered to have a clear meaning [only when confirmed] by this quarter-verse.
Discrepancy with specific scriptural injunctions, greatness, manifestation of true qualities, perceived irrationality, equality, the capacity of the agent, and mixture. (Manu 2.4.2)
The arguments presented in the prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣa) are well-established;
however, such arguments as those for the final conclusion were themselves proclaimed by the Blessed One.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Intrinsic nature, alteration, non-existence, existence, and what has been otherwise stated;
non-distinction, distinction, coexistence, and mixture. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.1.1)

Contradictory statement, coexistence, futility, and inconsistency—these are the logical arguments for the prima facie position, which serve the purpose of demonstrating the superiority of [the author's] own qualities. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.1.2)

Occurrence, twofold nature, superiority, conformity, fitness, predominance, distinction, absence of cause, postulation, and lack of another alternative— these are the means of establishing a philosophical tenet (siddhānta). MAnu 3.1.3.
The Blessed One, by means of the word "atha" (now), has declared the abandonment of the restrictive rules regarding the union of seed, person, and womb, as well as the cause thereof.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Subsequent non-perception, the time of consciousness, suffering, distinctness, difference of location, contradiction, parity of reasoning, and arising from itself. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.1)
The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), disjunction, sublation by reasoning,
contrariety, manifoldness, and enticement— these belong to the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
The incapacity for agency, powerlessness, innate ignorance, as well as the non-creation of means of knowledge, the establishment of false authority, extreme meanness, and non-existence; Mānu 3.2.3.
And in the statement regarding inference from specific observation (*viśeṣadṛṣṭi*), the power of the person (*puṃśakti*) is a clear illustration;
[the characteristics of such a person are] transcendence of the worldly (*alaukikatva*), excellence (*ādhikya*), autonomy (*svātantrya*), and the certainty of valid cognition (*nirṇayapramā*).
The latent impressions (vāsanās) of all things, acquired through beginningless experience,
truly exist within the minds of all living beings, abiding there from time immemorial.
The mind, consisting of the three qualities, exists indeed as long as liberation lasts, persisting eternally;
it is therein that all latent impressions (saṃskāras) are always accumulated.
At the time of dissolution, it exists as subtle and is augmented by primordial material nature;
at the time of creation, when that [nature] is not present, how could there be the establishment of the cycle of existence?
Having created the manifold world through formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the Blessed One himself manifests it during the state of dreaming; for the waking state is indeed nothing but an illusion.
When an entity has not been seen or heard, no such entity arises;
from an entity that has not been seen or heard, no entity arises.
Thus, the statement found in the Śrutis and Purāṇas is appropriate because [the Veda] is beginningless; for even that which is at times unfit for perception exists there in its divided form.
That which is seen as having a common substratum is indeed perceived, yet it is an illusion;
because its root is merely latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it lacks the clarity found in waking perception. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.11)
The question of whether there is difference, non-difference, or a pair [of both] is not tenable, because for all people, the dreamer is seen as distinct from the dream. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.12)
For there are four defects of a question: self-contradiction, incoherence, tautology, and futility; by means of these, the determination of truth cannot be achieved. (Manu 3.2.13)

For even in a formal debate (*vāda*), defeat consists in contradicting the determination of reality; it must indeed be pointed out [by the opponent], otherwise the conclusion of the discussion would not occur. (MAnu 3.2.14)
In a debate between those seeking victory, however, the grounds for ending the discussion are as follows:
even when there is an avoidance [of the point], the fact that [the opponent's position] is already established constitutes a refutation for the respondent;
for in the case of a thesis, it is precisely the establishment of something other than that which serves as the proof.

The fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the unestablished substratum (*vyāśrayāsiddhi*), as well as the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*), are for some [logicians] defects; yet these are not defects at all when pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists.
There is indeed a logical contradiction in proving the existence of a human horn;
but where there is no such contradiction, what excessive attachment could there be in proving it?

For all principles of reasoning (nyāya) are indeed rooted in perception and scripture; those that lack such roots are fallacies of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa). Furthermore, these two [perception and scripture] are themselves the root of any other reasoning.
When no deviation has been observed, it is clear that this [reason] is a prover;
it is known by the witness alone, provided there is no sublation by a means of valid cognition. Otherwise, it would not be so. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.19)
Since the validity of means of knowledge is determined by the witness alone,
whereas the validity of that which is not a means of knowledge would be unstable due to its lack of being a means of knowledge.
Even that which is obtained by way of a general rule (*utsarga*), provided it is free from exceptions (*apavāda*),
shall indeed be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) unless it is contradicted by an exception.
For this reason, the inference that food and other such things are means to achieve a desired end is always the authority for worldly conduct; however, there is indeed deviation in that regard.

If there is pervasion, how indeed can being the locus of that pervasion be a fault? For when it is said, "The rising of Rohiṇī is imminent because Kṛttikā has risen," is this not a valid proof? Indeed, in this case, it is not merely a command that establishes the point.
Furthermore, the claim that "the universe is other than being and non-being" is a contradiction;
if there were a pervasion (vyāpti) [between these terms], what fault would there be in proving what is already established? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.24)
And in that case, pervasion is understood through negative concomitance (vyatireka) by those very [means].
When it is maintained that the probans (liṅga) serves as the means of proving a probandum (sādhya) that is not yet established,
by what means of knowledge is this specific distinction in the statement of the probans understood?
When a proof for something unestablished, such as an atom, is sought, why then must this [proof] not be accepted exactly according to experience? (MĀnuv 3.2.26)
Where there is no over-extension and where the means of knowledge do not fail,
it is extremely difficult to assert that what is to be established here is accomplished by afflicted conceptualization alone.
Mutual dependence, circularity, self-dependence, and so forth—
these must be accepted by all as means of establishing what is unestablished, even without the five-membered syllogism. What, then, is the basis for that restriction?
And if there were proof of what is already established, the discussion would never reach its conclusion;
moreover, deviation and the unestablished nature of the reason are defects even when they pertain to only one side.
If a qualification is added to the example, there is a deficiency of either the probandum or the probans;
furthermore, such a qualification is useless if one [of the two] is unestablished, for it results in the very non-establishment of the qualified [reason].

The fault regarding the first question is its lack of purpose; that which consists of questions about established facts and the like would fall into the category of redundancy at the end. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.31)
In some cases, presumption, analogy, and non-existence are included within inference;
and non-existence is included within perception, as is the case with pleasure and the like by necessity.

Elsewhere, all logical arguments—such as those concerning the beginning [of creation], those based on "suddenness" (*khaḍiti*), those intended to establish the meaning of scripture, and those involving necessary pervasion—are rendered futile. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.33)
Sentence, context, position, and likewise name—
these are distinct from them because they are established separately, like the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
One should establish one's own position by means of one's own principles, but refute the opponent's position by means of their own principles;
and the refutation of the opponent should be carried out by means of those [principles] which have been established for him.

Propounded for the sake of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), they do not invalidate one's own established tenet (*siddhānta*). Sophistry (*chala*) and futility (*jāti*) are recognized as two distinct types of contradiction: futility should be understood as self-contradiction, while sophistry is a rejoinder that shifts to a different meaning.

Thus, because it has been thoroughly purified by its consistency with logic and the eternal scriptures, that which is "inexpressible" is not what is intended here by the term "mere illusion" (māyāmātra). MĀnu 3.2.37.
For it is self-contradictory to say that [Brahman] is "distinct from both being and non-being";
furthermore, this would entail the admission that Brahman possesses a counter-correlative.
If the state of being a counter-correlate were false, then there would indeed be no distinction;
if non-distinction were real, then Brahman would consequently be false.
If the existence of that which is inexpressible is not [admitted], then there would be no properties whatsoever;
thus, Brahman itself would not be an object of inquiry, for inquiry is the determination of properties.
The purpose of the desire to know is the knowledge that "this is thus"; for its property is its state of being thus, and if that were not so, there would be no status as a counter-correlate.
And all the Śrutis declare that the dharmas consist of this very nature;
for even qualities such as invisibility and the like have been proclaimed by the Lord as belonging to Him.
If such qualities as omniscience and the like were to exist, why would they not [be present]?
If they were dependent on something else, then their existence would likewise be restricted by place and time.
For existence is never observed anywhere that is independent of place and time;
what, then, can be understood through scripture regarding this [self] which is devoid of all dharmas?
Furthermore, since the Veda is the ordainer of false doctrines, it lacks authority;
how could the Veda attain the status of a valid means of knowledge by inducing an unattained error?
For without the Veda, Brahman cannot be known, nor can the duties contained therein;
if that which is known through the Veda were false, how could oneness [of the self] not be so as well?

For even the superimposition of a property occurs when there is the perception of general properties and so forth; for in this case, when something is the subject characterized by "this-ness" and the like, another property is indeed conceptualized here.
Where can the superimposition of phenomena be seen upon that which is devoid of all phenomena?
If there is a superimposition of phenomena for that purpose, it would lead to an infinite regress.

For it is by that very semblance of a means of knowledge (mānābhāsa) through which the error of the entire universe is postulated—[an error] preceded by [the notions of] God, His knowledge, the Veda, perception, inference, and the knower. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.49)
Since that very essence undergoes change, why should the reality of the universe not exist?
Why is this world not imagined as an illusion, and why is that illusion not attributed to Him alone? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.50)
If that [world] were erroneous, then the Lord and others would indeed be non-erroneous;
for human errors could never belong to the Lord and such beings in any way whatsoever.
If that which is established by the senses is held to be erroneous because it is illusory,
then from what source could the authority of scripture— other than perception— be derived?
For it is through the direct perception of the witness that the validity of all means of knowledge is established;
since the witness is self-luminous, there is no infinite regress. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.53)
When the validity of sense-perception is only temporary,
why should the validity of the scripture on unity not likewise be so,
if its validity regarding unity is false while the reality of the universe remains? (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.2.54)
If the validity of the scripture on unity is held to be uncontradicted, why is the validity of that which is born of the senses not also held to be uncontradicted? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.55)
Since there is no distinction whatsoever due to the commonality of the loss of non-duality,
if validity were intrinsic, why would you not accept the existence of all things?

Furthermore, the very limit of validity would be contradicted by time; for if it were not a means of knowledge at another time, how could it possess the status of a means of knowledge now? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.57)
Is the conceit of falsity not also a conceit regarding liberation? Let it be said:
if it were a valid cognition (māna), non-duality would be lost; if it were not a valid cognition, there would be no liberation. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.58)
When false pride no longer exists as the re-occurrence of the universe, that is [liberation];
if it does exist, there is the state of bondage, and otherwise, there is the occurrence of duality.
Likewise, liberation depends on time, for liberation is indeed subject to time.
Time alone declares liberation even when time has ceased;
therefore, there would be a cessation of liberation itself, and consequently, the state of transmigratory existence would persist.
And where is it that the identity of the body with the self—which is attained through perception—is not sublated by inference?
For if that were not attained through perception anywhere, there would be no valid cognition such as "this is my body," but rather [the cognition] "I am the body. (Manu 3.2.61)

And just as the metaphorical attribution "I am black" occurs when mud is smeared upon a garment, so it would be if that [blackness] were produced by an adventitious condition (upādhi); for then, just like its inherent whiteness, one would perceive "the blackness is not mine. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.62)
And how is it that the distinction between the body and so forth and the self is not perceived?
Immediately upon birth, deer, cattle, elephants, birds,
and humans recognize the causes for fear, fearlessness, their own enjoyment, and the like.
If there is no memory of one's previous body, how could that consciousness arise when there is a lapse of recollection regarding positive and negative concomitance and so forth?

When there is knowledge of another body, how can there be the conviction of identity with the current body? Because the self is all-pervading, yet it lacks proficiency in worldly activities within the body.

Even when there is knowledge of distinction, as in the case of charcoal and fire, or things that appear as if not distinct from themselves, worldly transactions proceed; for indeed, [distinctions] do not always follow what is perceived by direct perception.
For people are capable of explaining objects exactly as they experience them;
therefore, what is established by direct perception cannot be sublated by anything else.
If it were possible to restrain that [karma] anywhere when it has not yet entered its objective range,
how then could future time and liberation be understood as its domain?
For even scripture, once the general [principle] has been established through perception, can only lead to the understanding of a specific [application];
otherwise, how could there be a grasp of the word's power?
Once the apprehension of the word's power has occurred regarding past and future objects, a sentence may convey every particularity; it cannot do so for one who has not yet apprehended that power.
If the capacity [to denote] existed only in the present, one could not speak of the past and the future;
if the apprehension of that capacity occurs elsewhere, how could it exist if that [other thing] is not apprehended?
If this [inference] were to lead to something else based merely on what is observed in common,
how could it lead to the true nature of a thing that is devoid of generality?
Nowhere has anyone ever accepted a universal called "self-nature" (svarūpatva).
If self-nature were pervasive, what would be excluded therein? And if it were excluded, how could it be pervasive? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.73)
For it is held that among all inclusive properties (anugata-dharma), selfhood (svatva) is the ultimate;

when asked "What is excluded?", the only answer can be "its own nature" (svarūpa). If there were anything other than that, then for us, that [nature] itself would not be selfhood. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.2.74)
Likewise, even when the apprehension of a word's power occurs with respect to an excluded form,
how could that [apprehension] take place without a general cognition of it?
Therefore, everything is accepted as having both specific and general forms;
and that which is a generality when excluded [from others] is itself the particular.
Nor is there a single nature among things by virtue of that [similarity],
because their similarity is perceived only through the observation of the difference between their respective properties.
Therefore, all objects, by virtue of their commonality, come within the range of the witness-consciousness;
otherwise, how could there be the cognition "all" regarding all things?
Furthermore, through the cognition of even slight similarity,
there may be the apprehension of the expressive power of words for every object, by means of that respective similarity.
When direct perception and mental cognition have as their object a past thing,
then they possess the status of memory-cognition, being specifically characterized by that pastness.
When something that was previously experienced is considered to have passed away, why should it not be regarded as authoritative? For in this case, there is no sublation of memory.
The status of being a means of valid cognition belongs to recognition as well, for it is experienced by everyone;
moreover, that recognition is seen to have as its object a subject characterized by both past and present existence.
And that [cognition] does not consist of mere memory, because it arises from the simultaneous grasping of "that" and "this";
therefore, there would be no restriction to the present alone in a perception produced by the senses.

And there can be no such thing as "cognition" (pramiti) anywhere other than through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); since there is no evidence for it and because such a postulation would be cumbersome, what is the use of this [separate category]?
The thought "this has been known by me" refers to the object of knowledge as apprehended by a witness-consciousness;
therefore, no cognition other than that very knowledge is seen which could be called a valid result (pramiti).
There is no destruction whatsoever of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and the cognitions;
nor is any sublation of these ever observed even in dreams.
In this state, there is only the singularity of being awake; otherwise, it is clearly seen as something else.
Therefore, the dream is false, yet it is not [absolutely] non-existent; rather, it is just like the waking state, which is itself waking.
Just as the self exists somewhere, so too the self may indeed be the object of delusion;
yet for that reason alone, it is not false, whether in a dream or likewise in the waking state.
If that which is seen otherwise in the self were also erroneous here,
then from what source would the error of dreams and the like arise, given that they persist without being sublated?

And there is no valid cognition whatsoever regarding the universal delusion [of all things]; moreover, if everything were non-delusory, how could that [universal delusion] be a valid means of knowledge? How then could it be delusory?
Furthermore, that proponent of error necessarily accepts the erroneous nature of his own doctrine; since there is agreement on this point between the two disputants,
it follows that the entire universe must indeed be non-erroneous.
If there were both error and non-error, how could there not be truth in the non-erroneous?
That doctrine, corrupted by every defect, should be abandoned by those who desire their own welfare.
For he has always himself accepted that his own doctrine is to be rejected,
because its inherent impossibility is merely a proof of its being an error and is thus a mere ornament [to its refutation].
How could even a madman wish to accept his doctrine?
Because the power of the Lord is inconceivable, it has been set in motion by those who are greatly deranged.

Therefore, wisdom is here called "māyā," and it is indeed the material cause of the individual soul; the divine power is the primary instrumental cause, and that which is fashioned is the very protector.
Together with those two, and also separately, it is called "mere illusion" (māyāmātra).
From both together, and then from each separately, it is measured by its sovereignty and protected.
The mind is of the nature of wisdom, by which the latent impressions take the form of the mind;
for the Śruti directly declares that "intellect" and "fear" are indeed the mind itself.
As long as transmigratory existence lasts, this mind is indeed a mixture of consciousness and the unconscious;
by means of it, the individual soul perceives all these states at all times.
Objects of the mind are like those in a dream; they do not become gross as if external, and therefore their clarity is never such [as that of waking perception].
In some cases, even when these mental impressions (vāsanā) are clear,
they may disappear by the will of the Lord and be manifested again by Him.
Having created the manifold world from his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
the unborn Lord causes it to vanish by reducing it to the state of mere impression.

The Lord of Gods, being ever self-dependent, leads the individual soul—which is itself always subject to Him—through the states of deep sleep, delusion, and awakening; there is no other agent whatsoever for this.
There is no difference whatsoever in the Supreme Lord even due to a difference in location;
everywhere he is filled with every auspicious quality of consciousness and devoid of all defects.
But whatever is contrary to that [teaching] could never be authoritative in this context;
for how could it be authoritative here when it contradicts the primary purport? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.104)
The Vedic word is an authoritative means of knowledge only because it is the cause for the removal of suffering and the attainment of happiness;
that [authority] arises from the Lord alone when He is pleased, and not otherwise.
For clarity of mind arises solely from the knowledge of the excellence of virtues, and also from the thorough knowledge of their faultlessness; it does not arise through any other means whatsoever.
To him who knows me as one whose mass of defects is entirely exhausted and who is augmented by the totality of virtues— to him, being well-pleased, I shall grant liberation, and not otherwise.
He alone who knows me as being superior to all others truly knows me;
to him I grant all desires and the supreme state.
"That my enemies should revile me while I am thus free from delusion"—
this and other such statements from the Vedas and the Smṛtis establish this very point.
And liberation from the world comes through faith by virtue of recognizing those qualities;
for this very reason, there is a conflict with one whose primary intent is [worldly] greatness. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.2.110)

In no way can the meaning of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and other scriptures be considered defective, devoid of merit, or possessing only meager merit; for the meaning of all of them, which is contrary to that [false view], has been respectfully determined by Vāsudeva himself. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.111)
Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me;
by understanding this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done.
Therefore, because it contradicts all authentic scriptures, no inference applies there; by that [means], the Lord is determined to possess all excellent qualities.
Nor can it be established that the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from [the Lord] simply because it possesses consciousness, like the Lord himself;
for scripture clearly declares that this soul is merely a reflection.
Just as this shadow is spread upon this person,
and just as a shadow is seen to resemble the man and to be dependent on the man,
even so all beings, beginning with Brahmā, have the Supreme Self as their essence. (Manusmṛti 3.2.115)
Just as in matters concerning existence, cognition, and purposeful action, the individual is understood to be dependent on the Person (Puruṣa),
so too are the appearances and the liberated souls dependent upon the Supreme Self.
Chāyā is the wife of Viṣṇu, and Dhātṛ is the husband of Ramā; these two are the most distinguished among them.
From them were born Indra and Kāma, and from those two, all other beings as well.
Of these two—the song of Hari and that of Brahmā—Indra is the specific excellence;
and Māra is the illuminator of both, for all of them are dependent upon those two.

"All others have only limited power, while the supreme Hari possesses full power; even though they possess consciousness, they are distinct from Him. From such scriptural statements as these, it is indeed known that there is only difference. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.119)
For it has been determined that the individual soul (jīva) is a reflection (ābhāsa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman);
yet that is not logical, since a reflection is understood to depend upon a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Because there would be an absence of dependence on a preceptor, because it would contradict its nature as a mere appearance,
and because it would be a part due to its sentience, the unity of the aggregate would follow.
Therefore, a distinction arises between the whole and its constituent parts;
the designation "Lord" (Īśa) applies to the whole, just as it is applied to those who possess the form of a Lord.
Therefore, upon the removal of the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth, there arises equanimity;
or rather, there are manifestations in the form of the Lord, primarily like the reflections of the sun and other luminaries.
To dispel the apprehension that "in that case, there would be the destruction of the forms of the teacher's [speech]," the Lord, the Master of the Vedas, said: "Therefore,
it is indeed a comparison, distinguished by the appearance of something else" (Manu 3.2.124).

That which has been stated—that the soul is entirely dependent [on the Supreme] in all its states, and that its similarity [to Him] consists merely in being consciousness and nothing else—[is established]. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.125)
Their form consists merely in that appearance of the conscious selves;
it does not depend on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the like, nor is there excessive similarity with the illustrative examples.
Even a slight resemblance to pleasure and so forth appears to the gods and non-gods through the Lord;
therefore, it appears eternally, and it also appears as such.
Since its manifestation and existence are likewise non-different from it on all sides,
the individual soul (jīva) is always declared to be a mere reflection of the Supreme Self.

Because it is like the reflection of the sun and other luminaries in water, there is no dependence [of the reflection] upon that [water]; rather, there is only a certain similarity. This is clearly demonstrated by the entire authority contained within the Sūtra. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.129)
How could there be unity in a collection based solely on the perception of a difference between the individual soul and the Lord?
For Hari is free from all defects because of His omnipotence.
Therefore, it has been stated that she is "endowed with everything. Where is there unity for one who possesses defects?
If she is endowed with all powers by virtue of her sovereignty, how could she be possessed of defects?
If unity were devoid of recollection, it would not be oneness;
in the case of the unity of conscious beings, recollection alone is the proof, and nothing else.
If it is argued that there is indeed a unity of the aggregate even without conscious investigation,
then let that [unity] exist among sentient beings as a mere name, for such is the case.
If there were a continuous connection [to objects] even in liberation, it would be a state of false knowledge;
for that [liberation] does not exist at all, since the Omniscient One does not maintain a connection with unity [with objects].
If there were subsequent reflection later on, it would constitute false knowledge;
if there were no reflection while it was present, it would result in ignorance.
If there were a seventh taste, then a unity of non-existent things might occur later;
therefore, a unity of a collection is always and from afar rejected.
Therefore, as long as he is indeed endowed with all virtues and free from defects, he alone is called "Lord" (Īśvara); in that regard, there is no distinction whatsoever.
"Here there is no diversity whatsoever; this is He, and that is He"—by such scriptural authority, all individual souls are indeed portions of Him. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 12.138)
If, by necessity, there were an inherent unity between the parts and the whole,
then the synthesis of all parts would exist even for that which is extremely minute.
Whatever portion of him is born on earth experiences the pleasure, pain, and so forth associated with that state; however, there may be some distinction made by the Lord.
Because the Lord possesses inconceivable power, there is nothing anywhere that is impossible for Him.
If His identity with the individual soul were indeed established, then His lordship would be untenable;
for it is a contradiction according to all means of valid knowledge to claim lordship for one who is not a lord.
If the Śruti teaches that [the Self] is known as the Lord by way of being the non-Lord, or conversely, that it is known as the non-Lord by way of being the Lord; MAnu 3.2.142.

Because it contradicts that which must be lived by, it will not attain the status of an authoritative means of knowledge; for this very reason, since its lordship is not established, nothing can be accomplished by it.
When sovereignty has been correctly revealed by the Śruti through the distinction between the Lord and the non-Lord,
even that which is otherwise improper becomes proper by virtue of that power.
Therefore, even in other cases, whatever is observed is to be attributed to the Lord alone;
for even that which is obtained from a semblance of scripture does not contradict his status as the Lord.
"The Lord is powerless, the world is false, the one who suffers is liberated, and there is no duality"—
this contradiction of one's own proposition is the most excessive of all faults.

Thus, this doctrine of the identity of the individual soul and the Lord, as propounded by the Brahmatarka, should be utterly rejected by all who desire their own spiritual welfare. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.147)
There is nothing whatsoever that is improper for a lord which does not contradict his lordship;
whatever would contradict his lordship is truly and immediately improper.
Having reconciled all means of valid cognition without contradicting [the Lord's] sovereignty,
and since sovereignty is established, one should not attribute even what is improper to the Lord.
"Everything obtained through pride should never be applied to one's name";
such is the statement from the *Brahmatarka*, and therefore what has been said here is appropriate. (Manu 3.2.150)
And because his form is non-material, he is formless; yet his form, consisting of his own qualities, is held to consist of head, hands, feet, and so forth.
Therefore, there is no impermanence, nor indeed any contradiction with the two scriptural statements;
for just as the scripture says that the Self alone is the light even when the light of fire has been set aside, so does it declare the Lord to be the light of the individual soul.

According to the degree of their devotion to Him, there is a corresponding gradation in the attainment of liberation for all beings, beginning with Brahmā, in respect of bliss and other qualities, in due order.
Their bliss, like their other qualities, is merely a reflection;
it is dependent upon the qualities of Nārāyaṇa and is exceedingly small in comparison to them.
Therefore, knowledge is always distinct from the Supreme Being; indeed, the knowledge of individual souls is one thing, while bliss and lordship are another.
"Since the sovereignty belongs primarily to the Supreme Lord and only secondarily to the individual soul, it is stated in the Śruti that creation and destruction are dependent upon Him;
however, because maintenance is His very nature, it does not stand to reason that it should depend on Him. (Manusmṛti 3.2.156)
Since the entire nature of everything is dependent upon the Lord,
Hari is perceived by his devotees through his own power, even though he is unmanifest.

All the qualities (guṇas), being eternally non-different from that [Prakṛti], exist specifically as qualities and as possessing qualities, and as the enjoyer and the enjoyed. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.158)
Because they exist eternally both as specific entities and as the nature of eternal power,
there is no impermanence in the dharmas such as action and the like.
Nor is this nature of distinction an impermanent form of power;
for that very [power] would have to possess distinction, yet there is no other distinction here.
Nevertheless, for the sake of one's own maintenance, it may be done specifically;
for it is known as a specific [duty] by all means of valid cognition.
For the distinction that "he emits" and "he withdraws" is indeed understood;
yet by the very Vedic text itself, the identity of those two as "that same [act]" is also understood, and thus their non-difference is perceived.
If the distinction belongs to the distinct thing, how can that distinction [itself] be distinct from the distinct thing?
If it were distinct, there would be an infinite regress; if it were non-distinct, why was it not so before?
It is not accepted by him that a distinction is indeed non-different;
for if the non-different were devoid of distinction, how could there be the state of being a distinction? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.164)
When one thinks, "This is distinct from that," this is simply differentiation;
since this differentiation is observed in many ways, what further answer can there be? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.165)
For non-difference and difference indeed constitute the essential nature of the differentiator;
if there were no distinction between these two, the words expressing them would be synonymous.
And who could say that the words "non-difference" and "difference" are synonyms?
If difference and mutual non-difference were to exist as distinctions through a differentiator, [then they would not be synonymous]. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.2.167)

How can there be difference in that which is without distinction? Likewise, how can there be identity for one who possesses difference? Furthermore, the distinction between those two would arise merely from being the possessor of difference.
If a distinction is perceived between the divider and that which is divided,
then what distinction is there between non-difference and the non-different, or between difference and the different?
If all transactions were to proceed everywhere by means of distinction alone,
then why would one postulate a separate category [of "difference"] at all, since it would only result in the burden of conceptual construction?
Due to the absence of the cognition of identity, there is indeed a difference between a cow and a horse;
for when there is the cognition "it is that very same thing," it is called a "particularity" (viśeṣa).
Indeed, even by a proponent of illusion (māyin), this distinction must be admitted for the sake of establishing that "Being," "Existence," and so forth are not synonyms;

for if there were no such distinction, it would have to be accepted that different words are used merely to exclude [their respective] non-existent qualifiers individually. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.172)
If that [truth] were likewise qualified by the absence of a specific distinction from illusion, then even truth would become [illusory]; and if that were so, there would be an infinite regress.
If there were no distinction regarding truth, then there would be no mention of it;
yet, since it is perceived by that [truth], the object to be characterized would likewise be specified.
Furthermore, even if one were to characterize it repeatedly, there would be an infinite regress;
for you have already admitted that it is characterized by non-existence.
In that case, your [opponent's] position would likewise result in the absence of non-omniscience and so forth;
then, because of the positive sense of the two negatives, there would simply be omniscience itself.

If such [knowledge] were not to be accepted because it does not turn away from suffering and because it is a cognition of non-existence, then non-existence and so forth would likewise [not be accepted].
If it is admitted that [virtue] is opposed to falsehood and the like, why is its opposition to a lack of sovereignty not likewise admitted? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.178)
Thus, even by one who maintains that [the self] is partless, a distinction must be accepted through a mind that is itself fragmented, because otherwise no such state is possible. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.179)

That [work] must indeed be borne upon the head with great reverence by those who advocate for its being either unbroken or broken, and likewise by those who maintain it to be both broken and unbroken; for it possesses a special distinction.

Therefore, by means of three illustrations, the Blessed One has declared with emphasis the non-differentiation of the qualities; and that [view] is not the one in which the meaning follows from the literal sequence of words.
When there is a general release from all specific details,
the understanding of those specifics may arise even from a single word in the response.
Since there is no such thing as a unity among all particularities of an object,
therefore, what is known in a general way may later become known in a specific way through the power of another word; by this, there is the status of being an "anvita" (correlated) expression.
Since it is only when the word's own meaning is connected with some particularity that one understands "by this [person]"— for this is indeed known through experience by the very statement itself.
If this word were to express its own meaning here without any connection at all, then who would ever establish a connection again for all the other words as well? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.185)
For a word has no function other than the manifestation of its own meaning;
likewise, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his duty by speaking but once. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.186)
How can there be knowledge of the relation [of words] when its status as the meaning of a word is not established?
For at that very time, those words would be utterances whose meanings are unrelated.
The meaning of a word would not be coherent, for that coherence belongs to the meaning of the sentence;
indeed, the wise declare that a sentence consists solely of words that are mutually expectant.
And that state of being free from expectancy arises through the expression of those respective meanings.
First, expectancy is required for the sake of completing the meanings;
but once the object, the agent, and the action are complete, what other syntactic connection could there be?
If there is no fulfillment by means of the words spoken, how can it be fulfilled by a human horn?
And if their function exists, why does it not occur even when they are not spoken?

If it is claimed that an action is required for the sake of establishing [the object] in the mind, why would they not have made the effort to establish it in the mind beforehand? And if their dependence on a person is admitted, that [dependence] remains the same afterwards as well. (Manusmṛti 3.2.192)
If it is argued that the male alone is the underlying referent (*anvaya*) of these [words] when considered subsequently,

then since those words would have denoted unrelated things, how could there be any connection at all, even if one were to exert effort regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word in the case of different meanings? (Mbh 3.2.193)

Because it suffers from defects such as the excessive complexity of conceptual construction and because it contradicts direct experience, the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of already-denoted meanings) must indeed be rejected by the wise.
For when the word for the agent has been expressed, because its general property is already known, one asks "Why? precisely while seeking its specific property. (Manu 3.2.195)

Since words denote [objects] as already connected [with other meanings], once the specific properties such as qualities and actions have been stated, there arises a state of being free from expectancy. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.196)
Therefore, the Blessed One alone is said by all the Vedas to be the one whose nature consists of infinite qualities; yet those Vedas themselves are entirely distinct from him.
All [beings] possess the nature of all qualities and are indeed the agents of all actions;
nevertheless, they are also distinct from one another, both by their specific characteristics and through the discernment of the wise.
And by various such words, the Supreme is expressed and appropriately designated through instruction,
by way of similarity to other forms of bliss and so forth, and by way of its being concordant with them.
Their greatness, such as fullness and other qualities, is heard of in the Śruti as a distinction:
"He is the full one, the controller of all without exception, the most excellent bliss, and the single part. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.200)
This collection of qualities is Vāsudeva, yet he is devoid of parts;
this very Vedic revelation concerning Vāsudeva speaks of the supreme qualities of Hari.
The Unborn One, always perceiving the dharmas and adharma of all living beings existing without number since beginningless time, awakens them at his own will.
To some of them, Acyuta himself bestows the fruit;
it is said that they never perform any distinction, such as instigation or the like. Therefore, he is independent in the primary sense of the term.
And those actions are in every respect nothing but volitions;
though their bodies are insentient, they partake in the fruits of their own karma.
In each of these, there are likewise infinite actions of this kind; and that they are thus is the unsurpassed, boundless power of the Lord.
Indeed, the single sin of killing a Brahmin, as described by Varāha and Hariṇa,
departed from the king's body solely through the hymn to Brahmā’s Pāra.
By the greatness of that hymn of praise, she was again restored from her state of being a hunter;
having attained supreme knowledge, she likewise always obtained other [spiritual benefits] as well.
Thus indeed have the infinite various karmas ripening within saṃsāra been described by the Lord Kapila.
Therefore, Janārdana, who possesses an infinite multitude of majestic qualities, is to be propitiated with supreme devotion; such is the meaning of the word "pāda."
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Through detachment comes firmness of devotion; by that, when worship occurs, direct perception of Viṣṇu arises—such is the sequence of the stages. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.1)

Having understood the meaning of the Vedas through reasoning, having set aside other [non-Vedic] conventions, and having removed all contradictions found within the entirety of the scriptural texts; MĀn 3.3.2.
Having become the internal *praṇava* because of its proximity [to the self],
it is so called because many contradictions [of other views] appear therein, and because the Vedic revelation supports that very position.
Having resolved the contradictions among the Vedic texts concerning the vital breaths and the skin,
and having set aside those points of conflict, he was gratified by their favor.
Having recognized the Lord as the creator of the body, and because of the remembrance of Him as its father,
one should develop a special affection for Him that exceeds [the affection felt] toward the creator of all else.

Having produced great respect for that [state] because of the extreme suffering elsewhere, and having generated an even greater detachment by perceiving the superiority of its qualities, [one should remain there]. // Manu 3.6 //
And because everything is under its control, having attained firmness in devotion,
one should strive for worship alone through the excellence of a distinguished teacher.

When it is stated that "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken," if a doubt arises as to why this is so, and even when "therefore" (ataḥ) is uttered, because no specific reason has yet been stated, [the next verse follows]. (Mānavadharmaśāstra 3.3.8)
"Since he is heard in scripture to be the agent of creation, bondage, liberation, and so forth, and since he is the bestower of liberation and other goals, he alone is to be sought after by you.
Thus he spoke of that Supreme Brahman, known as Vyāsa, who possesses rays of knowledge. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.9)
That very path by which bondage and liberation occur is reached through inquiry;
the Lord becomes well-pleased, and through such inquiry, He grants him liberation.

If it is asked, "How is it understood that the Lord is the giver of liberation and so forth? [the answer is: "Because He has the scripture as His source; for the giver of liberation is known through scripture. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.11)
If liberation could somehow arise from things determined by direct perception,
why would all these creatures be submerged in beginningless saṃsāra?
Because the certain destruction of suffering occurs through direct perception,
all subjects run toward him alone, as if toward a king.
If liberation were accessible through inference, then inference itself—
just as in the case of ordinary men— would preclude its being the bestower of liberation.
Only he who is accessible through that scripture is certainly the giver of liberation;
and there is no one other than Keśava who is accessible through scripture as the giver of liberation.
For he who is independent would be the giver of liberation; but how could one who is himself dependent while engaged in creation be capable of granting ultimate liberation alone? (Manu 3.16)
If He were to grant liberation through another locus, He alone would indeed do so;
however, not being followed by that [other locus], He would not grant liberation based on the words of another.
Therefore, for that purpose as well, Viṣṇu should be known by those seeking liberation.

By the scriptural passages "whomsoever he [Brahman] chooses" and "him alone," those who uphold the Veda understand with reverence that this very [Brahman] is the source of the scriptures. (Manu Smṛti 1.3.18)
"He who knows this becomes immortal"—thus it is said; and that which goes to the ocean is determined by the Veda to be the supreme Brahman. (Manu 3.3.19)
Because [the Veda] was produced from Him, Hari is therefore said to be the source of creation;
it is understood that there is no other source for the scripture in the primary sense.
For its origin in scripture is known through systematic coherence; indeed, by means of the prefix *sam*, the word "coherence" (*samanvaya*) expresses the sense of the supreme primary meaning.

Thus, because the Śruti declares that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme and primary meaning, the Lord of the Vedas proclaimed "not what is not based on the Word" (nā-śabdam) in order to establish this definitively. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.22)
How is the concordance to be known by men who know only a few branches? For the Veda is indeed infinite; thus the Śruti declares its infinity.
The determination of infinite suffering is like crossing the ocean of the great dissolution; therefore, no further synthesis need be understood here.
To dispel such doubts, that Mine of Compassion said:
"Even though this ocean, which has the scriptures as its shore, is impossible to cross, I alone shall determine it by means of the dissolution of a single pore of my skin. (Manu 3.3.25)
Even though the meaning of the entire Veda is difficult for all human beings to grasp,
it attains the state of a subtle atom within the unmanifest space of my knowledge.
Thus revealing the state of being an object of knowledge for the entire Veda as well, the Lord of the Universe clearly stated the commonality of its interpretation.
Who indeed, other than that single Bādarāyaṇa, could declare the commonality of destiny for those endowed with infinite traditional knowledge, were it not for the sun of his wisdom?
Even another person of small intelligence, knowing wealth consisting of four or five branches, might say, "I know it by inference," through his favor. (Manu 3.29)
Thus, because he is the Lord who primarily knows all states of existence in their commonality,
he made a firm promise which even the gods find difficult to fulfill.

Therefore, although the harmonious convergence (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedas is thus established, [the author], having clearly explained the meaning, has stated the convergence again separately. (Manu 3.31)

In this regard, first of all, there is the coordination (*samanvaya*) of words well-established elsewhere; here, they apply solely to the expressed meaning (*vācya*), like the breaking of a great wrestler. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.32)
Even though this [attainment] is far superior to that, no one at all has the qualification for that Great Consecration (mahāsamanvaya) proclaimed in the fourth quarter.
In that [practice], the Brahmin alone is primarily authorized, while others are so in due order;
and because it is difficult to master, it has not been directly declared as the first [duty] for others.

But for the sake of determining those words well-known elsewhere, the Lord first set forth [this work]; therein, qualities such as bliss and the like were determined to belong to the Lord alone, by relying upon scripture and reasoning. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.3.35)

All those who abide within other deities truly speak only of Viṣṇu himself as the cause of the application of their names; they do so directly through that connection, or figuratively through secondary usage.
In this world, some speak of other gods because they describe their specific qualities;
yet others declare Viṣṇu alone to be supreme—thus it is for all others without exception.
Thus, when the entire collection of words "uru" (vast/great), which are established elsewhere,
is known to have its complete application in Viṣṇu through these indicative marks, this [present] application is indeed established.
"But if they were directed toward something else, there would be no correct coordination;
thus, all marks without exception have their coordination in Brahman alone. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.39)

"Or rather, there may be a state of belonging to both; therefore, for the sake of removing doubt regarding the gender and the word, [it is established] because it is perceived in both ways. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.40)
The primary application of words currently in use, along with their specific grammatical genders,
pertains exclusively to Hara and not to anything else.
Since words and indicative marks have no independence elsewhere, when things are not independent,
the word's application is not based on primary denotation.
Therefore, since they have attained the status of being the meaning of words by depending upon that [quality],
the function of a word occurs through a quality that is indeed very slight.

Just as iron possesses the quality of burning, so too that very Lord, by virtue of His independence, must be accepted by the wise as the primary meaning of the word "Self. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.44)
Thus he says: "And even though the convergence of all words in Nārāyaṇa is thus established, it is in no way appropriate for all words [to be used] in that manner. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.45)
If it is argued that this would result in the attainment of even contradictions such as inferiority and so forth, [we reply: for inferiority and the like are indeed observed to be of two kinds.
Even one who, being himself another, is the cause of another's inferiority,
is indeed the referent of the word "inferior," just as a king might be victorious over another.
In Keśava, there exists the first [of these two], which experiences inferiority;
the second exists as the individual soul (jīva) alone, and because of its independence, there is no fault.
Since it has been stated by Hari that there is thus a complete coordination of all words with one who is free from contradiction,
therefore the Lord has effected the removal of all contradictions without exception.

Once the determination of reality has been achieved through both systematic correlation and non-contradiction, the thought of the qualified seeker will be: "What must be done by me? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.50).
In that regard, since devotion has been described as the means for warding off the succession of misfortunes for those lacking it,

and since the entire collection of supreme qualities has been proclaimed, the practice of worship must indeed be performed with diligence as a constant duty in order to strengthen that devotion. (Manu 3.51)
And that worship is of two kinds: consisting of the study of the scriptures, and the higher form consisting of meditation; its ancillaries include concentration (dhāraṇā) and the rest.
Likewise, Bādarāyaṇa has declared that in this section there is meditation characterized by both aspects; he has explained it extensively, preceded by scriptural authority, O Adhvaryu.

A separate view, impossibility, lack of determination, combination, perception of a specific quality, omission of the effect, mention of various things, and swiftness [are the grounds for the application of the particle *ca*]. (Manu 3.3.54)
Error, removal, a mark, lack of finality, non-distinction, lack of purpose, over-extension, and reliance on what is not remote. (Manu 3.55)
A distinguished cause is desired; visible deformity, elevation, non-mention, lack of effort, firm bonds, and defeat [are also such causes]. (3.56)
Equality with men, renunciation of what has been acquired, uncertainty regarding causes, delusion, perception of distinctions, speech, equality of qualities, and the view of separateness. (Manu 3.57)
The pursuit of forbidden paths is the connection; the absence of conceptualization is the desired fruit;
purity and deformity are the limbs; and the vision of no distinction is the action.
The arguments for the prima facie position, ease of comprehension, the performance of injunctions, greatness, limited capacity, the fruit according to fitness, and rebirth. (Manu Smṛti 3.59)
Equality of results, distinction, superiority of qualities, predominance,
action according to one's capacity, alliance, proof, strength, and submission.
The cause, the excellence of the effect, intrinsic nature, the refutation of the entity,
counter-action, contradiction, connection, and non-deficiency.
Skill in the refinement of speech, self-determination, mastery over objects, particularity, non-authoritativeness, preeminence, affection, and tradition. (Manu 3.62)

Steadfastness, the attainment of what has been performed, the expansion of beginningless virtues, the excellence of the means of accomplishment, the vision of diversity, instruction, and non-deficiency.
Absence of obstacles, absence of contradiction, excellence of qualities,
and scriptural authority— these arguments are always unassailable in the determination of a final conclusion.
Having mastered all the Vedas according to one's capacity, there should be worship;
for in that regard, the complete comprehension of the entire Veda belongs truly to Brahman alone.
The complete knowledge of others is required according to their respective fitness;
by that much alone, every person becomes fit for worship.
"O Nārada, it is not at all the case that Janārdana attains satisfaction merely because one praises him after having understood the supreme limit of his greatness. (Manu 3.3.67)
But for that devotee who always praises [Him] with unwavering devotion in accordance with self-knowledge, Hari is forever pleased.

From the context of such passages, there arises a universal knowledge appropriate to one's capacity, which conforms to the knowledge of the Self through inquiry according to one's ability. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.69)
Otherwise, the futility of such statements as "the entire Veda is to be mastered" and "there shall be the study of one's own recitation" cannot be avoided.
Even today, the gods and others always hear, reflect upon, and meditate upon it as appropriate, until the final determination of the matter; therefore,
hearing and reflection must indeed be performed in every way.

The supreme teacher knows the specific distinctions regarding intellect, sacred learning, meditation, and time; indeed, for one who acts according to the path of his instruction, true insight shall arise.
Hearing, reflection,
and meditation on the perceived reality are for the sake of perceiving that which is other than this, through the attainment of extraordinary bliss.
If such a teacher is not available, one should perform the determined rites of hearing and so forth according to the established tenets of one who knows the final determination.
Without hearing [the Veda] and so forth, one should not remain idle for even a single moment;
however, in the event of extreme incapacity due to sleep or other such causes, one should begin once again.
In the absence of one who knows the definitive conclusion, he should always listen to the true scriptures, provided that an abundance of correct knowledge is found therein.
One should dispel the doubts of those devoted to Viṣṇu to the best of one's ability;
and in the absence of someone superior to oneself, one should practice them by oneself.
The state of being completely full of all virtues, the total eradication of all defects,
and that everything else is dependent upon Viṣṇu— this is the correct determination.
Its independence is always [established], as is its distinction from everything else;
this is for the sake of proving its faultlessness, since it persists even when there is no difference.
And even for those who are liberated, there remains dependence upon Him in order to perfect His qualities; moreover,
there is indeed distinction among the liberated, for it is never observed that what is distinct attains non-distinction, and the absence of such distinction is supported by experience.

If there were no distinction from the former [state], the Lord would be subject to defects; therefore, His absolute transcendence is established, being perfectly equal even to Nārāyaṇa and the liberated souls.
Even if there were both difference and non-difference, faults would still arise due to the aspect of non-difference;
likewise, Lakṣmī’s faultlessness and her state of being inseparable from Him [would be compromised].
Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Indra, Śeṣa, Rudra, and their consorts, as well as Śakra, Kāma, and others, are likewise liberated in due order. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.83)
This is to be known as the established doctrine, determined by Hari himself;
everything that contradicts this leads only to blinding darkness.
"The Veda declares most clearly: 'They enter into blinding darkness';
and so do all the Śrutis and the entire Pañcarātra. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.85)
The Mūlarāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, all the Smṛtis, the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas, and the two supreme systems of Sāṅkhya and Yoga. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.86)
The Brahmatarka and the Mīmāṃsā constitute an infinite ocean of words,
as well as the subsequent logical arguments rooted in perception and scripture.
This supreme truth applies entirely to the direct perception of Īśvara, as well as to Rāmā and the others, whether they are liberated or not yet liberated.
That which reveals [the truth] respectfully, leaving no room for another [view], is alone a true scripture; anything other than that is a false scripture. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.89)
One should constantly study the true scripture and abandon false scripture; for through the certain determination of reality, there arises the vision of Brahman. (Manu 3.3.90)
In accordance with the degree of their correct or erroneous understanding,
the fruit for human beings shall consist of happiness or suffering, varying according to that degree.
And through correct and superior knowledge, there shall be an increase in happiness for human beings;
therefore, one should engage in hearing and reflection according to one's own capacity.
Due to attachment to sense objects, doubt regarding the eternal,
and the mind's longing for something else, the Supreme is not realized.
For this is indeed the statement of the *Bhārata*: "One who is free from these defects and endowed with constant worship beholds Vāsudeva. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.94)
The defects, bound to [the self] from beginningless time, are the obstacles to liberation;
they generally exist in men, and for that reason, liberation does not arise.
All these [qualities] are seen among living beings in varying degrees.
Among those who are upright, there is only one [quality]: the absence of excessive zeal.
Because it consists merely in the lack of such qualities, it is not contradicted by the state of being non-upright.

Therefore, for one who desires the goals of human existence, supreme devotion to Viṣṇu and to his devotees, such as Ramā and others, should be practiced according to their relative degree of excellence.
For respect toward all living beings is indeed established by their very nature;
it is even greater toward those who are superior to oneself, in accordance with that degree of superiority.
One who desires welfare in every respect should practice [the stages] ending with Vāsudeva;
he should never abandon that [practice], but should increase it gradually.
One should feel affection for equals as for oneself, and compassion for others who are virtuous;
by acting thus, the Lord is quickly perceived through direct realization.
He who perceives equality with Viṣṇu even in the liberation of Ramā, Brahmā, Śiva, and others, shall go to that blinding darkness.
How much more so for one who perceives superiority, for one who considers him devoid of virtues,
for one who knows his faults, for one who sees no difference [between himself and him], and likewise for one who sees both [his virtues and faults].
Thus says the sacred scripture: one should worship Hari, who is endowed with the qualities thus proclaimed; having seen Him, liberation arises through that very means. (Manusmṛti 3.3.103)
That which is spoken out of malice, and that which contradicts the words of the Vedas; those who are enemies of Rāma, being devoid of devotion due to their aversion,
remain eternally situated in the blinding darkness of the state of hostility.
Those who hate Hari go to darkness, as do those who identify with him [as being different from Brahman],
those who know him to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and even those who perceive his defects.
From such scriptural passages as these, it follows that hatred leads one to darkness; even Hiraṇyakaśipu fell into darkness through his reviling of the Blessed One,
whereas Vidhikṣu transcended it, O son, by virtue of Prahlāda’s power.
"Since my father censured me, who am devoted to you, and was thus possessed of sin, may my father be purified from that wretched and insurmountable evil. (Manu 3.107)
He who, hearing the censure of the Blessed One or of others devoted to him,
does not depart from it, he too goes to hell, fallen from his merit.
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form, being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. (Manu 3.109)
Futile are their hopes, futile their actions, and futile their knowledge;
devoid of discernment, they have taken refuge in a delusive nature, that of the Rākṣasas and the Asuras.

Those malicious people who hate me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others— I cast those cruel haters, the lowest of men, perpetually into transmigrations within the wombs of the Asuras alone, which are inauspicious.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they do not reach me, O son of Kuntī, but from there go to an even lower state.
How could he who hates the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the best of the wise gods, not become an object of hatred for anyone as long as the world endures? (Manu 3.113)
"O best of the wise, the ancestors of one who hates the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, sink into hell for eternal years"—
from such a multitude of scriptural statements, it follows that for the hater there is indeed only darkness. (Manu 3.114)
Those who stand by the Lokāyata doctrine say that there is no liberation at all;
enjoyment lasts only as long as the body, after which it turns to ashes.
Thus, by what means of knowledge has this been seen by one who asserts perception?
For the non-existence of liberation is certainly not determined by the means of knowledge that is perception.
The view that liberation is possible for a great man is consistent;
however, there is no way whatsoever for one who says "it is not" to possess greatness.
How can one who accomplishes that which is common to all be considered unique?
Yet, in this world, men are seen who know both the higher and the lower.
Those established in yoga, possessing direct vision and pure eyes,
having perceived the deity directly and obtained prosperity through its grace, [attain their goal].
How can men be prevented from [attaining] knowledge, discernment, and supreme wisdom?
For the great majesty and immense power of those sages is clearly seen.
If even those [means of knowledge] are rejected, why is your own statement not also rejected—
that the authority of the spoken word is perceived through direct perception?
For even boons and other gifts granted by him always remain true;
moreover, the lack of authority in his speech is determined by its being mere idle talk.
Indeed, there is no purpose whatsoever in preventing [others] from the next world;
if one were to kill [them] in vain with vain words, what answer would he have? What man of intelligence would speak so as to bring about the ruin of his own life? (Manu Smṛti 3.123)

Could there even be doubt regarding the authority of those two men? For such doubt would apply even to one who speaks contrary to his own life, or to an ignorant person who has witnessed [an event]. (Manu 3.124)
He who hears the words of gods beyond the reach of the senses, who has seen both the higher and the lower, and who makes known all that is past and future through his experience of the worlds—
for this reason, because he is accessible to direct perception, the Veda itself is clearly [established].

If the scripture were not authoritative, then the same would apply to what is perceived by the senses; and if what is perceived by the senses were authoritative, why should that not also apply to the scripture? Furthermore, the distinction between the words of common worldly usage and the scripture is established through their non-deviation [from reality].
Liberation exists through dharma and also through knowledge of reality as it is;
furthermore, the validity of inference is established for the purpose of proving the Jina’s status as a trustworthy authority.
And from his words arises the instruction regarding dharma, right knowledge, and discernment;
for dharma is centered on non-violence and nothing else, while knowledge is the vision of the true person (pudgala).
Thus, how could that [scripture] be authoritative for the Jains by means of inference?
For it is declared that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the sense organ established toward its objects;
and "inference" (*anumā*) is so designated in accordance with the word *pratyakṣa*. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.129)
Because it causes both dharma and adharma to reach the supreme state on all sides,
and because it possesses other qualities beyond the reach of the senses, it is therefore known as Āgama.
For this very reason, each of these is accepted as a means of valid knowledge;
for their own nature is established otherwise than through a means of knowledge. (Manu 3.131)
Therefore, how could inference reveal either a dharma or a person?
For the faults of the person's own nature have already been stated, as has Ānanda’s [view]:
"He does not conceive of the person; rather, the absence of suffering is itself happiness. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.132)

Since an excess of pleasure is observed through an excess of the enjoyment of sense-objects, by what means could pleasure not be non-existent? And why should it not be the reverse? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.133)
If there were even some kind of existence, how could that very thing possess non-existence?
If all things were non-existent, they would, by virtue of their mutual relation, possess existence.
If there were the state of being the absence of absence, what would be lost for us then?
Existence is the nature of affirmation, while non-existence is the nature of negation. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.135)
Even the negation of a prohibition would necessarily result in a positive state;
however, the first cognition is that which determines the existence or non-existence of a thing.
And the cognition of a person (pudgala) never bestows liberation;
for because the person lacks independence, even when known, it does not grant happiness. (Manu 3.137)
For the state of being afflicted does not cease merely by the full knowledge of suffering.

If one could somehow become free from suffering through the cognition of a person (pudgala), then why would even an embodied being not be free from suffering? What could ever be superior to such knowledge? (Manu 3.138)
For one who maintains that God is the cause, the agency of time and other factors would exist in accordance with the Lord's will;
however, because it is insentient, karma can never be the cause [of anything].
Just as there is no cause for the dissolution of all suffering now,
so too there would be none hereafter, since inference is based on what has been previously observed.
If the knowledge of another who is capable [of liberation] generates that same joy, then the destruction of bondage would occur through that very means; what fault could there possibly be in this?
By whose own knowledge has the destruction of bondage ever been observed anywhere? By what means of valid cognition is it understood that non-violence is dharma?
If it is argued that violence itself is dharma, what answer could there be? (Manusmṛti 3.142)
By whom is it understood that dharma is a cause of happiness? And from what means of valid cognition is the fact that killing is a cause of liberation prevented? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.143)
If liberation could not possibly come about through the thorough knowledge of emptiness and even through the cultivation of emptiness, why would it not exist now? MĀnuv 3.144.
For one who desires to inspire confidence in others, delay is indeed appropriate;
for if [the teaching] were not dependent on human desire, by what could there be any delay? (Manu Smṛti 3.145)
Even in other cases, let there be delays caused by the will of the Lord;
otherwise, if the cause were present, why would the effect not arise?
For when the cause exists, the existence of the effect is indeed strictly determined.
For the Vijñānavādins as well,
liberation is nowhere possible through the realization of the non-duality of consciousness, nor through the cultivation of consciousness.
Because one perceives internal cognition and external momentariness,
yet fails to cultivate them according to the taught path, one is not liberated due to the absence of valid means of knowledge.
"The discrimination between *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa* is the means to liberation"— this doubt arises, yet there is no authoritative proof for this [view] except through the grace of the Lord.
Since the Śrutis and Smṛtis declare that liberation is attained through the grace of the Lord according to fixed rules, how could it possibly exist without Him?

Even Kaṇāda, Yoga, and Akṣapāda, though they proclaim liberation through the grace of the Lord, declare that the exhaustion of karmas occurs only through experience; for how could this [exhaustion] occur otherwise than when the Lord of the World is propitiated? (Manu 3.3.151)
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away,
and one's karmas are exhausted upon seeing the Lord, the Self, even here and now"—
for this is established by such statements from the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other sources. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.153)

Nor is there any other path [to liberation] through the grace of Śiva and others taught by the Pāśupatas and other sects; for it is stated in the Śruti that [liberation comes] from the knowledge of the Puruṣa. (Manu Smṛti 3.154)
All moments were born from that Puruṣa who is lightning;
thus the word "Puruṣa" is applied to Hari, who reclines upon the ocean.
"No one has power over him; his name is Great Glory.
Thus, the status of being a sovereign lord over him is itself prohibited by the Veda.
"Viśvataḥ paramāṃ nityaṃ viśvaṃ nārāyaṇaṃ harim"—by this statement of His being superior to all, even the possibility of equality is excluded;
for since He lacks anything equal or superior, He is not a person who exists merely figuratively. (Manu Smṛti 12.123)
The Person alone is all this—that which has been and that which is to be;
moreover, he is the lord of immortality, as well as of that which grows by means of food.
The Śruti declares that he possesses the state of being both the liberated and the supreme Lord;
for by the word "Amṛteśāna," his lordship over all is proclaimed.
If it is argued that the word "uta" implies "all," then that is futile; for this word "uta" would merely express a conjunction with lordship (*īśatva*). (Manu 3.160)
Regarding that [Puruṣa], the Brāhmaṇa declares: "This world is pervaded by the Puruṣa"; for the words "so great is his majesty" refer to his majesty. (Manu 3.3.161)
"He is the lord of immortality and fearlessness, having transcended mortal food"—
thus, having restated the sovereignty over the unliberated mentioned in the first half-verse, [the second half-verse follows].
And by the words "the lord of immortality," it ordains his status as the Lord of Liberation.

Therefore, liberation arises solely from the thorough knowledge of Viṣṇu and not from anything else; for according to the Śruti, "Just as... [and so forth], from that [knowledge] the destruction of karma occurs. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.163)
Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.

The meaning stated [in this verse] is also determined by such words of the Blessed One as: "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in me alone; I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.165)

"By performing obligatory and occasional rites and abandoning others, one is liberated from saṃsāra; this very point has also been refuted by this [verse]. Knowledge alone—this is the meaning that the King of the Vedas himself has declared. (Manu Smṛti 3.166)
