"That there can be no liberation without action, even through knowledge"—this is indeed what that Śruti respectfully prohibits by stating, "There is no other path. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.167)
The Lord [the Veda] carefully prohibits even worship performed otherwise by stating "it is thus," lest one mistake a mere symbol for the actual object.
"And those who worship ignorance enter into blind darkness"—because of this contradiction with the Vedic scripture, there can be no other mode of worship. (Manu 3.169)
Nor is one liberated merely by the knowledge of oneness according to the logic already stated;
having thus understood everything through all means of reasoning and sacred tradition,
one should constantly worship Hari through His very qualities by means of one's own yoga.

Brahmā is [superior] by virtue of all qualities and by the generality of his actions; Gīḥ (Speech) by the generality of qualities; Rudra by the generality of qualities; and the others by the generality of their substance.

Through the distinction of their respective offices, there is a difference among the deities and others by virtue of devotion, knowledge, bliss, and so forth; and this difference is especially evident in regard to liberation.
There is no contradiction to that extent, because it is entirely free from fault;
whereas for others and those inferior to them, it is in every respect merely an appearance.

Since all qualities and all actions of those who come later are invariably dependent upon the complete propitiation of their predecessors, they should never harbor envy or similar feelings toward them, just as one would not toward a good disciple. (Manu 3.174)
Nor are these others merely limited by time like the gods of the cycle of existence;
for in the Sūtra it is certain that for one who has merely begun [the practice], there is destruction through enjoyment alone.
"But the others [are exhausted] by experience when no effect has been initiated"—
since this was already enjoined, it is certain that these two [verses] state what has already been said, and thus involve tautology.

Uṣas, Svāhā, Parjanya, Mitra, Agni, Varuṇa, Vidhu, Pravaha, Aniruddha, Indra, Rudra, Vāṇī, and the Maruts— these, each succeeding one, attain liberation through all their respective qualities. (Manu Smṛti 3.197)
Soma, Manu, Dakṣa, Bṛhaspati, Śacī, Rati, Aniruddha, Tārā, and Mitra were equal [in their conduct]. (3.178)
But offspring is like Soma, the Virāj is like Agni,
Vāruṇī is like Parjanya, and likewise Saṃjñā and Rohiṇī.
The Dharmī is proclaimed as Prāvahī because of her friendship;
the Aśvins are the lords of obstacles and wealth, being friends, fathers-in-law, and mediators.
Bhṛgu is equal to Agni; Mitra is in the middle, O sons of Brahmā;
Varuṇa is between Agni and that [Mitra], and Nārada is generally like Indra. (Manu Smṛti 3.181)
Kāma is like Suparṇin, Umāva is like Indra, he is proclaimed to be like Rudra;
Viśvāmitra is like Nirṛti and like Mitra, and he is like Kasūnu.
Vaivasvata Manu and the Aśvins were first; others followed after them as his descendants.
Then came Cyavana, Ucathya, Vainya, Śaśabindu, and Haihaya.
And likewise, even here, there was a certain distinction among Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
In the same way, Priyavrata [had] one hundred other deities as his wives; those others, however, were born from within the interval between Pajra and Nimiṣa, and they were inferior to him.
May there always be even greater prosperity for those who are liberated, especially;
there is no one superior to them, nor anyone else but Hari himself.
In the *Bṛhatī-saṃhitā*, it was declared by the Blessed One himself:

"All this—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and that which consists of the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*)—as well as the vision [of Indra] immediately following Indra, is according to one's capacity. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.186)
The primary cause for attaining the vision [of the Truth] is the correct grace of the Guru;
furthermore, hearing [the teachings] and other such practices must be performed, for otherwise the vision can never be attained.
Having obtained a teacher who is superior in qualities, one should never resort to one who is inferior;
however, the opposite must be done by one who desires liberation in every respect.
It would be the very same conceptualization, and the prior permission would be required in every case;
therefore, for the sake of attaining the supreme Guru, a prior permission is not sought.
The teacher is the foremost of all [gurus], and Sarasvatī is the embodiment of knowledge;
the Lord Viṣṇu is the deity of all without distinction.
Through his grace alone may liberation be attained, and not by any other means whatsoever.
It is taught that for all people, their own superiors are the gurus in due order;
the instruction of Brahman, however, leads to the liberation of everyone.
Devotion superior to all means of accomplishment exists nowhere else;
and devotion to Hara alone is primary, while elsewhere it is secondary, according to the sequence.
Indeed, that devotion—which is characterized by bliss and leads to liberation—continues everywhere, even toward those superior to oneself, and proceeds in due order;
therefore, one should perform worship preceded by that [devotion] through the [prescribed] qualities for the sake of liberation. (Manu 3.193)
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Thus, from constantly beholding the Blessed One who is free from defects,
there is the attainment of the desired fruit, because one does not overstep what has been undertaken.
For gods, sages, humans, and others, [the rites] follow their respective species;
that which was taught by Jaimini pertains to humans, as do certain specific details thereof.
The Blessed One has declared a general rule for gods and others specifically;
however, when a powerful contradiction exists, the teaching of Jaimini and others is accepted.
For those who possess right vision, there is never any stain from improper action;
nor is there any loss of excellence for Brahman, because it is beyond all action.

Even for the gods, there is generally no reduction of what has been ordained; yet, in some cases, it may occur through a great transgression of duty. Nevertheless, that [ordinance] remains ordained; therefore, there is no absolute rule.
And for Candra and Sugrīva, because they took wives who were their own sisters,
there was indeed no loss of what they had acquired, nor any loss of what was ordained, in any way whatsoever.
Even for humans and others, there may be a diminution of bliss through wrongful action;
this occurs especially in the case of those of high status due to their transgressions, even regarding liberation.
Regarding the sin of one who possesses higher knowledge (*jñāna*), it is said that there is no taint in the fourth [case];
its fruit is that impurity and the like do not affect him.
Herein, the certainty of liberation as the very fruit of knowledge is declared. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.8)

Just as death resulting from consuming poison may occur even when it is destined by *prārabdha* karma, so too, although such results are unavoidable once attained, their suppression is taught here for gods and others respectively, through the conscious experience of having partially enjoyed them.
For the full experience of even that very *prārabdha* karma occurs through the totality of one's being;
however, even for one who perceives Brahman, there is a reduction in its fruit.

If there were a total loss of fruit for karma that has not yet begun [to bear fruit], then the injunctions for optional rites would be rendered useless; thus the aforementioned rule would hold. This has been clearly stated even today in the *Tantrabhāgavata*. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.11)
If there were no gradation in the fruit [of liberation], how could the Śruti speak of Brahmā and the others as "free from sin" and "unassailed by desire," and having declared their liberation,
further describe their bliss individually in varying degrees? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.12)
If this gradation exists only within saṃsāra and not in its primary sense,
then the meaning of the term "unassailed by desire" and our state of being free from sin would not exist.
"Where the desires of desire are attained, there make me immortal"—thus the Veda declares the characteristic of liberation, and it is an authoritative testimony. (Manu 3.4.14)
How could one who has attained all desires not be unassailed by desire?
When the attainment of desires occurs without effort, that alone is the state of being unassailed by desire; how could it be otherwise?
But where has desirelessness ever been observed in a conscious person who is not asleep?
It is merely the non-manifestation of desires, not their destruction, as in the states of delusion or sleep. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.16)
Why is it that one awakens with the very same desire with which one fell asleep? Why does one speak even against one's will? And how can there be a lack of desire while one is asleep? (Manu 3.4.17)
He obtains all desires and, attaining liberation, goes with Brahmā;
there he wanders about, laughing, playing, and experiencing delight.

"Taking whatever he desires as food, assuming whatever form he desires, and wandering through these worlds, he remains singing the Sāman, liberated"—such is the firm authority of the Śruti. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.19)

"How can one who has desires resting in his heart be liberated from desire?"—thus the Śruti speaks specifically of the liberation of those desires residing within the internal organ by using the word "in the heart" (hṛdi); for if this were not so, the qualification would be meaningless. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.20)
The position that "this [Veda] is the refuge for them" does not appear plausible,
since the Śruti in various recensions (śākhās) speaks of the desires of those who are liberated.
Therefore, freedom from being overcome by desire belongs primarily only to those who are liberated;
for those who employ deceptive means, the abandonment of the primary meaning of a term is merely an ornament.
Freedom from sin, freedom from suffering, and freedom from crookedness are declared here;
for "sin" (vṛjinam) is that which is unpleasant, suffering is pain, and "crookedness" (arjam) is a piercing sting.
"Because it is the cause of that, it is called 'pāpa' or 'vṛjina'";
thus was the meaning of the name explained by the Lord himself in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.

Indeed, for one who possesses knowledge, there is no state of sinlessness as long as saṃsāra persists; for even such a person still possesses the suffering resulting from previously initiated evil karma.

Therefore, to assume that "from each of these [comes] freedom from desire" is an assumption not found in the scripture; moreover, since the text says "struck by desire," the abandonment of what is explicitly stated is also evident.
In some cases, due to the absence of desire in a lustful man, and in other instances,
the experience that there is enjoyment of the pleasures of Indra and others is indeed contradicted.
Therefore, having separately stated the gradations of happiness for those who are not yet liberated,
the Śruti says "and that which [is for] the liberated"; this declares a gradation in their happiness,
and its subtlety is understood from the word "and" (ca) itself.
One who is "cooked" (rāddha) or "fully perfected" (saṃsiddha) is understood to be liberated;
one joined with the virtuous Viṣṇu is considered a liberated youth.
Since youth is eternal for this liberated one, he is "the Youthful" (Yuvan); and because he has attained the fruit of study, he is called "the Student" (Adhyāyaka).
He is praised as "learned" (āśiṣṭa) because he has attained the bliss of the cessation [of mental fluctuations],
and he is declared "most steadfast" (dṛḍhiṣṭha) because he remains established without deviation from that state.
One who is powerful by nature becomes liberated solely [of that power];
the statement "this earth is his," and so forth, is made with reference to his previous state of existence.
Having stated that "he alone" experiences happiness within the course of worldly existence,
he further declares that for the Vedic scholar there is a state of self-hood a hundred times greater than that of the liberated man.
For one who has entered the cycle of existence, it is fitting that the merit of one who has departed from it be more than a hundredfold;
this is seen to be declared by the Śruti for one who is liberated from the liberated.
And it is logical that there should be a superiority of the result corresponding to the superiority of the means, as seen among the gods and others;
for if there were no such superiority in the result, why would there be effort in the means?

And great effort is observed on the part of those high-souled ones; for where there is an abundance of means, there is an abundance of the goal to be accomplished. If this were not seen as a rule, they would not exert themselves so readily.
It is precisely because of the difficulty of its accomplishment that it is not spoken of as if it were liberation.
Rudra performed penance for ten kalpas in the salt ocean; having renounced all pleasures, he was tormented by the salty water. (Manu 3.4.37)
For ten million years, Śakra drank smoke with extreme suffering;
and for ten thousand years, Sūrya performed austerities with his head hanging downwards.
Having renounced pleasure with great difficulty through dharma, he who slept in the open air drank the mass of my nectar for a thousand years with the utmost reverence.
"For even those who know Brahman exert effort with great difficulty;
how can all this be so, given that there is no difference in their liberation? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.40)
"The divine nature leads to liberation, while the demonic is considered to lead to bondage"—
thus has the distinction regarding liberation been declared by the Blessed One himself.

Therefore, you should worship that very one with your own mental dispositions, through the virtues of mind, speech, and body, and by means of your own duties— being free from deceit— for the sake of accomplishing the goals determined by your respective capacities, at the lotus feet of the wish-fulfilling tree.
Friends with eyes and ears have become unequal in the swiftness of their thoughts;
some appear like ponds reaching to the mouth or the armpits, while others look as if they have bathed in deep lakes.
And such statements as these clearly declare the gradation leading to liberation; by what, then, could equality among those who are liberated be understood? (Manusmṛti 3.4.44)
And the equality expressed in the scriptural statement of equality is understood as the equality in the absence of suffering and so forth;
for while inequality exists due to the presence of qualities such as devotion and the like, it is stated in the *Bhārata* that excellence in means is also mentioned everywhere.
The nature of the Lord, who is of terrible form and the destroyer of the three worlds, is difficult to comprehend even for the gods, the sages, the perfected ones, and the great yogis.
By those who are ever-disciplined, highly fortunate, liberated from the fear of afflictions, possessed of great energy and great fortitude, steadfast in their being, and resolute; (4.47)

By those who know the origin and dissolution of the knowledge of the past and the future, and who are endowed with purity, self-study, contentment, austerity, truthfulness, and compassion; (Manu 3.4.48)
How much less so by mortals who are beset by fear, delusion, distraction, and the affliction of disease,
and whose lifespan, vigor, intellect, courage, resolve, learning, and vows are all meager?
O God, it is difficult for anyone other than me to know You, who are both intoxicated and sober;
only Brahman knows something of You, for indeed no one else can.
"Even among those who are liberated and perfected, O Great-minded One, one whose soul is perfectly tranquil and who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa is extremely rare, even among tens of millions."
From whom this creation arose— whether he fashioned it or whether he did not—
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he truly knows, or perhaps even he does not know.
He who has himself realized the manifestation of his own self-illusion—how could others, such as the wind-god, know him?
Even Brahmā does not truly know him here; how then could other gods, lords of sages, or mortals?
Salutations to you, the immeasurable reality and the source of dharma and the other goals;
you are beyond all qualities and the supreme limit—how could I know you, and how much less anyone else?
Neither I, nor the sages headed by Marīci, know that which has been created by Him, for they too are attached to beings;
and since even the lords, Daityas, and mortals have their minds deluded by His māyā, what need is there to mention those whose conduct is eternally unwholesome?

I am Mahendra, Nirṛti, Pracetas, Soma, Agni, Īśa, Pavana, Arka, and Viriñca; likewise the Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the hosts of Rudras together with the Siddhas. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.56)

And others who are creators of the universe, lords of the immortals, such as Bhṛgu and the rest—who, though their nature is dominated by goodness (sattva), are touched by Māyā and do not know His purpose—how much less so those others who are touched by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas)? ||| 3.4.57 ||
O King, Brahmā is traditionally held to have been born at the beginning of the eon; immediately after that deity, he knows the foremost of gods, and even more than that, O ruler of men.
They shall not surpass you in any way even in liberation;
through the yoga of devotion to me and through knowledge, you shall surpass them all.
Just as a distinction in devotion is seen here toward Puruṣottama,
so too is there a distinction in liberation for the knowers when the subtle body is cast off.
Even though all the gods and others have attained union [with the Divine], they nevertheless remain in a state of gradation; for there is indeed a gradation in their spiritual practice.
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection;
and even among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
He who shall proclaim this supreme secret among my devotees,
having established the highest devotion toward me, will undoubtedly come to me alone.
And among human beings, there shall be no one who does me greater service than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he.
And whoever shall study this righteous dialogue between us, by him I am worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction.
Even that man who merely hears this with faith and without malice shall be liberated and attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
Some perceive the Self within the self by means of meditation through the self;
others by means of Sāṅkhya yoga, and still others by means of the yoga of action.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others;
they too certainly cross over death, being devoted to what they have heard.
Lord Viṣṇu, though he is of all forms, always perceives his own self together with all its subtlest and most minute particulars.
And everywhere else, nothing else is likewise unseen by him anywhere;
however, even Ramā herself beholds the Lord everywhere and at all times.
Yet they do not perceive him as superior to others through all his particular qualities;
for he indeed perceives his own self and everything else in their entirety at all times.
Brahmā indeed perceives the all-pervading [Self] as superior even to the qualities (guṇas);
however, one who has not attained liberation does not perceive it in that way at all times.
But once liberated, he should always perceive [all things] through his omnipresence;
for like Ramā, he would never be able to perceive specific objects.
One should always perceive one's own self and others through all their specific qualities; likewise, one should perceive speech along with its various forms, yet not as limited to them.
Beyond the three gunas, one should behold Hari, who pervades everything a hundredfold.
Giriśa and Garuḍa indeed perceive Hari as having entered into pure darkness;
yet they do not perceive even those particularities that are seen by speech.
As long as Umā and Suparṇī perceive the Great Principle (mahattattva),
they shall never perceive the specific manifestations (viśeṣa) seen by Rudra.
Except for the liberated ones, all the gods— including Indra, Kāma, and Brahmā, down to the level of the ego— know both their own true nature and other natures.
Manu, Dakṣa, and the others, perceiving Hari, see him as abiding in the principle of the intellect (buddhi);
but Soma and Sūrya perceive the Supreme Lord as abiding in the mind (manas).
Other gods always perceive Viṣṇu abiding within the elements; after many thousands of years, they perceive him here and there within the principle of Mahat.
Others see Hari abiding within the cosmic egg according to their fitness;
others see him as the Lord of Śvetadvīpa within their hearts; and even there, some occasionally behold Keśava.
O Umā, as many infinite portions of Vāsudeva’s specific qualities as were previously perceived, those very same ones are subsequently observed when they are described.
And Śakra, Kāma, and the others declare that even the specific excellences residing in Brahmā are but a hundredth part of those possessed by the enlightened ones, such as Umā and the rest.
From such statements in the Vedas and Smṛtis,
a gradation of both the liberated souls and their means of attainment is seen according to their true nature.
By whom could this unobserved discrepancy between the goal and the means be imagined?
Through that [discrepancy], both partiality and cruelty would accrue to the Supreme Lord;
however, these two objections are refuted by the Lord of Knowledge on the grounds that He is dependent [on other factors]. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.84)
Due to the gradations of the means of accomplishment, there is a corresponding gradation of the results;
yet, because the Lord is sovereign, there is always no partiality or inequality in the Supreme Lord.

"Even though the Supreme Lord possesses absolute sovereignty, there is no fault in His dependence on beginningless diversity [of karma] regarding the means of accomplishment and so forth; such is His teaching.
For it has been stated that this is indeed logical because of its beginninglessness. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.86)
The nature of the goal exists in accordance with the disparity of the means employed;
with what [rule] of mine would this be in conflict? It is observed even in the case of kings and others.
The renunciation of what is perceived and the postulation of the unperceived are extremely difficult to accomplish;
why should these be undertaken by anyone other than the illusionists, and for what purpose by other disputants?
In this world, deceivers are recognized by their neglecting what they have heard and their grasping for what they have not heard;
even in these signs of deceivers, what faults could be greater than those? (Manu 3.4.89)
For those whose defects have been entirely eliminated over many births, direct perception of Hari indeed arises; how then could hatred, envy, or the like exist for them?
If envy and the like were to arise even toward equals, why would they not feel it?
Even those possessed of hatred, envy, and other such traits are seen in the world to be tormented upon seeing their equals; therefore, it is these very defects that are the cause in this matter.
If there is faultlessness in that [other system], why is it excessively censured?
If envy and the like are restrained because of the absence of seeing other [systems],
how can lack of interest and the like be restrained by that same reason of not seeing them?

Even Brahmā, having previously seen [the world] alone, felt a lack of delight; he did not find joy being solitary, for no one finds joy in solitude. Therefore, the Vedas declare that he desired a second.
If it is imagined that there is no desire for that [result] at all, such an assumption is false;
why not simply accept the very faultlessness declared by the Śruti? 3.4.94.
But having completely set aside gradation, desire, and sacred revelation,
by what person who considers himself logical could equality be postulated for those who have not heard the scriptures?
What measure of equality do you perceive among those who are liberated?
Why this futile insistence on abandoning what has been heard and grasping what has not been heard? (Manu 3.96)
"Even in liberation there is gradation because of sentience, just as before"—what answer have you, who propound a doctrine based on mere imagination, to this? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.97)
Nor can suffering and the like be attributed [to him], by virtue of the scriptural statement that he is free from suffering:
"The knower of the Self transcends sorrow; having crossed over, he partakes in no suffering whatsoever. (Manu 3.4.98)
By which one becomes truly joyful and never grieves;
he is the remover of sin, the winner of paternal wealth, the benefactor here, and the lord.

"Whatever end one desires to reach, that he shall attain here through his resolve"—such scriptural passages are the authority for the attainment of states such as freedom from suffering. (Manu 3.4.100)
Therefore, no room is found here for an inference based on suffering and the like;
thus, an inference based on gradation would not lead to an over-extension.
Thus, through the very power of scripture and reasoning, this gradation is discerned;
therefore, who here is capable of creating a contradiction even regarding liberation?
Who is able to restrain the fitness for beginning [the study] and its limit, which is the Lord of Speech at the end of the Kali age, when it is elevated by the power of reasoning and scripture?
Time, when associated with excess, leads to dispute apart from Brahman; for let this time not become a source of pride for those who measure by means of inference. (Manu 3.4.104)
The word "other" (anya) is employed with the intention of denoting those other than Hari, Śrī, and one's own kinsmen;
it does not constitute a fault when applied to Rudra and others according to reason.
Even for those who are liberated, there can be no superiority over Brahman;
rather, there would be a manifestation of bliss, but not an increase in the bliss itself.
Moreover, Brahman always possesses superiority in strength and knowledge over them;
for no proof is found that this superiority is non-eternal.
The hero is heard of as subduing every fierce one, leading each one beyond the other;
Indra, the king of both worlds whose enmity increases, overcomes the human tribes.
Indra casts aside his friendships with the former ones and moves forward, racing with others; shaking off those who have not attained him, Indra traverses many autumns.
Day after day, he drove away the dark ones who were like others from their dwellings;
the bull, desiring wealth, slew the two Dāsas, Varcin and Śambara, within the enclosure of the waters.

The gods meditated upon it as "Bhūti" (Prosperity); they became prosperous, and therefore even now, when one sleeps, one breathes out saying, "Bhū-bhū. The Asuras meditated upon it as "Abhūti" (Non-prosperity), and they were utterly defeated.

Just as a weaver takes a measure of cloth and weaves another form that is newer and more beautiful, even so this Self, having cast off this body and caused ignorance to depart, fashions for itself another form that is newer and more beautiful—whether belonging to the fathers, or... (the text continues with other realms).
Whether it be the Gāndharva, the Daiva, the Prājāpatya, the Brāhma, or that of other beings.
They swiftly attain the supreme perfection pertaining to this world and the next—
a state that is unattainable by all the asuras, imperishable, and free from affliction;
no men reach that goal except for the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas).
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
Futile are their hopes, futile their actions, and futile their knowledge;
they are devoid of discernment, having resorted to a delusive nature that is both demonic and titanic.
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.117.

Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, refraining from slander, compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (Manu Smṛti 3.118)
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and freedom from excessive pride—these belong to one born with a divine nature, O Bhārata. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.119)
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness,
and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.

Those who hate me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being envious and malicious— those cruel haters, the lowest of men, I perpetually cast into transmigrations among the very wombs of the Asuras, which are inauspicious.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they fail to reach me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state.
In this world, the creation of beings is of two kinds: divine and demonic;
that which is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu is divine, while the opposite is demonic.
The supreme duty of the gods is always ritual acts such as sacrifices,
the study of the Vedas, the knowledge of reality, and the traditional teaching of devotion to the worship of Viṣṇu.
The Daityas possess strength of arm, envy, skill in battle,
proficiency in the treatises on policy, devotion to the worship of Śiva, and traditional learning.
Adherence to the conduct of one's caste and stage of life, Vedic study, and devotion to Acyuta,
Śiva, Sūrya, and likewise to the Goddess— this is known as the natural state of humanity.
The deities are by their very nature eternal Vaiṣṇavas from time immemorial; the Daityas, on the other hand, have always been their opposites since beginningless time.

"Human beings have mixed dispositions and mixed destinies as well"—from such a collection of statements, it is understood that there is beginningless fitness (*anādi-yogyatā*). *Mānava-dharma-śāstra* 3.4.128.
If the specific difference is beginningless, how can it be so at present?
Furthermore, by asserting that the unseen arises solely from the unseen, all theorists have accepted [this very principle].

If it is claimed that a particular excellence occurs spontaneously in some cases where no visible cause is seen, then everything would be spontaneous; there would be no dependence on an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*).
If this particular excellence arises from the unseen, then why is its beginninglessness not accepted?
And no difference is perceived in Viṣṇu by those who perceive Him, as there is in other distinct things;
rather, it is recognition alone that is seen even among His many forms.
Furthermore, plurality is not established by any distinction whatsoever;
and those for whom there is recognition [of identity]—they too have their vision obscured by that [ignorance]. (Manu 3.4.132)
They do not perceive any distinction within themselves, nor do they perceive any distinction from others;
Hari reveals himself to them in this way, and not otherwise.
Thus, a statement in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* is not found in the Purāṇas;
one who speaks merely according to worldly observation would be able to contradict the Veda. (Manu 3.4.134)
One who possesses an unexamined view and one who views things preceded by critical examination are both capable of refuting [an opponent], yet only the latter is capable of contradicting the Veda.
And there is no scriptural authority for the perception of a difference that has already been ascertained;
for in some cases, a statement is understood there as referring to a perception that is still indistinct.
In this matter, the piercing and other such rites of the presiding deity are indeed unexamined;
no one anywhere ever perceives them when subjected to critical examination.
Brahmā beheld him as entirely faultless and possessing every form; Rudra likewise saw him as faultless, and Purandara saw him as faultless.
"The forms of this [Viṣṇu] have been seen as faultless by the best of the gods;
all others are possessed of faults, but Hari alone is faultless. From this statement in the *Barku-śruti*, it follows that his vision is not defective.
"Though unpierced, Viṣṇu appears as if pierced; though unborn, he falsely appears as if born;
and though unbound, he appears as if bound—thus does the Paiṅgi Śruti proclaim the faultlessness of Hari. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.140)
"Only by an unexamined vision is Hari seen as having faults;
in the vision of examination, no fault of Hari is ever seen.
Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti, for that which has been examined is indeed the authoritative means of knowledge.

There would be no infinite regress of investigation, for that which is established by direct perception is free from doubt. Faults may exist in mental cognition, but certainly not in direct perception. That wherein a most firm conviction arises should be known as direct perception. (Manu Smṛti 8.142)

Desire, knowledge, pleasure, pain, fear, fearlessness, compassion, and so forth, are established by the witness-consciousness; for no one anywhere has any doubt regarding them. As for that mental perception which might sometimes be erroneous, it is indeed [only] that [which is fallible]. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.143)
That perception alone is to be considered examined, in which the validity of even mental and visual perception has been well-ascertained by the witness-consciousness.
Its validity is not seen by means of mere intellectual insight;
rather, its validity regarding pleasure and other such experiences is invariably within the range of direct perception.
The Witness always perceives the validity of knowledge with absolute certainty,
for the measure of validity is determined by the Witness alone, who is the apprehender of cognition.
In the absence of defects, the status of being a valid means of knowledge is established by the witness-consciousness;
and in some cases, the validity of cognition is held to be self-evident.
Therefore, the validity of all means of knowledge would not be established;
rather, that which is ascertained by a witness is the defining characteristic of validity.
For no person entertains doubt regarding pleasure and the like,
nor does every person ascertain all means of valid cognition.
Therefore, why should one deny that which is established by experience? Furthermore, the witness perceives correctly the absence of defects and so forth.
There is no fault whatsoever in Viṣṇu when He is measured by such a standard;
for in what matter is there not found a perspective that fails to examine?
Therefore, when a matter contradicts what is perceived by direct perception, even scripture lacks authority;
for in such a case, that which is born of the senses is what must be relied upon, whereas in other cases, it is the opposite.
In this worldly transaction, perception is that upon which [the other means of knowledge] depend; in the observation of the descent [of the sacred law], scripture is that upon which they depend.
For it is by means of scripture that Viṣṇu-hood is known; thus, a fault is imputed here [to one who denies it].
If he were not [Viṣṇu], then another would be faulty; for the defining characteristic is established by the sacred texts.

If the mere fact that someone possesses faults were sufficient for it to be produced by the senses, then there would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Viṣṇu’s possession of faults; however, such direct perception does not occur spontaneously.
Some perceive faults even in this [Vedic injunction], yet it is not something produced by the senses;
the ancient word itself is what contradicts that [perception] through its very revelation.
The Veda alone is the source upon which the Purāṇa depends, and nothing else; how then could it be an authority when it contradicts that Veda? (Manu 3.4.157)
And how could that which is seen without examination be born of the senses?
If this were so, why would an error regarding Devadatta and others not also be born of the senses?

In an investigation according to one's ability, there is no fault in subverting that which is being relied upon; however, if it has not been purified, the fault remains, for mere reliance is not sufficient.
Even in an error, there exists a portion that is not erroneous;

for it is by depending upon that alone that the operation of a subverting cognition occurs. However, this is not the case when [an object] has been thoroughly examined, because every means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) functions precisely by depending upon that [thorough examination].

How is that Brahman to be known? It is characterized by omniscience and other such qualities; for if it were merely its own essential nature, it would have to be abandoned as something indeterminate. (Manu 3.4.161)
To the extent that dependence upon this [teacher] is excluded,
to that same extent there is no dependence whatsoever on the *svarapa* itself.
If, however, it is said that the essential nature [of the self] is endowed with all characteristics, then let it be so;
for us there would be no loss at all, and this would directly support our own position.
Since the meaning of words is in every respect always accompanied by both the particular and the universal, their entire nature consists of these two.

In the case of an error regarding Devadatta and others, the properties beginning with "being present before one" exclude that form [of the object] solely by means of Caitra, even without [the cognition of] Devadatta himself.
Since Brahman is devoid of distinctions, what indeed could it exclude?
If [the opponent claims exclusion] from some object or other whatsoever, then that would merely be proving what is already established.
And for one who maintains that there is no distinction, pure consciousness alone cannot be desired;
if that were all there is, why would omniscience not belong to it? (Manu 3.4.167)
Even though the non-difference from pure consciousness is what is to be proven, that [consciousness] is already established for the opponent;
for he himself accepts his own non-difference from it, since he holds that even his own self is consciousness.
If it is argued that omniscience arises from dependence on all [objects], that is not so;
for consciousness itself is knowledge, and knowledge is never devoid of an object of knowledge.
Furthermore, he does not consider this [object] to be "knowable by itself" in an absolute sense;

even the word "self" (sva) is dependent upon something else. Therefore, it is taught that the meaning of the word "self" is indeed exclusion (vyāvṛtti). If it were not so, what would "own-form" (svarūpa) actually be?
Because it is already complete by the word "form" (rūpa), that [word] expresses a general property;
it cannot denote the specific intrinsic nature (svarūpa) itself, for that would result in the redundancy of the suffix.
For the very nature of consciousness is proclaimed to be sentience;
therefore, sentience possesses a multiplicity of specific qualities by virtue of its particularity.

For knowledge can never exist anywhere devoid of both the object of knowledge and the knower; nor is there any authority for the claim that there exists a knower devoid of both the object of knowledge and knowledge itself.
If knowledge were devoid of both the knower and the knowable,
then the act of eating would be a mere eating, just as striking would be a mere striking if it were devoid of both the striker and the struck.

If it is argued that because it is eternal, such [speech] would exist, then even eternal speech would be devoid of both the expressed object and the speaker; yet it is not the case that it is of such a nature.
For there are indeed seers of the Vedic words, and the things to be expressed are directly present;
and the Blessed One himself is both the eternal seer and the object to be expressed.
For there is never any speech devoid of a speaker or devoid of a subject to be expressed;
likewise, knowledge devoid of a knower and an object to be known would not even exist.
For there exists no speaker, even if eternal, who is devoid of sentence and its referent;
likewise, there exists no knower, even if he is wise, who is bereft of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Furthermore, by what means of knowledge is the annihilation of everything apprehended?
If that statement and its meaning are grasped along with everything else, then there can be no denial of anything on account of the absence of that [statement]. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.179)
If it is not perceived, then by that same logic, there can be no denial anywhere;
for the meaning of a statement devoid of logical justification is not understood.
For among the marks such as direct application and the rest, each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding;
and among the means of proof beginning with direct audition, each preceding one is stronger, according to the determination of the Brahma-tarka.

When direct perception, logical reasoning, and many scriptural authorities conflict, and there is no objective reality that does not contradict the inferential mark (liṅga). Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.182.
How can that very same meaning be accepted when a consistent and primary sense is available? Where is such a figurative interpretation ever prohibited? (Manu 3.4.183)
Therefore, Brahman alone is indeed endowed with all qualities and is worthy of acceptance;
moreover, the denial of everything is in no way tenable.

And the fitness for non-attachment has been stated; therefore, it must be accepted in every respect. Furthermore, the gradations among those who are liberated cannot be overturned by the aforementioned means of valid cognition.
Since even the wise always perform only what is auspicious,
the degree of excellence in liberation is determined by that very same [performance].
If there were no gradation in liberation, why would they perform auspicious deeds again?
For these very people practice austerity, knowledge, and ritual action even with great difficulty.
They always fear the inauspicious and always desire the auspicious;
yet this is not merely their inherent nature, because they proceed with fear as a precursor and because they practice what is auspicious again and again only with great difficulty. (Manu 3.188)
If such a nature were to belong even to an ignorant person, then it would be so;
for if there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its fruitfulness, that applies equally to the learned person as well. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.189)
Action performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is called "withdrawn" (nivṛtta) here;
by practicing that which is withdrawn, one attains the eternal Brahman.
Through auspiciousness there shall be an increase in joy, whereas through inauspiciousness there is indeed a decline;
therefore, even for the wise, they must perform only what is auspicious.
He who worships the Self does not perish, nor is his ritual action lost;
for from this very Self he creates whatever he desires. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.192)
"For even one who performs many rituals, if he is ignorant, shall obtain only a finite result;
but whatever one performs with knowledge, that indeed becomes exceedingly powerful"—by the force of such statements, there exists a gradation leading to liberation. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.193)
And here it is not the fruit of the lay follower alone that is said to be inexhaustible;
for nowhere can there be inexhaustibility of fruit without knowledge. If [the inexhaustibility] is by way of knowledge, then it does not contradict our position.
For even in this way, the knowledge of Jñānottara is indeed inexhaustible, and not otherwise;
for the merit of previous virtuous deeds finds its fulfillment through knowledge alone.
But for those actions already commenced, their entry into liberation occurs through experience; otherwise, there would be no performance of them subsequent to that knowledge.
All auspicious acts performed prior to the attainment of knowledge are for the sake of achieving that knowledge;
those performed without desire and those prohibited lead to the obstruction of knowledge and to worldly enjoyment.
And whatever abundance of merit exists from the beginning by the force of one's fitness—that is indeed an abundance of knowledge; it is not the cause of anything else.
Because devotion is a constituent part of knowledge, devotion is said to be knowledge;
that which is called devotion is simply a particular form of knowledge.
Just as the qualities of being indirect and direct belong to knowledge,
so too the connection with affection would likewise be a quality belonging to the object of knowledge.
With this intention, the Śrutis generally declare that knowledge alone leads to liberation; yet, this distinction is also indeed proclaimed.
Devotion and knowledge— never indeed is a vision joined with hatred conducive to the goals of human life, for it contradicts all the sacred scriptures.
For the conscious being, there are two things to be experienced: saṃsāra and liberation.
Therein, saṃsāra is threefold: heaven, the intermediate state, and the lower realms. (Manu 3.203)

In that regard, liberation is of two kinds: eternal happiness and likewise the other, which should be known as eternal suffering; even within the cycle of worldly existence, the means [to these] consist of desirable action and prohibited action—this is the certainty regarding ignorance.
"Both hatred and devotion bring about two kinds of liberation," according to the Paiṅgi Śruti; thus, hatred is certainly not a cause for true liberation. (Manu 3.4.205)
And Keśava is the cause of non-liberation and of liberation;
for he grants liberation, which is denoted by the word "mukti," to his own devotees. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.206)
If liberation were possible even through hatred, it would obstruct the great purpose [of spiritual life];
rather, all the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Āgamas declare that liberation comes from the God through devotion and grace, by praising His very qualities.

If liberation were to come through hatred, then the entire collection of faults would have to be stated; for it is with this very purpose that the Blessed One sometimes spoke of virtues as if out of hatred, like the words of one who is angry, as in the Purāṇas. (Manu 3.4.208)
Just as an angry father, having first uttered a reproach such as "Kill my son," speaks thus for the sake of another task, so it is said in the Purāṇas.
A statement that directly contradicts the Vedas, contradicts itself,
or conflicts with many traditional scriptures cannot be a declaration of liberation, especially if it arises from malice.
"Through hatred they go to darkness, and likewise through devotion to liberation;
[they attain it] in Viṣṇu by Viṣṇu’s grace, or swiftly by the reverse. Thus, even the statement regarding the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) serves as a regulator for the meaning already stated.
And if the great purport is obstructed, how can a statement attain the status of valid authority? For the great purport is held to consist of all the meanings [of the sentence]. (Manu 3.4.212)
For the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is indeed the capacity to denote, that which all sounds signify;
how could such a meaning be abandoned when there is doubt regarding even a single word?
Therefore, through knowledge and devotion, the supreme human goal shall be attained. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.213)
For that great-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the teacher as he does the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly.

From devotion comes knowledge, from that comes devotion, from that comes vision, and from that, liberation; thereafter, there is devotion again—that very same devotion which is the embodiment of bliss.
The Blessed One, pleased by devotion, would grant untroubled knowledge;
having attained his vision through that very devotion, he would grant liberation through it.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form; one may grant liberation only through this [knowledge].
But by means of undivided devotion alone, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe.
"From such statements as these, this aforementioned meaning is understood:
one does not obtain grace through hatred, but one may attain him through devotion.
Thus, even the conformity with observed experience is understood in this matter. (Manu 3.4.219)
Those qualities of Viṣṇu which have been respectfully set forth separately by the Veda—those alone must be accepted when they are perceived to be consistent; nothing else.
Other [matters] may also be accepted regarding Vāsudeva according to what is observed,
provided that one does not abandon those absences of fault which have been declared by the Vedas.
Moreover, even those [rules] not explicitly stated are to be understood through the power of the great purport;
for it is thus that the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* declares its own established doctrine.
Since devotion toward his devotees is also determined by degrees of excellence, this devotion too must be practiced in accordance with worldly custom and the Vedas. (Manu 3.223)
For he who is devoted to the principal [teacher] is necessarily seen to be devoted to his [the teacher's] dependents as well; conversely, the opposite is true in the case of the reverse.
If there is infidelity in any case, a decline in devotion is to be inferred here;
for this is a defect of devotion, namely that one is not devoted even toward those who are devoted to Him.
Devotion toward them should be performed according to their relative degree, as observed in actual experience and in accordance with the grace of Viṣṇu; otherwise, there is fault.
Affection is indeed seen even in the world to follow from one's own affection;
by this very means, the knowledge of degrees of excellence is also established.
Lakṣmī, Viriñca, Vāṇīśa, Girijā, Indrāṅgiras,
and the Sun and others, in their respective order, are the objects of the Blessed One’s favor.
Devotion to these must always be practiced in due order by those seeking liberation;
for all of them are indeed the gurus of a person at all times.
"Therefore, Hari is to be honored, saluted, and meditated upon on all sides"—
from this statement regarding the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), this meaning is also determined.
Devotion to Hari leads in due order to the remembrance of His devotees,
the praise of Hari, the remembrance of Him, the praise of them, and the worship of Hari.

"Renunciation prescribed for that worship is indeed the gradual means to liberation; for by this rule, all [means] are to be practiced constantly until their goal is achieved. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.232)
Thus, when the discourse on the means of accomplishment has proceeded toward its determination,
there is indeed an absolute certainty regarding the means once the Pañcarātra has been set in motion.
Hatred toward Hari does not bestow auspiciousness,

because it is hatred [toward a worthy object], just as [hatred] toward a teacher [does not]. Conversely, devotion [toward him] gradually becomes the cause of Hari’s pleasure, for it approaches that which is dear to him.
For devotion toward him is just as it is toward oneself; such is the reasoning applied here.
Devotion is supreme when it conforms to the degree of preeminence [of the object],
because it brings joy to Hari, just as devotion directed toward oneself does.
Or rather, the fruit of knowledge, action, and so forth accrues to these [officiants] in successive order;
for the fruit of those who possess the fruit arises according to the degree of their independence.

But for these [servants], even an impure object becomes pure because of their independence, their joy, and the command of Hari; and it never fails to become a source of enjoyment when directed toward others.
"He attains merit alone, not sin; he does not reach the gods"—such scriptural passages (śruti) are the authority for this matter, as are other logical arguments (yukti). Mānava 3.4.238.
For the fruit of the dharma of worship is residence in another body,
by the command of Vāsudeva and in accordance with one's prior karma.
For they constantly impel living beings toward merit and sin;
being free from both attachment and aversion, how could they incur any fault?
Merely by carrying out Hari’s command, merit is obtained by these [servants];
how then could they not attain auspiciousness through the performance of Hari’s worship?
Therefore, O gods, the fruit of dharma and knowledge is swiftly attained by all living beings, from the lowest creatures up to Brahmā, in due order.
For indeed, among the gods, the gods themselves are the most distinguished and the controllers;
but Brahmā is the controller of all the gods and of men.
Therefore, he attains more of all excellent qualities than anyone else.

The fruit of the gods' [sacrifices] is superior due to their independence over the materials, their consciousness, and their effort; for even that which belongs to others among them is indeed [the fruit] of Brahmā.
This statement regarding the determination of results was uttered by Hari in the *Bṛhattantra*;
for even in the world, an abundance of results is indeed observed through such qualities.
And thus, for those Asuras who were preceded by the Kali age, there would always be a great fruit in their evil deeds, such as false knowledge and the like.
The gods and the asuras shall obtain the fruits of their good and evil deeds in due order, according to their capacity and according to who was the instigator of each act.
"Even though they may incite others to sin, the gods do not incur sin";
thus indeed did Hari declare directly in the *Prakāśikā*. (Manu 3.4.248)
Even so, although there is great fruit for both gods and Daityas from good and evil deeds, it shall accrue to the doer exactly as has been described.
Therefore, starting from the highest of men, gods experience the enjoyments of hell, the human realm, heaven, and liberation; however, [the gods] exclude hell.
"But the Asuras, without liberation, shall even attain blinding darkness"—this is the word spoken by the Blessed One himself in the *Tattvaviveka*. (Manu 3.4.251)
Moreover, teachers who bestow knowledge shall obtain a special reward;
the preceptor receives eight times the merit of the disciple, provided it is auspicious.

The teacher is twice as venerable as that; the son of the teacher is twice as venerable as him; others are equal to that [teacher] plus a half; and the gods are ten thousand times more venerable than those, in successive order.
"Brahmā has thus determined the fruit as multiplied by a great flood;
so the Blessed One himself declared in the treatise titled *Guruvṛtta*.
And that is logical: one who gives a cow shall not obtain merely the fruit of a single cow."
He who shall proclaim this supreme secret among my devotees,
having established supreme devotion toward me, will undoubtedly come to me alone.
"And there shall be no one among men who does more for me than he,
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he"—
thus the Blessed One has spoken; yet even so, the recipient is taken into account.
In this very way, through non-opposition, knowledge is declared to have its fruit seen in the very karma that has already begun; and liberation is attained even here in this world.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

When the reality [of Brahman] has been established through both positive concomitance and non-contradiction, and when all possible means of proof have been specifically examined in their entirety; (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.1)
That which must always be done, the means that will certainly come to pass, should first be considered; in that regard, the performance of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth occurs but once.
When there is doubt as to whether repetition should be performed or not, repetition must indeed be performed;
for the instruction "That thou art," and so forth, occurs precisely more than once.
Before Lātavya, from the lineage of Ṛju, after a hundred generations,
he heard of one named Ugratapas who was worthy of the station of Rudra.
For half a parārdha, he remained constantly diligent in devotion to the qualities of Viṣṇu; with a concentrated mind, he performed worship for one-third of that period.

For ten *manvantaras*, Sunanda heard from Garuḍa that he was worthy of Śakra’s position; from Sumana, who was himself worthy of that position, he heard it as well. Diligently devoted, he performed his service for four sets of *manvantaras*.
Possessing great splendor, they were worthy of the feet of the sun and the moon;
Surūpa and Śāntarūpa remained for four *manvantaras*, serving with well-disposed minds those who did not hear [the Veda]. (Manu 4.1.7)

Then all of them— Bhakti, Ugratapas, and the others— having been thus addressed by Viṣṇu himself in the work known as the *Sattattva*, beheld the Supreme Viṣṇu, ever nourished by His grace. (Manusmṛti 4.1.8)
Indeed, the name "Ātman" is declared to be that of Nārāyaṇa himself;
he is the Self, Brahman, the Great One, the Savior, the Supreme Lord, and the one of pure fame.
"Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Ananta—thus is the Lord of Śrī proclaimed.
So says the Piṅga-śruti, and likewise the Parama-śruti.
Oṃ! The Blessed Viṣṇu is the Self, the bliss of the Self, the imperishable, the self-ruling Lord;
he is the protector of the universe, Nṛsiṃha, the unborn, Nārāyaṇa, and the wide-striding.
In the same way, Anasūyā bore to Atri sinless sons born from the self, Īśa, and Brahmā: Datta, Durvāsas, and Soma. (Manu 4.12)
Thus it is stated in the Bhāgavata; therefore, Janārdana is the Self, and consequently, Viṣṇu is to be worshipped—this should always be known by the virtuous.
The virtuous worship Him in that very way and likewise instruct others in that same manner.
Furthermore, because it signifies the act of taking possession (*ādāna*), this word "Self" (*ātman*) denotes the Lord;
thus, one should rightly and eternally worship Viṣṇu as "Viṣṇu is my Master. (Manu Smṛti 4.14)
The meditation "Viṣṇu is the Lord" should be performed by means of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified;
this must be done in every way and should never be forgotten.
Thus, the truth concerning the principles of existence and the supreme discourse on the six qualities:
"My master is Hari, who is eternally the Lord of all"—in this way, the imperishable Blessed Viṣṇu should always be meditated upon. (Manusmṛti 4.16)
One should not perform the meditation on Viṣṇu by treating him as a mere symbol (*pratīka*), for the symbol is not Viṣṇu himself; indeed, false worship leads to misfortune.
What sin is not committed by that thief who steals his own self, who perceives the Self and the Lord as something other than they truly are? (Manu 4.18)
What sin is not committed by that thief who steals the Lord, who represents himself as one thing while being another? (Manu 4.19)
What sin has not been committed by that thief in the guise of a religious student who perceives Viṣṇu, who exists in one way, as being otherwise?
Whether one meditates upon oneself, or a statue, or another deity, or something else sentient or insentient, thinking "this is Keśava"—
what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals the Lord? (Manu Smṛti 4.121)
He who meditates upon another as Viṣṇu, or likewise knows Hari as such,
shall sink into blind darkness from which there is no emergence anywhere.
He who meditates on Viṣṇu as being something else, or thinks that Viṣṇu is something else,
sinks into the great darkness by the fault of such erroneous meditation.
He who meditates on Viṣṇu as being something else, or on something else as being Viṣṇu,
has no emergence at all from the great darkness into which he has sunk.
Whatever is meditated upon incorrectly as being otherwise than it truly is, that immediately brings great fault upon the meditator; how much more so in the case of Hari, the Lord of All?
Whatever is established as one thing but is knowingly perceived otherwise, that causes great fault; how much more so in the case of Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords?
Whatever exists in one way and is perceived in another way is a cause of misfortune in this world; how much more so the Lord of all lords?
Nothing whatsoever should be known or meditated upon by him as being otherwise anywhere;
how much less should Viṣṇu, the supreme of all, ever be perceived as inferior?
Therefore, an object should always be known and meditated upon exactly as it is, for it is the cause of human purpose; otherwise, it never becomes so at any time.
Thus, by the force of the statements in the Śruti and Purāṇas, [Viṣṇu] is not a mere symbol (pratīka);
for Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon as such in some instances, since false knowledge brings about harm.
Having this in mind, the Lord, the Master, said "not indeed he"; Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon as being established in the symbol (pratīka), and not otherwise.
And the Lord Viṣṇu should always be meditated upon as Brahman;
for the meaning of the word "Brahman" is preeminent, since "brahman-ness" consists in perfection.
"Even for one whose mind is distracted by the causes of mental or physical affliction, the state of Brahman must always be meditated upon through uninterrupted devotion to Viṣṇu";
such is the statement uttered by Viṣṇu in the *Prakāśikā*. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.1.33)
The aphorism "Not the Self" establishes that the Lord is not the individual soul (jīva);

for, taking the word "Self" as the reason, the King of the Vedas [the Upanishads] excluded the individual soul, stating that the vital breath is not [the Self] because of its own specific designation. Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.34.
If the word "Self" (ātman) applies even to the individual soul (jīva), how could it exclude [Viṣṇu]?
Therefore, he who is designated by the word "Self" is Viṣṇu alone, and no other.
Words such as "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman" do not denote that immutable Viṣṇu, because perfection in all qualities is never attained by them;
for the Vaiṣṇava scripture states: "That which pertains to the inner self is indeed Nārāyaṇa. (Manusmṛti 12.123).

If one considers the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), as well as the identity of the knower of the Veda (vedapati), then how can one logically exclude the word "Self" (ātman) from applying to that [Lord]? (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.1.37)
The Lord of the World, with full intention, stated the designation, the maintenance, and the consumption of distinctions as the reason for the firm establishment of those distinctions. (Manu 4.1.38)
If this distinction is merely conventional, where then does the non-conventional exist?
The very statement "it is conventional" itself is conventional.
But if, in the alternative "or not," it were merely conventional,
and if even that were subject to sublation, then the distinction would be ultimate.
If this difference were non-conventional and yet attained the status of reality,
then when one of two contradictory things is unreal,
who could prevent the other from being real? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.41)
When it is said, "I have not spoken an untruth," people understand that truth has been spoken;
but when it is said, "I have not spoken the truth," they also understand the untruthfulness of what was said. (Manu 4.1.42)
Even in a dream, duality is not false; for therein one [aspect] is indeed real.
How could both existence and non-existence therein be false?
For when an entity is negated, there is no negation of its non-existence;
if the unreality of one's own word were thus established, then from that follows the reality of difference.
Therefore, the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) is understood through the reasoning already stated;
for this reason, this word "ātman" must be a designation for the Supreme Self (paramātman).

The visualization of Viṣṇu upon a symbol (pratīka) does not constitute that [visualization] by virtue of the symbol being the object; rather, the worship should indeed be performed with the thought, "Viṣṇu is in this symbol. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.46)
And when the position is that Viṣṇu is not the object of meditation as the "Self" because he is a mere symbol (pratīka),
such that the perception of Brahman here would be contradicted—
then the logical principle "He is not [that]" applies there as well, and thus the contradiction remains as stated.
Even if worship were performed based merely on superiority,
such superiority would belong to the Self as well, since it is conscious compared to that which is unconscious;
therefore, those who know the Veda hold the view that what is not the ultimate reality (atattva) is not to be worshipped.
If, through meditation on Brahman as superior, a fruit were to arise immediately,
why would no calamity not arise from meditating on Brahman as inferior?
Brahman is never pleased by the meditation on himself as being insentient;
rather, like people in the world, Brahman becomes angry when a base person meditates upon himself as identical with his own Self.
When it is said that "the Caṇḍāla is the king," then the king is also the Caṇḍāla;
once the king is fully recognized as such, what distinction could possibly remain?
If a Caṇḍāla is honored in the presence of a king like a king himself, why would the king not become angry? For the king observes the world.
But when it is said in the presence of the king, "The king is a Caṇḍāla," or "He is himself [a Caṇḍāla]," he becomes as if enraged at the mere mention of such words. (MDh 4.153)
If there were no difference between these two, what distinction would there be either in their meditation or even in their speech?
For when it is said of both a Caṇḍāla and a king, "This is a king;
you [are the king]," yet when it is said, "This is a Caṇḍāla," the resulting defilement is exactly the same.
If, when one person meditates, that state [of Brahman] arises for him, why does it not arise for another?
And yet, that Brahman is never unknown to the Omniscient One anywhere.
Therefore, every statement asserting that anything else is Brahman is unrefined;
consequently, Brahman should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation according to the path as it has been described.
In the same way, when Brahman is directly perceived through such meditation, it reduces all prior sin to ashes; it renders even subsequent [sin] non-attached,
and likewise renders the hatred of those who hate it non-attached, as well as the destruction of merit.

In the verse beginning with "yadeva vidyayā," the action previously mentioned is indeed distinguished from what was said before: whereas previously it was enjoined as being efficacious for the sake of attaining heaven and other such rewards, it is subsequently taught that when joined with knowledge, it bestows efficacy toward liberation. (Manu 4.1.58)
Then, having exhausted both merit and its opposite through experience,
one who hates the Veda and one who views the Veda as such attain darkness and liberation respectively.
The destruction of the merit previously begun occurs one hundred kalpas before the end of Brahmā’s life;
for Brahmā himself it lasts for fifty [kalpas],
for Rudra twenty, and for Indra, the Sun, and the others, ten.
"For others, however, there is the destruction of the commenced [karman] at the end of the life of Brahmā;
and then, together with Brahmā himself, he shall go to the supreme Nārāyaṇa"—this statement regarding the true nature of reality was spoken by the Blessed One himself. (Manu 4.1.61)
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
For gods and humans, this much indeed is equal;
however, the paths of departure for the gods will not generally belong to humans.
The exhaustion of karma, the true departure [of the soul], the path, and enjoyment— these four are declared as the fruit,
liberation, taught respectively in the chapters.
But at the dissolution of Brahmā, the entry of those to be created occurs into the creators themselves;
this is declared to be the path of the gods, neither the path of light nor the upward departure.
The body of the Creator, who has become the food, shall undergo dissolution therein;
for there can be no departure of the soul from the God who is the object of creation.
And since the worlds beginning with the Radiant (arcis) also dissolve entirely,
how could there be a path for those entering [heaven] by their own power to reach the supreme state?
Whenever the paths of departure (utkrānti) exist for those born in the world of humans or among the gods, liberation is not then desired.
But the settled conclusion of the scriptures is that even for others, liberation shall be attained directly upon reaching that Hari, together with Brahmā.

When the Supreme Self-existent One, whose nature consists of the three qualities, having experienced his own supreme time and desiring to withdraw [the universe], enters the unmanifest state surrounded by earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, the senses, the objects of the senses, the primary elements, and so forth; (Manu 1.56).
Thus, having passed away and entered into the Blessed One, those yogis who have conquered their breath and mind,
who are free from passion, and who are devoid of egoistic pride, go together with Him alone to the immortal, ancient Person— the Brahman that is the Pradhāna.
Even those yogins who have reached the Blessed One, together with Brahmā,
attain supreme liberation through the dissolution of the subtle body (liṅgabhaṅga).
Having reached the Supreme God together with Brahmā,
they again attain the full manifestation of bliss through the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga*).
This is understood through the force of the statements in the Śrutis and Purāṇas;
for enjoyment exists for all the gods as well as for humans and others. (Manu 4.2.12)
In that regard, the entry of the gods is said to proceed from one to the next in successive order; and the same is true for the functions residing within the body.

In this regard, the proponents of various doctrines describe the nature of liberation differently, based on their own intuition; for the intellects of men arise individually according to the distinction of their qualities, while through darkness alone, misconception arises. (Manu Smṛti 4.2.14)

The intellect of those who have transcended the qualities is unmixed with passion (rajas) and possesses the nature of pure goodness (sattva), because the intellect of the liberated is pure consciousness.
Then, through the power of that very majesty,
Śrī’s intellect became balanced, constant, abundant, exceedingly clear, and indeed lucid.
Because it is the Great Pure Consciousness, it is therefore an even greater consciousness;
it is the vision in which all vast particularities are perceived with extreme clarity.
This supreme intellect of Nārāyaṇa is eternal and of a single uniform nature.
Like the radiance of the sun, they illuminate everything without interruption;
they are untainted, free from defects, and eternally changeless.
Having abandoned the specific qualities residing in the shoulders and for the most part their characteristic marks of beauty,
[the body] remains merely due to the absence of clarity and its dependence on those [qualities];
however, the beauty of Brahman is not like that, for it is for the most part exactly as it was before.
But for those others who have been liberated, existence appears like the waves of the ocean;
and for those whose memory remains, it is like a flame of fire.
Regarding such forms of knowledge, those whose vision is obscured by darkness—

possessing only a very meager understanding like that of a firefly and perceiving things erroneously— propound various views on liberation by relying on diverse doctrines. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.2.21)
Relying on his supreme intuition, the Jina declared therein that liberation from the cage called the body occurs through knowledge and the exhaustion of karma.
Like a bird released from a cage, the person (pudgala), possessing hands and feet, moves eternally upward, having the sky as his domain.

Thus, by what means of knowledge is that which has the nature of liberation perceived? And since upward movement is painful because it is a form of movement, just like worldly movement—what is the answer for one who relies solely on inference when this is said? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.24)

If the inability to fly upward were the limiting condition for the bird in that case, then the suffering experienced during flight to a great height would not follow from the probandum. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.25)
A counter-inference (pratisādhana) is not a refutation of an inference;
for a "counterform" (pratirūpa) is merely a [flawed] means of proof, and nothing else.
Moreover, in this case, corporeality cannot possibly be the limiting condition (*upādhi*),
because corporeality follows upon the probans (*sādhana*) wherever there is the state of being a transmigrator.
Since this reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) does not follow from the scriptures,
it is not the fault of deviating from a tenet (apasiddhānta); for if that were a fault in a reductio, then there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), and no reductio would ever be possible.

If it is argued that "being located in the space of the world" is the limiting condition (upādhi) that follows upon the probans (sādhana), then when this is said, one might ask: what would follow from that? Would he [the teacher] be one proclaimed by the Veda? 4.2.29.

Although Viṣṇu himself is indeed the Lord and the omniscient one who brings about liberation, he established the Buddhist doctrine solely for the purpose of deluding [those who would otherwise follow the path of unrighteousness].
Because it is intended for the Asuras— who are unfit for the path of the Vedas— and because it has the Asuras as its authority, their doctrine should never be accepted anywhere.
That void consciousness is said to be of four kinds:
that which has external reality as its object of inference, and likewise that which has external reality as its object of direct perception. MAnu 4.2.32.
Thus, those who, deluded by ignorance, proclaim emptiness therein,
would speak of liberation in such a manner, just like those who are deceitful and free from doubt.
In the state of liberation, there is nothing belonging to a self or to what belongs to a self;
once one is released from saṃsāra, nothing whatsoever remains.
This distinction between the sentient and the insentient exists only through conventional reality;
when conventional reality is destroyed, there is nothing but the undifferentiated emptiness.
Neither existence nor non-existence is found in the reality of emptiness;
there is neither happiness nor suffering, nor is there any distinction whatsoever.
It is without distinction, self-luminous, untainted, undecaying, and immortal;
it is the void reality, unobstructed, and free from the concealment of manifold appearances.
That which is free from all defects, beyond the reach of mind and speech, and untainted by various conventionalities, is called "liberation" by the wise. (Manu 4.2.38)
The state of cyclic existence (saṃsṛti) is to be understood as being distinguished by conventional reality alone;
for both by its persistence and by its destruction, there is what is called "cyclic existence" and also "liberation."
Some among them have stated otherwise: "The great void, though undivided, is described in many ways through conventional designation by various names such as 'person' (pudgala). (MAnu 4.2.40)
He for whom the state of being of a single flavor with emptiness has departed through knowledge—
that person, liberated from individuality, shall attain the Great Emptiness.
"But conventionally, another [self], being delimited, experiences various sufferings to its full extent"—
thus say the proponents of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), who maintain that all is an illusion.
And according to the view of many living beings, their conventional reality is indeed illusion;
because they speak of it as being without distinction, for us there is no difference between the void and Brahman.
And for one who asserts the indivisible [reality], what is there such as truth, consciousness, bliss, and so forth, and from what could they be excluded?
However, for the proponent of emptiness, there exists a distinction consisting merely of exclusion.
Indeed, he himself considers [the self] to be the exclusion of falsehood and so forth;
for, due to their lack of distinguishing attributes, there is no difference whatsoever between Brahman and the Void.
For the authority and other qualities of the Veda are indeed equal [to those of other means of knowledge] in their results;

however, that which does not reveal reality is therefore called a non-authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), since the wise consider the state of not revealing reality to be non-authoritativeness. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.46)
If scripture were a means of valid cognition that does not reveal reality because it produces long-lasting delusion,
then it would lack authority even more than the cognition of a snake in a rope,
since it instills a great delusion that cannot be dispelled.
The cognition of blue color and so forth would attain the status of valid knowledge regarding space;
likewise, the cognition of the umbrella-like shape [of the moon] and the notion that the moon is the size of a span [would be valid]. (Manu 4.2.48)
Furthermore, he has always accepted the indivisibility of emptiness;
for both [of us] agree that there is an absence of dharmas such as existence and non-existence.
For emptiness is not intended by him to be the state of having an existent counter-correlative;
nor indeed is bliss intended to be anything other than the opposition to suffering.
Even for the illusionist who maintains the position of emptiness, cognition is opposed to insentience;
yet even for him, those properties do not exist at all. What, then, is the difference between the two?
The Lord has already refuted such positions by the very fact that they undermine his own position, as stated in the words, "it is not non-existence. (Manu 4.2.52)
In the absence of a self, what would be the goal of man, since the limit of the desired object is the self?
If liberation were not limited by the self, then liberation would be the emptiness of a jar;
for that [emptiness] is the same even for a magician, because particularities are merely imagined.
If there were no distinction even when a specific difference is perceived,
then the absence of a jar would be indistinguishable from its future non-existence.
