Liberation is not something subject to dispute, because it is bodiless, like the emptiness of a jar; what could one who relies solely on inference as his authority say when this is stated? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.55)
And a deceiver should not speak there by the very path previously mentioned;
for that [scripture] is not an authority, nor does it teach the absence of a body.

A certain scriptural passage teaches that the state of being bodiless pertains to a non-material body, since scripture declares that there is enjoyment in liberation, saying, "eating and playing. (Manu 4.2.57)

"Because it is free from suffering, that [state] is not liberation, just as has been established"—what kind of refutation by inference could there be between two proponents who maintain the doctrine of emptiness? (MĀnuv 4.2.58)
Because suffering is non-different from [the nature of] suffering, liberation would undoubtedly also be suffering;
if there were difference, there would necessarily be duality, and so forth— due to such boundless faults,
the wise should reject the doctrine of emptiness along with the doctrine of illusion.

In this way, even the Vijñānavāda, by virtue of its distinction as "consciousness-only," would incur the same stated faults; for if one were to set aside its specific qualities such as transience and so forth, it would directly become the doctrine of non-duality (advaita).
Time is not possessed of absolute knowledge because it is time, like that which has already passed; since this inference precludes it, such a state cannot be the nature of liberation.
If it is argued that time also does not exist, the answer to the question "When? is as follows:
what will he say when he describes a state? That [state] would then become the subject of debate (pakṣatā).
For the reason is indeed "because it is a state," and when asked "When does that occur?", time must be specified; therefore, there can be no lack of timing.

When there is a general prohibition stating "it is not the [proper] time," a specific authoritative rule regarding that time must be stated to set it aside; therefore, there would be no such thing as "non-time."
But if the position of a single soul were held, this valid cognition— being deprived of time—
would, in its anger, seize upon time and thereby establish duality itself.
"The disputed time possesses manifoldness because it is time, like that which is already established"—
this other inference would likewise preclude the oneness of the individual soul.
The doctrines of Kāla, Śabda, Īśvara, and Ekatva have likewise been refuted, for they are equal to the aforementioned positions in their logical flaws.
Knowledge is held to have an eternal continuity by means of its own inherent flow;
however, according to the other two Buddhist schools, even there, inference is declared to be its adversary.
Liberation is not for one who possesses a stream of pure consciousness alone after death;
rather, it belongs to one who has practiced accordingly—this is the inference that constitutes the reply.

All inferences have been refuted by means of counter-arguments through the very same method of disintegration already stated; and the Vedic scriptures that follow our own assertions are likewise [refuted].
The followers of Sāṅkhya, the Naiyāyikas, and others declare that liberation is indeed devoid of happiness,
consisting in the total dissolution even of desire, aversion, effort, and so forth.
Regarding this, they say that even this is not appropriate here, because the revealed scriptures (śruti) indeed declare that both great bliss and enjoyment follow as a necessary consequence.
The loss of what is dear to one's nature is called "contact with the unpleasant";
that which is disagreeable is termed "the adverse," and it is designated by that term without distinction.

For there is no suffering whatsoever for the existing living being that is not natural; its very nature is dear to it, according to such scriptural statements as "Bliss, indeed, is its nature. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.74)

Because that which is unpleasant must be abandoned, and because the loss of what is pleasant is undesirable, it is not logical to say that liberation consists in the absence of all that is pleasant. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.75)
For the very nature of what is unpleasant is heard of only among the Asuras:
"The Asuras are not thus, nor are they thus, nor are they not thus"—all [of which applies] to human beings.
What wise person would strive for the sake of destroying his own pleasure? (Manu 4.2.76)
For even the notion that "there is no perception" does not mean that for him the knowable has not been expressed;
because his subsequent teaching speaks precisely of the non-cessation of phenomena.
Fearing a loss of his knowledge, Yājñavalkya said to Maitreyī,
who had addressed him as "Sir," "I do not speak of delusion to you";
for by saying this, he spoke of the non-destruction of one's true nature.
"Since for that which is of the nature of gnosis, non-destruction consists precisely in its destruction"—
in order to refute such a nihilistic view, [the Buddha] taught once again those dharmas preceded by bliss,
which are uninterrupted and which have been rejected by the logicians.
Likewise, the Mādhyandina Śruti also speaks of contact with women during their fertile period.
And he rejected that doctrine according to which there is no consumption of objects;
for the Śruti [rejects it] because the absence of enjoyment through the sense of smell and so forth is undesirable to the heart.
"By what means does one know this entire world, as well as the knower himself?
By what, then, could one know that [knower]?"—for such a thing is altogether impossible. (Manu 4.2.81)
For Viṣṇu is not the knower of everything, nor is he necessarily unknowable;
indeed, it is for the purpose of knowing him that all the Vedas have been set forth.
Moreover, because it is experienced as not contradicting perception, scripture, or self-knowledge,
no contradiction whatsoever is perceived regarding one's own state of consciousness.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction between the agent and the object, as well as a contradiction with constant experience;
how could such a position ever be reached? For contradiction is the sublation of what is perceived.
"He enjoys all desires and, being a master of his own will, assumes forms at will"—for scriptural passages such as these indeed express the very meaning already stated. (Manu 4.2.85)

It has been stated that [the world] is like this due to a lack of independence and so forth, and not because of the non-existence of duality; for if it were otherwise, it would follow from the statement "He became the Self alone" that there is no distinction whatsoever.

In the various types of metaphors where independence is absent, it is proclaimed as being "like"; and what was stated in response to Maitreyī is called the "principle of sound" (śabdatattva). MAnu 4.2.87.
Furthermore, what would be the purpose of liberation if it involved the loss of pleasure and other qualities?
If its aim were the removal of suffering, then the destruction of pleasure would be a misfortune. (Manu 4.2.88)
Moreover, from the destruction of those two [pleasure and pain], the loss of pleasure would indeed be greater than the loss of pain;
for even when encountering very great suffering, people strive to obtain a mere fragment of pleasure. Indeed, what man would strive for liberation if it meant the total loss of pleasure? (Manu 4.89)
For people fear the loss of even a small amount of pleasure exceedingly, and they undergo great suffering in order to prevent the destruction of their pleasure. (Manu 4.2.90)
Nor is that the sign of passion;
for even those free from passion, such as Nārada and others, readily endure suffering for the sake of pleasure, since they watch spectacles like battles even with great distress. (Manu 4.2.91)
"Even when Indra and Virocana were scorched by the Brahmā-missiles of Nārada and the others, they did not abandon the passion for battle.
Since this is the word of the Skanda Purāṇa, who would strive for the absence of pleasure? (Manu 4.2.92)
Since one who is conscious, being in a state of suffering, is seen to experience pleasure upon attaining it, by what means can this inference be refuted? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.93)
Because the state of happiness is described in all the Śrutis and Purāṇas,
the wise should not accept this view that there is an absence of happiness in liberation.
Thus, being liberated from [worldly] bliss, he clearly becomes blissful,
fixing his mind clearly upon me, the qualityless Brahman;
he attains supreme bliss wherein all desire comes to rest.
There is no deity equal to Viṣṇu, no happiness equal to liberation,
no word equal to the Veda, and no syllable equal to the letter *A*.
Where joys, delights, pleasures, and raptures abide,
where all the desires of desire are attained— there make me immortal.
For thus do the Śrutis and Purāṇas declare here and there;
therefore, the claim that there is an absence of happiness in liberation is indeed trivial.
Furthermore, the absence of a head, hands, and so forth would never belong to one who is liberated;
for there are many scriptural texts and Purāṇas that serve as authority on this point.
There, where neither passion nor darkness prevails, nor is goodness mixed with them, and where there is no power of time;
there, where there is no illusion—how much less others—there dwell those devoted to Hari, who are honored by both gods and demons.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with eyes like lotus petals, clad in saffron-colored garments, they were of excellent luster and beautiful form;
all had four arms, wore necklaces and ornaments of choice gems that seemed to sparkle, and possessed great splendor.

It shines brilliantly on all sides with the rows of radiant celestial chariots belonging to the great-souled ones, who possess the luster of coral, lapis lazuli, and lotus stalks, and who wear shimmering earrings, crowns, and garlands.

Where Śrī herself, in embodied form, pays homage in many ways with her manifold splendors at the feet of the Wide-Ranging One (Viṣṇu), as the sky is graced by rows of clouds accompanied by flashing lightning and the most excellent celestial nymphs.
One, having nourished it, sits chanting the growth of the *ṛc* verses; another sings the *gāyatra* chant upon the *śakvarī* meters;
a third speaks as a *brahmán* priest the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice. (Manu 4.104)
There is no fault in this, for according to the aforementioned Vedic scripture stating that "he moves about assuming various forms at will," as well as by the declarations of the Purāṇas,
it is indeed understood that even for those who have attained liberation, the body is of the very nature of their own essential self.
Since even those who possess heads, hands, and so forth are now endowed with liberation,
and since inference preceded by "as it is" (yathā) brings about the attainment of the limbs and other parts of the nature of the living soul.
The embodied soul does not attain the actual nature of Brahman even upon liberation;
rather, through valid knowledge, he somehow partakes in all enjoyments together with Brahman, having approached that ocean of bliss.
Having attained that supreme light and having regained his own true nature, the individual soul enjoys its desires;
he is called the Divine, the Supreme Person, the Unborn, and the Self, on account of the fullness of his qualities.

"He is the bridge, the god, the lord of those who partake in all liberation, and the master of immortality here"—by such statements, even though he has attained liberation, he remains under the control of the Blessed Lord and enjoys all pleasures. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.109)

"Time also is not united with the Supreme, just as time is [distinct] from the individual soul (jīva)"; such inferences are also authoritative for establishing the distinctness of the individual soul from the Supreme in the state of liberation. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.110)

And how can it be logically sound that he who did not exist previously is the very same person who exists later? For it has never been observed that something which did not exist before subsequently comes into being; how then could this be so?

Furthermore, it does not stand to reason that in liberation there should be either separateness or identity for Hari; for nowhere has any distinction or non-distinction ever been observed between consciousness and a conscious being.

Thus, because these doctrines are born of delusion, even worldly people here do not correctly know liberation, though it is their goal; they merely think, "May there be happiness for me" and "May this endure. (Manu 4.2.113)

In the fourth quarter [of this chapter], magnanimity, manifold power, firmness of one's own character, innate nature, sovereignty, full capacity for excellence, and the removal of contradictions are described. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.2.114)

The establishment of distinctions, the maintenance of general prohibitions and injunctions, the differentiation of the four stages of life, and their successful accomplishment—these are the reasons that oppose the attainment of the opposite state. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.115)

Ease, constant renown, discernment, arrangement, reflection, the knowledge of names, various activities, and the fulfillment of one's duties—these are the arguments for the opposite side regarding the section on the past. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.116)
Great fruitfulness, seclusion, the grasping of the connection, the means, the fulfillment of the task,
the specific purpose, and the establishment of the action— these are the well-reasoned arguments leading to a conclusion regarding one's own position.

Intermixture, the performance of a task, the arrangement of objects, extreme firmness, dependence, common characteristics, and the remaining of what has been done— these are the worldly analogies that follow the views of the ancients.
The scriptural mention of specific equality, opulence, equal dissolution, greatness, distinction,
fulfillment of purpose, and eternal persistence are the distinguished reasons for the determination of the final doctrine.
Furthermore, the primary wind here, though it has entered into the elements as the one called "Vāyu," is also logically [designated] by that term;

for in the Śruti it is extensively stated that "it blows" (*pavate*), and since it is the bringer of the elements (*bhūtamānī*), it is also called by that word because it is both the great measurer (*mahāmānī*) and the subtle measurer (*alpamānī*). (Manu 4.2.120)
In that [Brahmā], all beings go to their dissolution in due order without contradiction; he himself [goes] into Viṣṇu.
The dissolution of Indra and the others therein follows a specific sequence as it has been declared, and not otherwise.

Therefore, all living beings, having entered into the Daughter of the Mountain along with her, and into Rudra along with him, and having reached Vāṇī along with her, and having reached their Lord along with him, attain dissolution in Hari.
Soma, joined with Varuṇa, enters Aniruddha; he [Aniruddha] enters Kāma, and he [Kāma] enters Vāruṇī.
She [Vāruṇī] enters the god Śeṣa, she enters Speech, and she indeed enters Vāyu directly—this is the conclusion here.

At the time of liberation, the Vedic speech declares that Umā and the Lord of the Mountains are Bhāratī and Rāva; likewise, it speaks of the consort of the Lord of Serpents and the Serpent King, and the consort of Viriñca and Viriñca himself.

At the very time that living beings attain that state by worshipping these [deities], they enter into them at the time of becoming Brahman; such is the meaning conveyed by the statement. (Manu 4.2.125)
The sun, joined with fire, having reached Jupiter, goes together with him to Indra; with him [Indra] to the wife of Suparṇa;
with her to Suparṇa; with him to Vāṇī; and reaching Brahmā, he goes from there to this [world]. ||| 4.2.126 ||
When it is stated here that there is an entry into Indra, then *Umā* herself is indeed the wife of *Suparṇa*;
and since *Suparṇa* is referred to by the name *Girīśa*, there is no contradiction whatsoever in this matter. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.127)
Bhṛgu and the others, having obtained Dakṣa, and through him Indra, and through him the wife of Suparṇa;
those Manus and chief kings who enter Manu, having entered Manu here, go to Mahendra.
Having entered the sky and the earth, he went by that very same path to the god Indra;
likewise, ascetics who have attained self-realization enter into the Supreme Spirit at will, while the rest enter the sacrificial fire.
Men devoted to the conduct of their castes and stages of life follow the Dharma of Manu; he too, in due time, follows it.
All the ancestors, along with the gods, follow him alone; all [the gods] follow Kubera, and he in turn follows Soma alone.
At the time of liberation, they repeatedly enter [the body] and enjoy the pleasures contained within that body;
their bliss becomes perfectly manifest there, and thus they are indeed considered to have emerged.
They play again and re-enter those very same [bodies]; this is what they call *sāyujya* (union).

All those who have not attained *sāyujya* enter [the Supreme] during dissolution and emerge from it again at the time of creation by the aforementioned path; however, even at other times, there is entry for those who possess *sāyujya*.
"All that has been declared is indeed stated in the supreme scripture; however, the reversal [of the order] follows the sequence of creation.
Just as dissolution occurs during liberation, so too does dissolution occur through reversal," thus spoke the Lord of Speech. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.133)

Since this dissolution (*laya*) is the liberation of the gods, and it is that which he will specifically describe as enjoyment (*bhoga*), the relationship between the original image and its reflection has been stated in accordance with the dissolution taught in the *Piṅga* scripture. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.2.134)
The dissolution of the images [of the elements] into that [Vāyu] is certain for liberation, and the conscious selves (cidātman) are always subject to its power.
Having attained the glory named Tejas, Vāyu was first born as the son of Viṣṇu;
then, having entered Viṣṇu again, he remains here liberated at the time of cosmic dissolution.
All those hosts of liberated beings, while fully enjoying their own intense and dense bliss even in its entirety,
remain as they are during the dissolution in the body of the Lord, and then go outward again at the time of creation.

Dharma goes to Nirṛti, Śakra to the hosts of Maruts, and likewise the attendants to Aniruddha; all the commanders of the armies and so forth go to Tvaṣṭṛ—such is this liberation. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.137)
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

The path of departure, that which is to be reached by the liberated, the seed arising from the feet, the two strides, the lineage-born, attainment, and the state of being sought— these are the speculative theories of other systems regarding the nature of the soul.

Attainment of excellence, reaching greatness, gradual passion, and the continuation of what has been told; those men who possess these, which bring about the determination of the final doctrine, as well as the body and so forth which are merely its outward signs—[for them, this is the end]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.3.2)
They worship Him in His presence and shall attain Brahmā; having attained us, they shall reach Viṣṇu.
Others also, having reached Him, shall thereafter go to Hari and partake in liberation at the end.
The third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
Transgression, speech, action, acquisition of wealth, the highest state, reaching the further shore, that abode,
the completion of all tasks, mastery, and the capacity for universal accomplishment— these are the arguments on the side of the other party.
General appearance, eloquence, wonder, artlessness, freedom from faults, the capacity for specific discernment, and tireless effort—these are the points for determining true greatness. (Manu 4.4.2)
The state of being a servant to none other than those mentioned here is taught for the purpose of precluding service to anyone else;
for the Veda indeed declares that Viṣṇu is the Lord even of these [gods], since it speaks of Hari as the Lord of immortality.
Moreover, these [gods] too, being endowed with the sovereignty of others and possessing minds other than Viṣṇu, are like ordinary men;
for it is inference alone that establishes their well-known status here, as it leads to certainty for the sake of proving what is intended.
"Even for those who have attained liberation, there exists a state of being a restrainer of their own kin, with Brahmā at their head;
by this god and by that one, I shall be honored as the supreme among those belonging to the worlds both beyond and below. (Manu 4.4.5)
The Veda declares that the fruit [of knowledge] arises from knowledge regarding liberation; and this is because it is a sign of the destruction of all that is inauspicious.

Furthermore, the *Tura-śruti* states that lordship over the world belongs to the Creator alone as the Self of all, and the statement "all the hosts of gods bring tribute" is logically applicable to none other than Him.

In this world as well, the word "worlds" (lokāḥ) is used by those who inhabit them; for indeed, among living beings, the sound "worlds" is always employed by all people, and thus those who pride themselves on that are designated by the term "world. But the *Paingins* have a sacred text stating: "The liberated ones here are called 'worlds' because they are the mutual lords of one another. (Manu 4.8.7)

By the word "light" (aloka), those who partake in liberation are meant; such a state is also appropriate here. For all those designated as "worlds" (loka) are indeed liberated, being eternally of the nature of illumination.
And the swift Veda declares that Brahman alone shall be the sovereign of the worlds, being liberated.
And here, the fruit of consciousness—lordship over the world—is not stated to reside in Hari [as the sun];
for that has already been stated separately previously, since the distinction between them and so forth was correctly explained.

Furthermore, if one were to disregard the suffix *-tva* and interpret the meaning here as "not by that form," then there would be many syntactical difficulties involving numerous faults if one were to abandon the word *aṇu* in the phrase "this comes into being" (*bhavaty asau*).

Therefore, Brahmā and the others, possessing full attributes and engaged in the activity of the world, remain seated in their own unborn state, eternally and intensely enjoying bliss. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.11)
Homage, homage to Puruṣottama, the sole abode of all excellent qualities without exception;
to him who bestows perfectly pure consciousness out of compassion for his devotees, whose nature consists of beloved and auspicious qualities that are free from all limiting adjuncts.
In the Vedic word, three divine forms of Him have been proclaimed: "That," "The Shining One," and likewise "The Great Splendor of the God.
The first is the wind; the second form is the speech of Rāma; and as for that third, which is honey—by inference regarding this, the work was composed concerning Keśava.
I bow to you, my beloved, who are free from every defect, possessed of all auspicious and excellent qualities, and worthy of worship by Bhūti, Svayambhū, Śarva, and the others.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
